docs.title: Opening a window
docs.text:
Create an AWindow, put views into it with AWindow::setContents and call AWindow::show:

#include <AUI/Platform/Entry.h>
#include <AUI/Platform/AWindow.h>
#include <AUI/View/ALabel.h>

AUI_ENTRY {
    auto window = _new<AWindow>("Hello AUI", 300_dp, 200_dp);
    window->setContents(Centered { Label { "Hello, world!" } });
    window->show();
    return 0;
}

Every window implicitly holds the application (see AApplication::Hold), so by default the application keeps running while at least one window is alive. This is adjustable: create an explicit hold with AApplication::hold() to keep the application running after the last window is closed, or release it to allow the application to exit. The window is owned by AUI while it is shown, so you don't have to store the pointer; store it only if you want to talk to the window later.

To open another window from the application (i.e., a settings dialog), do the same from any slot or callback on the UI thread:

connect(settingsButton->clicked, this, [this] {
    auto settings = _new<AWindow>("Settings", 400_dp, 300_dp);
    settings->setContents(Vertical { Label { "Settings go here" } });
    settings->show();
});

AWindow(title, width, height) creates an ordinary window with the OS-drawn titlebar. Anything else (a parent window, modality, custom titlebar, fixed size) is configured with AWindow::Init, see below. To close the window from code, use AWindow::close.

docs.title: Architecture
docs.text:
This document covers AUI's window management system, which provides cross‑platform window creation, lifecycle management, and event handling. The system abstracts native windowing APIs across Windows, Linux, macOS, Android, and iOS platforms while maintaining a unified interface for application developers.

AWindow is the concrete implementation of a UI surface that is backed by a native window. It inherits from ASurface – the generic surface API that can be used by other windowing API implementations (i.e., SDL3 or a game engine).

AWindow owns an IRenderingContext instance. The context bridges the window to the shared IRenderer – the actual rendering engine. The renderer performs all drawing primitives and is shared across all windows. The context handles platform‑specific tasks such as buffer swapping, resizing, and screenshot capture.

    AWindow2(AWindow) -->|has| IRenderingContext2(IRenderingContext)

docs.title: Creation, decorations and modality
docs.text:
AWindow is created with AWindow::Init - an aggregate describing everything that can't be changed afterwards:

_new<AWindow>(AWindow::Init {
    .title = "Settings",
    .width = 400_dp,
    .height = 300_dp,
    .parent = AWindow::Init::Parent { .window = *this, .modal = true },
    .decoration = AWindow::Init::DecorationDefault { .buttons = { .minimize = false, .maximize = false } },
    .resizable = false,
});

Meaningless combinations do not compile: modality exists only as a part of parent, window buttons exist only in decorations which have them.

Decoration What it is Replaces DecorationDefault { buttons } Ordinary OS-drawn titlebar and border. WindowStyle::DEFAULT, NO_MINIMIZE_MAXIMIZE DecorationExtended { buttons } Window contents extend into the titlebar. Native window controls are kept where the platform has them. ACustomCaptionWindow DecorationBorderless { shadow } No titlebar, no buttons. Native border, shadow and rounded corners are kept where possible. ACustomWindow, NO_DECORATORS

A modal window blocks user input of its parent until closed. Having parent without modal produces an ordinary child window - it does not block anything, even when it is not resizable.

docs.title: Titlebar of Extended and Borderless windows
docs.text:
declarative::Titlebar is a view you place into the window contents yourself; it is not created by the window. It is both a drag handle and a layout container for the titlebar contents. What it does depends on the decoration:

DecorationExtended DecorationBorderless Drags the window yes yes Double click maximizes/restores yes yes Window controls (close, minimize, maximize) yes: native or drawn by AUI, according to buttons no, declarative::Titlebar is just your contents Space reserved for native controls yes (AWindow::windowControlsInsets) no, zero

Without declarative::Titlebar a Borderless window can't be moved by the user at all, and an Extended window has no draggable area.

What can be put into declarative::Titlebar of a Borderless window: any view. Contents are laid out horizontally, the first and only child stretches over the full width. Put a label for a plain caption, or a Horizontal with a logo, title, search field, tool buttons and so on:

auto w = _new<AWindow>(AWindow::Init {
    .title = "Custom window without caption",
    .width = 400_dp,
    .height = 300_dp,
    .decoration = AWindow::Init::DecorationBorderless {},
});
w->setContents(Vertical {
    // an opaque caption strip: the window is dragged by it
    Titlebar { Label { "Drag me" } AUI_OVERRIDE_STYLE { Padding { 4_dp } } },
    Centered { Label { "Window contents" } } AUI_LET { it->setExpanding(); },
});
w->show();

Nothing is drawn by the window itself, so everything about the look (background, height, padding, border) is up to you and set by ASS on declarative::Titlebar or its contents. Interactive views inside the titlebar work as usual: buttons (AButton) and views with .override-title-dragging ASS class are not drag areas, everything else under declarative::Titlebar (labels, spacers, empty space, text fields included) starts window dragging.

With DecorationExtended the window contents extend under the system titlebar, so declarative::Titlebar is typically overlaid on top of the contents (see example for a complete example with a blurred backdrop):

setContents(Stacked {
    content,
    Vertical {
        Titlebar { Horizontal { Label { "My app" } } },
        SpacerExpanding {},
    },
});

docs.title: Window title inside the titlebar
docs.text:
You don't have to imitate the title of each OS yourself. Put declarative::WindowTitle into declarative::Titlebar (Titlebar {} without contents contains it) to mark where the title is, and the OS draws it there, the same way it does in its own titlebars, wherever it can:

Who draws the title Where macOS AppKit (the native title) centered over the window horizontally, centered in declarative::Titlebar vertically Linux GTK/adw GTK (the native header bar title) like in a header bar: centered over the window while it fits into declarative::WindowTitle, otherwise shifted into it Windows AUI: DWM does not draw the caption text of windows with the extended client area left-aligned label Linux X11, Borderless windows AUI centered label

The native title follows the system font, color and the inactive window look. It is drawn over the window contents, so neither ASS nor other views can affect it; it is shown only while declarative::WindowTitle is present (see AWindow::hasNativeWindowTitle). Where AUI draws the title, style it with t<AWindowTitle>().

The result looks like an ordinary titlebar, but you control its background and can place your own views around the title:

setContents(Stacked {
    content,
    Vertical {
        Titlebar {},   // looks like the OS titlebar
        SpacerExpanding {},
    },
});

The window is the single source of truth for the title: AWindow::title is a property; the native title is the window title itself, and the AUI-drawn declarative::WindowTitle is bound to it. Change the title with AWindow::setTitle (or title() = ...), and the taskbar, window switcher and the title in your titlebar update together. Do not duplicate the title in a Label with a string literal. If you need a label of your own (for example, with a prefix), bind it to the property:

Titlebar {
    Horizontal {
        Icon { ":img/logo.svg" },
        Label { .text = AUI_REACT("{} - Editor"_format(*window->title())) },
    },
}

If you don't need contents in the titlebar area at all, use DecorationDefault: the OS draws the titlebar entirely.

docs.title: What Titlebar is and how its size is determined
docs.text:
declarative::Titlebar is not just a handle: it is a Horizontal { window controls (start), contents, window controls (end) } container which stretches horizontally over the whole width of its parent. Its size is not set by the window or the platform, it is regular AUI layout:

  • width: expanding, takes all the available width of the parent;
  • height: the maximum of the contents' height and the window controls' height (native controls height from AWindow::windowControlsInsets or AUI-drawn buttons height). To make the titlebar taller, put a taller view or padding into it. In a Borderless window it is just the height of the contents.

The rectangle occupied by declarative::Titlebar after layout is what the window treats as the caption area: it is used for dragging and, on macOS and GTK, to vertically center the native window controls inside it.

AWindow::windowControlsInsets is a property reporting the space occupied by native window controls (traffic lights on macOS, GtkWindowControls on GTK); AWindowControls uses it to keep the contents out of their way.

docs.title: Lifecycle
docs.text:
Only title and resizability can change at runtime:

What API title AWindow::title property (AWindow::setTitle, titleChanged) resizability AWindow::setResizable / AWindow::isResizable visibility AWindow::show / AWindow::hide, reversible closing AWindow::close, terminal

close() works the same on all platforms: closed is emitted exactly once, the modal parent is unblocked, the native window is destroyed. A closed window can't be shown again - create another one. Calling show() on a closed window logs an error and does nothing. Closing by the close button calls AWindow::onCloseButtonClicked, which calls close(); override it to refuse closing.

docs.title: Native handles
docs.text:
AWindow::nativeHandle returns the underlying native window object, which can be passed to platform APIs AUI does not wrap (DWM attributes, NSWindow tweaks, embedding into foreign toolkits, etc.). Its type is AWindowNativePtr and depends on the platform:

Platform AWindowNativePtr What it points to Windows HWND the window itself macOS void* NSWindow* (AUIView is its content view) Linux, GTK4 / libadwaita backend std::uintptr_t GtkWindow*; GtkPopover* for popups Linux, X11 backend std::uintptr_t X11 Window (XID) Android, iOS, web jobject / void* not available: always null, the surface is owned by the activity, view controller or canvas

The handle is null until the native window is created and after it is destroyed (see AWindow::close). It is owned by AUI: don't destroy it, don't keep it past AWindow::closed. Use it from the UI thread only.

#include <AUI/Platform/AWindow.h>

void tweakNativeWindow(AWindow& window) {
#if AUI_PLATFORM_WIN
    HWND hwnd = window.nativeHandle();
    SetWindowTextW(hwnd, L"Hello from Win32");
#elif AUI_PLATFORM_APPLE
    // in an Objective-C++ (.mm) file:
    NSWindow* nsWindow = static_cast<NSWindow*>(window.nativeHandle());
    nsWindow.level = NSFloatingWindowLevel;
#elif AUI_PLATFORM_LINUX
    // see below
#endif
}

docs.title: Linux
docs.text:
Linux has two core platform APIs, chosen at runtime (see APlatformAbstractionOptions); on the application side there is no compile-time way to tell which one is active, so the same uintptr_t means a different thing depending on the backend. Decide which one you have yourself, i.e., by pinning APlatformAbstractionOptions::initializationOrder to a single backend before creating windows:

// X11 only
APlatformAbstractionOptions::set({ .initializationOrder = { APlatformAbstractionOptions::X11{} } });
...
Window xid = static_cast<Window>(window.nativeHandle());
Display* display = XOpenDisplay(nullptr); // XIDs are valid on any connection to the same X server

// GTK4 / libadwaita only
APlatformAbstractionOptions::set({ .initializationOrder = { APlatformAbstractionOptions::Gtk4{} } });
...
auto* gtkWindow = reinterpret_cast<GtkWindow*>(window.nativeHandle());

AUI loads GTK dynamically, so it does not require GTK headers to build your application; include them yourself if you use the handle. To reach lower-level objects, go through GTK:

  • GdkSurface*: gtk_native_get_surface(GTK_NATIVE(gtkWindow))
  • Wayland wl_surface*: gdk_wayland_surface_get_wl_surface(gdkSurface) (when GDK_IS_WAYLAND_SURFACE)
  • X11 Window under GTK (i.e., GTK running on X11 or Xwayland): gdk_x11_surface_get_xid(gdkSurface) (when GDK_IS_X11_SURFACE)

On a Wayland session without pinning the backend you will get the GTK flavor; the X11 backend works through Xwayland there and its handle is an XID.

docs.title: Platform specifics
docs.text:
Windows macOS Linux GTK/adw Linux X11 Android, iOS, web Default buttons window style bits; disabled close is greyed style mask decoration-layout of the header bar Motif hints (window manager may ignore) ignored Extended window controls drawn by AUI, hit-tested natively (snap layouts) native traffic lights, aligned to declarative::Titlebar native GtkWindowControls drawn by AUI none Extended title (declarative::WindowTitle) drawn by AUI native, aligned to declarative::Titlebar vertically native header bar title drawn by AUI drawn by AUI Borderless shadow DWM frame system shadow CSD shadow not available, shadow is ignored ignored parent owner window child window transient transient ignored modal parent is disabled parent ignores input gtk_window_set_modal _NET_WM_STATE_MODAL, parent ignores input ignored

AProperty<ABoxFields> safeAreaInsets

Parts of the window covered by the system UI, in pixels.

Padding that guarantees the useful content is not overlapped by anything the application does not control: the status bar, display cutout and navigation bar on Android and iOS; the window controls strip of AWindow::Init::DecorationExtended on desktop. Put it into padding of the root view:

connect(window->safeAreaInsets, root, [root = root.get()](const ABoxFields& i) {
    root->setPadding(i);
});

The system UI itself is not part of the content area, so on desktop the value is zero if the window decoration is the OS' one (AWindow::Init::DecorationDefault) or there is none (AWindow::Init::DecorationBorderless): the OS (or you) already positions the content below the titlebar.

For AWindow::Init::DecorationExtended, top is the height of AWindow::windowControlsInsets; declarative::Titlebar lives inside that strip. Use AWindow::windowControlsInsets when you need to know which corners of the strip are occupied, since the controls take a corner of it, not the whole strip.

The software keyboard is not a part of the safe area.

void AWindow::close()

Closes the window.

Closing is terminal and works the same on all platforms: closed is emitted exactly once, the modal parent is unblocked, the native window is destroyed and the window is removed from the AWindowManager. The window can't be shown again after that; create another one. Calling close() on a closed window does nothing.

Use AWindow::hide to hide the window temporarily.

Examples:

glm::ivec2 AWindow::getMinimumSize()

The smallest size this window can be resized to.

In contrast to AView::getMinSize, which is the explicitly styled minimum, this one is measured from the window's contents: a window is never smaller than the space its contents need at their narrowest, so its layout is never squeezed into nothing. The styled minimum is respected as well.

The minimum height depends on the current width of the window (wrapped text needs less height in a wider window). Note that this differs from GTK and Qt, which use the height needed at the minimum width (a static value, the tallest the contents can be). As the minimum height changes along with the width, it is re-announced to the window manager on every layout; on win32 it may lag one resize step behind.

bool AWindow::hasNativeWindowControls()
Returns true if the platform draws the window controls (traffic lights, etc.) of `AWindow::Init::DecorationExtended` windows itself. Either way, they occupy `AWindow::windowControlsInsets`.

Hides the window without closing it.

A hidden window is still alive: it is counted as an open window, so it keeps the application running (see AApplication::quitOnLastWindowClosed). Use AWindow::close to destroy it.

A hidden window is not visible anywhere, including the taskbar.

Where the platform draws the window controls itself (macOS traffic lights, GTK window controls), AWindowControls is a blank space of the size of the native controls (AWindow::windowControlsInsets). Elsewhere (Windows, X11), these are AUI buttons following AWindow::Init::Buttons; their size is reported to AWindow::windowControlsInsets, so the property means the same everywhere.

AWindowControls is a part of ATitlebar and is not intended to be used standalone.

Example's page

This page describes an example listed in the ui category.

Backdrop effects demo.

This example demonstrates how ass::Backdrop effects can be used to produce rich visuals that conform modern design principles.

In this example, a combination of ass::Backdrop -enabled view and AScrollArea is used. To raise the ass::Backdrop above the AScrollArea, AStackedLayout layout is used.

#include <range/v3/all.hpp>

#include <AUI/Platform/Entry.h>
#include "AUI/Platform/AWindow.h"

#include "AUI/View/AScrollArea.h"
#include "AUI/View/ASpinnerV2.h"

#include "AUI/View/AText.h"
#include "AUI/View/ADrawableView.h"

using namespace declarative;
using namespace ass;

static auto headerWithContents(_<AView> content) {
    auto result = Stacked {
        AScrollArea::Builder().withContents(content).build() AUI_OVERRIDE_STYLE {
              Expanding(),
              Padding { 80_dp, 0, 0 },
            } AUI_LET { it->setExtraStylesheet(
                     AStylesheet {
                         {
                             t<AScrollAreaViewport>(),
                             AOverflow::VISIBLE,
                         },
                     }
                     ); },
        Vertical::Expanding {
          Centered {
            Horizontal {
                  Label { "boll" } AUI_OVERRIDE_STYLE {
                      FixedSize { 60_dp },
                      BorderRadius { 60_dp / 2.f },
                      Padding { 0 },
                      ATextAlign::CENTER,
                      Backdrop {
                          Backdrop::LiquidFluid {},
                      },
//                      Border { 1_dp, AColor::GRAY.transparentize(0.7f) },
                      BoxShadow { 0, 32_dp, 32_dp, AColor::BLACK.transparentize(0.8f) },
                  },
                  Label { "boll" } AUI_OVERRIDE_STYLE {
                      FixedSize { 60_dp },
                      BorderRadius { 60_dp / 2.f },
                      Padding { 0 },
                      ATextAlign::CENTER,
                      AOverflow::HIDDEN_FROM_THIS,
                      AOverflowMask::ROUNDED_RECT,
                      Backdrop {
                          Backdrop::LiquidFluid {},
                          Backdrop::GaussianBlur { 5_dp },
                      },
//                      Border { 1_dp, AColor::GRAY.transparentize(0.6f) },
                      BoxShadow { 0, 32_dp, 32_dp, AColor::BLACK.transparentize(0.8f) },
                      BackgroundSolid { AColor::WHITE.transparentize(0.5f) },
                  },
              }
          } AUI_OVERRIDE_STYLE { Padding { 50_dp } },
        },
    };
    return result;
}

AUI_ENTRY {
    auto window = _new<AWindow>("Backdrop test", 600_dp, 300_dp);

    window->setContents(headerWithContents(
        Centered {
          Vertical::Expanding {
            Centered {
              Icon { ":logo.svg" } AUI_OVERRIDE_STYLE { FixedSize { 128_dp } },
            } AUI_OVERRIDE_STYLE { FixedSize { 500_dp, {} } },
            AText::fromString(
                "    — Eh bien, mon prince. Gênes et Lucques ne sont plus que des apanages, des "
                "поместья, de la famille Buonaparte. Non, je vous préviens que si vous ne me dites pas "
                "que nous avons la guerre, si vous vous permettez encore de pallier toutes les infamies, "
                "toutes les atrocités de cet Antichrist (ma parole, j'y crois) — je ne vous connais "
                "plus, vous n'êtes plus mon ami, vous n'êtes plus мой верный раб, comme vous dites 1. "
                "Ну, здравствуйте, здравствуйте. Je vois que je vous fais peur, садитесь и "
                "рассказывайте."),
            AText::fromString(
                "    Так говорила в июле 1805 года известная Анна Павловна Шерер, фрейлина и "
                "приближенная императрицы Марии Феодоровны, встречая важного и чиновного князя Василия, "
                "первого приехавшего на ее вечер. Анна Павловна кашляла несколько дней, у нее был грипп, "
                "как она говорила (грипп был тогда новое слово, употреблявшееся только редкими). В "
                "записочках, разосланных утром с красным лакеем, было написано без различия во всех:"),
            AText::fromString(
                "    «Si vous n'avez rien de mieux à faire, Monsieur le comte (или mon prince), et si la "
                "perspective de passer la soirée chez une pauvre malade ne vous effraye pas trop, je "
                "serai charmée de vous voir chez moi entre 7 et 10 heures. Annette Scherer» 3."),
            AText::fromString(

                "вошедший князь, в придворном, шитом мундире, в чулках, башмаках и звездах, с светлым "
                "выражением плоского лица."),
            AText::fromString(
                "    Он говорил на том изысканном французском языке, на котором не только говорили, но и "
                "думали наши деды, и с теми, тихими, покровительственными интонациями, которые "
                "свойственны состаревшемуся в свете и при дворе значительному человеку. Он подошел к "
                "Анне Павловне, поцеловал ее руку, подставив ей свою надушенную и сияющую лысину, и "

docs.title: Code Style and Recommendations
docs.text:
AUI's code should be kept with the following code style:

  • No tabs; only four spaces (exception: for UI building, 2 spaces is acceptable)
  • Row length: up to 120 characters
  • Class names: CamelCase. Every framework public API class name starts with capital 'A'. Use GenericSpecific pattern (EventClose, not CloseEvent, PacketConnect, not ConnectPacket). Using that convention files group nicely in file lists.
  • Functions, variables: lowerCamelCase
  • Constants: UPPER_SNAKE_CASE
  • Member fields: m... (lineNumber -> mLineNumber)
  • Getters: ... (lineNumber -> lineNumber(), (field: mLineNumber )
  • Getters: set.../with... (lineNumber -> setLineNumber(...), accessible -> withAccessible(...))
  • Structures: commonly holds some data and does not have member functions; CamelCase. Also used for stl-like functionality (AUI/Traits), in that case, snake_case used for file names, struct name and its member functions.
  • Constructors and setters: move semantics. This allows caller to choose whether copy or move the passed object
  • Use const, noexcept and [[nodiscard]] whenever possible
  • Tend to not to use macros. UPPER_SNAKE_CASE prefixed with 'AUI_'
  • Use #pragma once instead of C-style include guards
  • Use Doxygen (@-style, not \)
  • Avoid global functions (at least put them to namespaces)
  • Every symbol (class, struct, namespace, file) prefixed with 'A', 'aui', 'AUI_' is a part of AUI's stable public API ready for the external usage. Symbols without such prefixes are called internal and can be also used (if possible) when needed. Be careful using internal symbols since there's no guarantee about their API stability.
  • Follow visibility in this order when possible: public, protected, private. Header's user is more interested in public APIs rather than in private.

Basic example: 

class User {
public:
  // User(const AString& username): mUsername(username) {} <--- outdated
  // use this instead:
  User(AString username) noexcept: mUsername(std::move(username)) {}

  [[nodiscard]
  const AString& username() const noexcept { // a typical getter; notice the const and noexcept keywords and [[nodiscard]] attribute
    return mUsername;
  }

  void setUsername(AString username) noexcept { // a typical setter; also uses noexcept
    mUsername = std::move(username);
  }

private:
  AString mUsername;

};

Note

With property-system, a better way of defining data models will be: 

struct User {
    AProperty<AString> username;
};
It allows aggregate initialization: User u { .username = "Test" };

docs.title: Assertions
docs.text:
The whole AUI framework's code filled with assertion checks so if you do something wrong the framework will tell you about it. Also in AUI almost every assertion contains a quick tip how to solve the problem. It is recommended to you to do the same. For example:

AUI_ASSERTX(mId == std::this_thread::get_id(),
            "AAbstractThread::processMessages() should not be called from other thread");

The code above ensures that the function was not called from some other thread.

Note

Do not put algorithm-necessary code inside assert(), AUI_ASSERT or AUI_ASSERTX since asserts are removed in release builds on some compilers, i.e. don't assert(("someAction failed!", someObject->someAction() != 0)) since it leads to hard-to-find bugs.

docs.title: Assert or exception?
docs.text:
Assert is an enemy for the production application since it terminates program execution. Use it when it's condition relies only on the developer. Quick example:

connect(mLoginButton->clicked, me::loginButtonClicked);
...
void loginButtonClicked() {
  AUI_ASSERT(mUsername->text().length() < 32); // bad! throw an exception instead so it can be handled: throw AException("username is too long!")
}

docs.title: Code style exceptions
docs.text: Commonly, any iterator-based algorithm (i.e. aui::binary_search), global functions, trait structs are STL-like functionality. The final goal is to avoid mixed-style expressions like AString::const_iterator which hurts eyes.

docs.title: Template metaprogramming and macros
docs.text:
Both C++ template instantiation mechanism and macro preprocessor are Turing complete. However, writing and understanding C++ template metaprogramming (TMP) and macro preprocessor code requires expert knowledge of C++ and a lot of time to understand. Use TMP deliberately.

Since TMP and macros often evolve custom syntax and usage scenarios, consider writing especially well documentation with examples when defining public API templates and macros.

docs.title: Try to break your templates
docs.text: After considering actions listed below, try your types/traits/concepts against various awkward types/arguments/use cases.

docs.title: Concepts are preferable
docs.text: Use concepts instead of SFINAE were possible.

docs.title: Raise static_assert messages
docs.text:
With static_assert with potentially helpful message, use ====================> prefix in your message to raise your message among a long list of compiler diagnostics.

/**
 * @brief Compile-time class introspection.
 * @ingroup reflection
 */
template<class T>
class AClass {
public:
    static_assert(!std::is_reference<T>::value, "====================> AClass: attempt to use AClass on a reference.");

docs.title: Single line comment error messages
docs.text:
You can exploit the fact that a compiler prints code lines in its diagnostics. Put a single line comment with long arrow prefix to put potentially helpful messages. Use Try to break your templates technique to discover the lines to put the comments in.

Cast failure example:

auto& [a] = const_cast<std::remove_cv_t<Clazz>&>(clazz); // ====================> aui::reflect: Clazz is not a SimpleAggregate.

Overload substitution failure example:

...
template<typename T>
requires requires(T& t) { std::hash<T>{}(t); }
constexpr std::size_t forEachKey(const T& value) { // ====================> std::hash based specialization
    return std::hash<T>{}(value);
}

template<typename T>
requires requires(T& t) { { t.base() } -> ranges::range; }
constexpr std::size_t forEachKey(const T& value) { // ====================> specialization for subranges
...

Produces the following diagnostics:

.../AForEachUI.h:220:92: error: no matching function for call to ‘forEachKey(...)’
220 |     return AForEachUIBase::Entry { .view = mFactory(t), .id = forEachKey(t) };
    |                                                               ~~~~~~~~~~^~~
...View/AForEachUI.h:34:23: note: candidate: template<class T> requires(T& t) {{}(t);} ...
34 | constexpr std::size_t forEachKey(const T& value) { // ====================> std::hash based specialization

This makes it obvious what does this overload do.

docs.title: .clang-format
docs.text:
clang-format is a de facto standard tool to auto format (C++) code with style described by .clang-format file that typically located inside your project's root directory. AUI has such file.

Since AUI abuses C++'s syntax, it's important to set up appropriate auto formatting, or you will often find yourself struggling with AUI's DSL especially in large portions of layout, despite the fact we recommend to decompose large AUI DSLs into smaller pieces (i.e., functions). For your project, we recommend to start with AUI's formatting configuration listed below. AUI's App Template has .clang-format already. Your IDE should pick up it without further configuration.

docs.title: Always Use Trailing Comma in Initializer Lists
docs.text:
When it comes to clang-format there's one an unobvious feature when using AUI's DSL. Consider the example:

With Trailing CommaWithout Trailing Comma 
setContents(Vertical {
  Label { "Up" },
  Label { "Down" },
});

setContents(Vertical {
  Label { "Up" },
  Label { "Down" }
});

See the difference? The second example lacks one comma. If we try to trigger clang-format (ALT+CTRL+L in CLion), we'll get the following results (assuming AUI's ".clang-format"):

With Trailing CommaWithout Trailing Comma 
setContents(Vertical {
  Label { "Up" },
  Label { "Down" },
});

setContents(Vertical {
  Label { "Up" }, Label { "Down" } });

The first example left as is (correct), the second example formatted confusingly.

When using any kind of AUI's DSL with initializer lists please always use trailing comma. Not only it helps with reordering, git diffs, etc..., but also .clang-format makes proper formatting for lists with trailing commas.

docs.title: Use clang-format off/on
docs.text:
In some scenarios clang-format may fight against you, especially with complicated syntax. You can use // clang-format off and // clang-format on to disable and enable clang-format, respectively.

struct DataOptional {
    int v1;
    int v2;
};

// clang-format off
AJSON_FIELDS(DataOptional,
             (v1, "v1")
             (v2, "v2", AJsonFieldFlags::OPTIONAL))
// clang-format on

docs.title: AUI's .clang-format
docs.text:
Place this .clang-format file in root of your project.

# options: https://clang.llvm.org/docs/ClangFormatStyleOptions.html
BasedOnStyle: Google
IndentWidth: 4
ColumnLimit: 120
# does (int) x instead of (int)x
SpaceAfterCStyleCast: true
# spaces, not tabs!
UseTab: Never
# if (x) doStuff()  is not allowed, bad style
AllowShortIfStatementsOnASingleLine: false
AlignTrailingComments: true
SpacesBeforeTrailingComments: 3
AlignConsecutiveMacros: Consecutive

# use \n instead of \r\n
UseCRLF: false

AccessModifierOffset: -4
EmptyLineBeforeAccessModifier: Always
EmptyLineAfterAccessModifier: Never

NamespaceIndentation: None
BreakConstructorInitializers: BeforeComma

# we have some problems with ranges-v3 and AUI's AUI_LET, so keep it disabled
SortIncludes: Never


################################################# UI BUILDING ##########################################################

BracedInitializerIndentWidth: 4
ConstructorInitializerIndentWidth: 4

# better spacing around AUI_OVERRIDE_STYLE and AUI_LET.
# before:
# view AUI_OVERRIDE_STYLE{Expanding()},
# view AUI_LET{printf("Hello");},
#
# after:
# view AUI_OVERRIDE_STYLE { Expanding() },
# view AUI_LET { printf("Hello"); },
Cpp11BracedListStyle: false
SpaceBeforeCpp11BracedList: true

# forces nested initializer lists to begin with their own lines.
# note: you should use comma after last element in initializer lists.
# before:
# Centered { Horizontal {
#
# after:
# Centered {
#   Horizontal {
PenaltyIndentedWhitespace: 1000
BreakBeforeBraces: Attach
BreakBeforeBinaryOperators: None

StatementAttributeLikeMacros:
  - emit

# fix AUI's scary macros.
Macros:
  - AUI_LET=+[]
  - AUI_THREADPOOL=[]
  - AUI_DECLARATIVE_FOR(a,b,c)=[v2=b,v3=c](a)
  - AUI_DECLARATIVE_FOR_EX(a,b,c,d)=[d,v2=b,v3=c](a)
  - AUI_OVERRIDE_STYLE=+std::vector

include(aui.boot.cmake)

# link AUI
auib_import(
    AUI https://github.com/aui-framework/aui 
    COMPONENTS core)


# Create the executable. This function automatically links all sources from the src/ folder, creates CMake target and
# places the resulting executable to bin/ folder.
aui_executable(project_template)

# Link required libs
target_link_libraries(project_template PRIVATE aui::core)

docs.title: src/main.cpp
docs.text:
#include <AUI/Platform/Entry.h>
#include <AUI/Logging/ALogger.h>

static constexpr auto LOG_TAG = "MyApp";

AUI_ENTRY {
    ALogger::info(LOG_TAG) << "Hello world!";
    return 0;
}

docs.title: Contributing to AUI
docs.text: AUI is maintained by 1 developer so community help and contributions are heavily appreciated. Here's some helpful information.

docs.title: Becoming a contributor
docs.text:
1. Follow AUI's code style.
  2. Anyone may become an AUI contributor: there are no restrictions.
  3. Tasks and todos are listed on the GitHub Issues page. Issues marked as good first issue are relatively simple and can be done without deep dive into AUI.
  4. AUI follows git flow-like branching model. master branch is a release candidate branch. Each feature of the framework is created in a separate branch from master in the feat/ folder. Pulling changes from your branch to master is possible only if the merge with your branch does not generate merge conflicts and does not break the build and tests.

That is, if you want to implement a feature, you should fork AUI's repository (if you don't have direct access to it's repository), checkout the master branch and create a new branch called feat/feature-name, where you work under your feature.

When you have finished your work, you should open a pull request from the feat/feature-name branch of your repository to the master branch of the AUI's original repository. 5. Contributing to AUI, you agree that your code will be released under AUI's license.

docs.title: AI
docs.text:
We'd happily accept your AI-assisted work, as soon as you take complete responsibility thereof, and you have complete understanding of the changes you propose. Make sure your AI-assisted work does not violate someone's copyright. Please manually review and adjust AI-generated code/documentation. We won't merge changes if they contain obvious AI traces:

  • hallucinations
  • AI assistant-specific unnecessary statements: "I'm happy to help", "Please let me know if you have questions", etc
  • overexplanation, repetitive points, fluff writing
  • excessive usage of bullet points: nobody writes a page filled with bullet points entirely but AI

Please treat AI as a tool, not as a complete replacement of a software engineer.

docs.title: Contributing from your project
docs.text:
Want to help make AUI better? You can work on AUI right from your own project!

  • Open your project. If you don't have one, clone https://github.com/aui-framework/example_app.

  • Expose AUI's source code: Open the file called CMakeLists.txt and add ADD_SUBDIRECTORY:

# import AUI
auib_import(aui https://github.com/aui-framework/aui
        COMPONENTS core views curl json crypt updater
        ADD_SUBDIRECTORY # <------- here
        VERSION ${AUI_VERSION})

Note: This disables use of precompiled packages, AUI will be built locally.

  • See AUI in your editor: Now, when you open the project in CLion, AUI will show up as a folder.

  • Make changes: You can now change things in the AUI folder. Fix bugs or add cool stuff.

  • Make your own copy of AUI: Go to GitHub and make a "fork" of AUI, if you don't have one already.

  • Open a terminal in AUI: Right-click on the AUI folder in CLion. Choose "Open In" and then "Terminal".

  • Send your changes: In the terminal window, type these commands (change "ololo" to your GitHub name):

git checkout master
git checkout -b feat/your-feature-name
git remote set-url origin git@github.com:ololo/aui
git add -A
git commit -m "your commit message here"
git push -u fork feat/your-feature-name

This saves your changes to your feature branch on your fork.

Note: If you already added a fork remote in a previous session, skip the git remote set-url line.

  • Share your work: Go to your fork on GitHub. It will ask if you want to make a "pull request". Just do it! Make sure the pull request targets the master branch of the original AUI repository.

docs.title: Story points
docs.text:
Story points are designed as relative measurements of work complexity, deliberately decoupled from time-based metrics ( hours/days/weeks). They provide a general indication of effort required for task completion. It's important to note that story point comparisons across different teams, departments, or organizations are inherently invalid.

For example, Team A's 100-point sprint delivery might represent more actual work than Team B's 200 points, as each team develops their own story point scale. While this guide isn't meant to standardize story points globally, it offers internal guidelines for consistent estimation.

Note: All stories include standard overhead for PR reviews, test verification, and deployment processes. This overhead should be factored into estimates and can sometimes exceed the time needed for the primary task.

This section explains how story points are assigned to tasks in the AUI framework project and their relationship to developer compensation.

docs.title: Financial compensation
docs.text:
The number of story points assigned to a GitHub issue in the AUI repository directly determines the financial compensation paid to the external developer who successfully resolves that issue.

For information about getting in touch regarding compensation, please refer to the contact details provided in our README. Pick a task which you want to resolve before contacting.

docs.title: 1 Point - Minimal Complexity
docs.text: These represent the simplest possible changes. They involve single-line or minimal code modifications, such as text corrections or content updates. Tasks typically involve simple configuration value modifications with no logic alterations or risk of breakage. There are no external dependencies, and all necessary information is self-contained within the ticket. The changes are covered by existing tests or basic smoke testing, with no test updates required.

docs.title: 2 Points - Low Complexity
docs.text: These tasks represent approximately double the effort of a 1-point story. They may include minor third-party dependency updates with API adjustments and basic method refactoring without output changes. New test creation might be necessary. External dependencies are straightforward, such as Docker image whitelisting, and follow clear documentation or known processes.

docs.title: 3 Points - Moderate Complexity
docs.text: This is the first level where significant uncertainty enters the picture. These tasks require a notable but manageable time investment and may involve multiple external dependencies. They often include major version updates of libraries with breaking changes. Some cross-team communication is required, though clarifications can typically be resolved through a single call or chat. This represents the upper range of typical story size.

docs.title: 5 Points - High Complexity
docs.text: These stories are an extended version of 3-point complexity, involving a substantial workload with multiple unknowns to resolve. They often include significant breaking changes across components and require extensive test modifications. Multiple cross-team meetings are likely necessary, and broader stakeholder involvement is common.

docs.title: 8 Points - Very High Complexity
docs.text: This represents the maximum reasonable scope for a single sprint. These stories involve major system changes or refactoring, new integrations, or complete rewrites. They come with significant unknowns at the start and should be considered for splitting into smaller stories. Examples include framework migrations or major library updates. Requirements often have high uncertainty.

docs.title: 13+ Points - Excessive Complexity
docs.text: Stories of this size exceed single sprint capacity and typically require multiple sprints to complete. They contain too many unknowns and variables, carrying a high risk of underestimation. Such stories should be split into smaller components or converted to epics. Examples include full API integrations or complete rebranding projects. These large-scale changes are too complex to estimate accurately and manage effectively within a single sprint.

docs.title: Creating an AUI module
docs.text:
Suppose whe want to create a module called aui::my_module:

  1. In the main CMakeLists.txt:
    1. Find the # define all components anchor, put define_aui_component(my_module).
    2. Find the # all components for exporting anchor, put my_module to AUI_ALL_COMPONENTS.
  2. If aui::my_module has external dependencies, handle them at # add dependencies in cmake/aui-config.cmake.in.
  3. Put the reference to the module in docs/index.md.
  4. Create aui.my_module dir.
  5. Copy & paste CMakeLists.txt from any small module (i.e. aui::xml) and configure it for your module.
  6. Use API_AUI_<your module> to export symbols from your module (it's created by the aui_module CMake function).

docs.title: Documentation
docs.text:
Recommended: easy way to contribute

Want to fix a typo or make a small documentation improvement? You can do it directly through GitHub:

  1. Navigate to top right corner of the page you would like to contribute to and click "Edit this page".
  2. On GitHub's edit page, you'll be prompted to fork the AUI repository if needed
  3. Make your changes in the editor.
  4. Commit your changes and create a pull request to https://github.com/aui-framework/aui
  5. Once our documentation pipelines verify the changes, we'll merge your contribution.

This process is perfect for minor documentation updates and doesn't require setting up a local development environment.

The docs found on aui-framework.github.io is generated with MkDocs.

To generate documentation, run the following command from the root of AUI repository:

Note

These commands are not tested on Windows.

git clone https://github.com/aui-framework/aui
cd aui
git checkout master 

# if you want to use venv
python3 -m venv .venv
source .venv/bin/activate

# only for the first time
python3 -m pip install -r docs/python/requirements.txt 

# generate docs
mkdocs serve --use-directory-urls

After the command is complete, you can visit docs at http://127.0.0.1:8000/.

In our pipelines, we use --strict flag to treat warnings as errors. If warnings were produced during generation, the CI/CD pipeline wouldn't pass.

mkdocs build --strict --use-directory-urls

Most functionality is provided by Material for MkDocs theme. In addition to md files found in docs/ dir, we have several python scripts to populate documentation:

  • docs/python/hooks.py - handles XML comments.
  • docs/python/doxygen.py - handles Doxygen-style documentation found in our C++ code. Doxygen, as the tool, does not participate in our documentation generation. We still use Doxygen style to maintain compatibility with documentation readers in IDEs.
  • docs/python/examples_page.py - generates pages related to examples.

docs.title: Background tasks and timers
docs.text: A GUI application must keep its UI thread free. This page shows how to move work off it, get the result back, stop it when it's no longer needed, and run something periodically.

docs.title: Running a task on the thread pool
docs.text:
AUI_THREADPOOL runs a lambda on the global AThreadPool and returns an AFuture of whatever the lambda returns. *future (or future->get()) blocks until the result is ready.

auto b = _new<bool>(false);
auto v8 = AUI_THREADPOOL{
        AThread::sleep(1000ms);
        *b = true;
        return 8;
};
auto v1231 = AUI_THREADPOOL{
        AThread::sleep(1000ms);
        *b = true;
        return 1231.f;
};
ASSERT_TRUE(!*b);
AThread::sleep(2000ms);
ASSERT_TRUE(*b);

ASSERT_EQ(*v8, 8);
ASSERT_EQ(*v1231, 1231.f);

Warning

A task lives as long as its AFuture. If you drop the future (for example by not storing the return value of AUI_THREADPOOL), the task is cancelled. Store the future in a field or hand it to an AAsyncHolder.

AUI_THREADPOOL captures by value, like [=]. If you need another capture list, use AUI_THREADPOOL_X followed by your own lambda: AUI_THREADPOOL_X [&] { ... }.

docs.title: Receiving the result without blocking
docs.text:
Blocking on a future in the UI thread defeats its purpose. Attach callbacks instead:

class Downloader: public AObject {
public:
    void start() {
        mAsync << (AUI_THREADPOOL {
            return heavyComputation();
        }).onSuccess([this](int result) {
            // callback thread is not specified, so jump to the UI thread when touching views
            AUI_UI_THREAD {
                mResult = result;
            };
        }).onError([](const AException& e) {
            ALogger::err("Downloader") << "Failed: " << e;
        });
    }

private:
    AAsyncHolder mAsync;
    int mResult = 0;
};

onSuccess, onError and onFinally are called exactly once when the future resolves, or immediately if it has already resolved. They don't keep the future alive, so something has to own it: that's the job of AAsyncHolder (a set of AFuture<> that cancels everything in the destructor, so a callback can't run on a dead this).

AUI_UI_THREAD { ... }; posts a lambda to the main thread's event loop.

docs.title: Cancelling
docs.text:
Cancel a future explicitly with cancel(), or just destroy the last copy. If the task is already running, its thread gets interrupted: blocking calls like AThread::sleep, waiting on an AConditionVariable and AThread::interruptionPoint() throw an exception that unwinds the task.

bool called = false;
auto future = AUI_THREADPOOL_X [&] {
    called = true;
    AThread::sleep(1000ms);
    ADD_FAILURE() << "this line should not have reached";
    return 0;
};
AThread::sleep(500ms);
future.cancel();
AThread::sleep(1000ms);
ASSERT_TRUE(called) << "lambda has not called either";

Use AThread::interruptionPoint() inside long loops to make them cancellable:

auto task = AUI_THREADPOOL_X [] {
    for (const auto& item : items) {
        AThread::interruptionPoint();
        process(item);
    }
};

docs.title: Coroutines
docs.text:
On compilers with C++20 coroutine support, an AFuture can be a coroutine return type and be awaited with co_await. The coroutine resumes on the thread that started it, so UI code can stay linear:

AFuture<> MyView::load() {
    co_await AThread::asyncSleep(500ms);
    auto result = co_await loadSomethingAsync();   // any function returning AFuture<T>
    setText(result);                               // we're back on the original thread
}

Keep the returned future in an AAsyncHolder.

docs.title: Periodic work with ATimer
docs.text:
ATimer emits fired every period until stopped. It is started explicitly:

class Clock: public AObject {
public:
    Clock() {
        connect(mTimer->fired, me::tick);
        mTimer->start();
    }

    void tick() {
        // ...
    }

private:
    _<ATimer> mTimer = _new<ATimer>(1s);
};

fired is emitted from a dedicated timer thread. If the receiver is a view (or any AObject with setSlotsCallsOnlyOnMyThread(true)), the slot is invoked on the receiver's thread instead. See signal_slot.

The complete example is in examples/app/game_of_life and examples/7guis/timer.

docs.title: Protecting shared data
docs.text:
A plain AMutex works with std::unique_lock. If the data should never be touched without the lock, wrap it in AMutexWrapper. Debug builds check that the mutex is held when you access the value.

AMutexWrapper<AVector<AString>> log;

void append(AString line) {
    std::unique_lock lock(log);
    log->push_back(std::move(line));
}

docs.title: Your own threads
docs.text:
Most of the time the thread pool is enough. If you need a dedicated thread, create an AThread:

auto thread = _new<AThread>([] {
    AThread::setName("Worker");
    while (!AThread::current()->isInterrupted()) {
        // ...
        AThread::sleep(100ms);
    }
});
thread->start();
// ...
thread->interrupt();
thread->join();

AThread::sleep throws on interruption, so a sleeping thread wakes immediately when interrupt() is called.

docs.title: Binary data, compression and identifiers
docs.text: This page is about bytes: holding them, encoding them as text, compressing, archiving, and generating identifiers. Reading and writing files is covered in Files, paths and streams, text in Working with text.

docs.title: Holding bytes
docs.text:
AByteBuffer is a growing array of bytes. Fill it with operator<< (it is an IOutputStream) or by constructing it from a pointer and size, and get a non-owning window into it with slice().

AByteBuffer buffer;
buffer << std::uint32_t(0xcafebabe) << "tail";       // raw bytes of the number, then the string

AByteBufferView head = buffer.slice(0, 4);           // first 4 bytes, no copy
AByteBuffer copy = AByteBuffer(head);                // own copy

Warning

Numbers are written as is, in the native byte order. If you exchange data between machines, agree on an encoding.

A buffer can be constructed from a string with AByteBuffer::fromString(), and read back as text with AString::fromUtf8(buffer). For a different text encoding, use the AString(AByteBufferView, AStringEncoding) constructor and AString::encode().

docs.title: Hex and Base64
docs.text:
std::string_view text = "Building beautiful programs in pure C++ without chromium embedded framework";
AByteBuffer buffer(text.data(), text.size());
auto base64 = buffer.toBase64String();
EXPECT_EQ(base64, "QnVpbGRpbmcgYmVhdXRpZnVsIHByb2dyYW1zIGluIHB1cmUgQysrIHdpdGhvdXQgY2hyb21pdW0gZW1iZWRkZWQgZnJhbWV3b3Jr");
auto decoded = AString::fromUtf8(AByteBuffer::fromBase64String(base64));
EXPECT_EQ(decoded, text);

toHexString() and AByteBuffer::fromHexString() work the same way for hexadecimal.

docs.title: Compression
docs.text:
aui::zlib::compress and aui::zlib::decompress from AUI/Util/LZ.h convert between AByteBuffers (both append to the destination buffer).

auto source = makeSource();

AByteBuffer compressed;
aui::zlib::compress(source, compressed);

EXPECT_LE(compressed.size(), source.size());

AByteBuffer decompressed;
aui::zlib::decompress(compressed, decompressed);

EXPECT_EQ(source, decompressed);

If the unpacked data is large, aui::zlib::decompressToStream returns an IInputStream which decompresses on the fly, so you can process it chunk by chunk.

docs.title: ZIP archives
docs.text:
AUI/Util/Archive.h reads and writes ZIP files.

To create an archive, wrap an AFileOutputStream (any seekable output stream works) in a aui::archive::zip::Writer and add files with a lambda that writes their contents:

{
    aui::archive::zip::Writer writer(std::make_unique<AFileOutputStream>("test.zip"));
    writer.openFileInZip(APath("test") / "test.txt", [](IOutputStream& os) {
        os << std::string_view("1234\n");
    });
}

bool called = false;
aui::archive::zip::read(AFileInputStream("test.zip"), [&](const aui::archive::FileEntry& e) {
    EXPECT_FALSE(called);
    called = true;
    EXPECT_EQ(e.name, "test/test.txt");
    EXPECT_EQ(AString(AByteBuffer::fromStream(e.open()), AStringEncoding::LATIN1), "1234\n");
});
EXPECT_TRUE(called);

To read, call aui::archive::zip::read with a seekable input stream and a visitor. It is called for each entry, and the entry's data is available through open(). Don't use the stream after the visitor returns.

aui::archive::zip::read(AFileInputStream("archive.zip"), [](const aui::archive::FileEntry& entry) {
    ALogger::info("Zip") << entry.name;
    auto data = AByteBuffer::fromStream(entry.open());
});

To simply unpack everything to a folder, pass the aui::archive::ExtractTo visitor:

aui::archive::zip::read(AFileInputStream("archive.zip"), aui::archive::ExtractTo { .prefix = "unpacked" });

docs.title: UUIDs and random data
docs.text:
AUuid parses and prints UUIDs in canonical and raw formats and throws AUuidException on malformed input.

AString s = "123e4567-e89b-12d3-a456-426655440000";
AUuid uuid = s;
ASSERT_EQ(uuid.toString(), s);

Use ARandom to generate new identifiers or random bytes:

ARandom random;
AUuid id = random.nextUuid();
AByteBuffer nonce = random.nextBytes(16);

Note

ARandom is not a cryptographically secure generator. For secrets, hashing and encryption use aui::crypt.

docs.title: Containers and optionals
docs.text:
AUI containers are thin wrappers around their std counterparts. They inherit from the standard type, so everything from the standard library keeps working (including range-based for, algorithms and ranges), and add helpers for the things you otherwise write by hand.

AUI type Based on Use it for AVector std::vector the default sequence ADeque std::deque insertion/removal at both ends AQueue std::queue FIFO queues ASet std::set sorted unique values AMap std::map sorted key-value pairs AUnorderedMap std::unordered_map hashed key-value pairs ASmallVector - few elements, with no heap allocation until needed AStaticVector - at most N elements, never allocates

docs.title: Filling and modifying a vector
docs.text:
operator<< appends one element or a whole container, and calls can be chained.

AVector<int> numbers = { 1, 2 };
numbers << 3 << 4;
numbers << AVector<int>{ 5, 6 };

Instead of the erase-remove idiom, use removeIf, removeAll, removeFirst or removeAt:

numbers.removeIf([](int i) { return i % 2 == 0; });  // { 1, 3, 5 }
numbers.removeFirst(3);                              // { 1, 5 }

first() and last() return references to the boundary elements. They assert that the vector is not empty, so they're safe to call only when you know there is something to return.

docs.title: Searching
docs.text:
contains answers a yes-or-no question, indexOf returns the index as an AOptional, findIf returns a pointer to the first element matching a predicate (or nullptr).

AVector<AString> names = { "Alice", "Bob", "Carol" };

if (names.contains("Bob")) {
    // ...
}
if (auto index = names.indexOf("Carol")) {
    ALogger::info("Demo") << "Carol is at " << *index;
}
if (auto* name = names.findIf([](const AString& s) { return s.startsWith("A"); })) {
    ALogger::info("Demo") << "Found " << *name;
}

For sorted data aui::binary_search from AUI/Traits/algorithms.h does a logarithmic search with your comparison callback.

docs.title: Transforming
docs.text:
map returns a new vector of transformed elements, filter keeps the elements for which the predicate returns true. toMap builds an AMap out of pairs and toSet makes an ASet.

AVector<int> numbers = { 1, 2, 3, 4 };
auto squares = numbers.map([](int i) { return i * i; });                // { 1, 4, 9, 16 }
auto labels = numbers.map([](int i) { return "item {}"_format(i); });   // AVector<AString>
auto byParity = numbers.toMap([](int i) { return std::pair(i, i % 2 == 0); });

docs.title: Maps
docs.text:
AMap and AUnorderedMap share the same extensions. Note that operator[] of a const map throws, instead of silently inserting like std::map does for non-const maps.

AMap<AString, int> scores;
scores["Alice"] = 10;

if (auto it = scores.contains("Alice")) {  // converts to bool, behaves like an iterator
    ALogger::info("Demo") << it->second;
}

AOptional<int> bob = scores.optional("Bob");          // empty, nothing was inserted
int total = scores.getOrInsert("Carol", [] { return 0; });
auto names = scores.keyVector();

at() throws AException if the key is missing. getOrInsert calls the factory only if there is no value for the key yet; the value type must be default constructible.

docs.title: Optional values
docs.text:
AOptional is an optional with a few extras: valueOr (accepts a value or a callback), valueOrException, map and support for references (AOptional<T&>). It is what AUI APIs return when a value might not exist, for example string to number conversions.

AOptional<int> parsed = "42"_as.toInt();

int value = parsed.valueOr(0);
AString text = parsed.map([](int i) { return AString::number(i); }).valueOr(AString("n/a"));
int mustExist = parsed.valueOrException("expected a number");

docs.title: Avoiding allocations
docs.text:
If a collection almost always has a handful of elements, ASmallVector stores up to N of them inside the object and switches to the heap only when it grows past N. AStaticVector never allocates and refuses to grow beyond N.

ASmallVector<int, 8> points;  // no heap allocation until the 9th element

docs.title: Files, paths and streams
docs.text: This page covers the most common file system tasks: building paths, reading and writing files, listing folders and using streams. Types here live in AUI/IO.

docs.title: Paths
docs.text:
APath is an AString with file system helpers, so it can be printed, compared and passed as a string. It always uses forward slashes, on Windows too.

APath dir = "/home/user/work";
APath file = dir / "report.txt";        // /home/user/work/report.txt
file.filename();                        // report.txt
file.filenameWithoutExtension();        // report
file.parent();                          // /home/user/work
file.extensionChanged("md");            // /home/user/work/report.md

EXPECT_EQ(APath("test.txt").extension(), "txt");
EXPECT_EQ(APath("te.st.txt").extension(), "txt");
EXPECT_EQ(APath("C:/te.st.txt").extension(), "txt");

Query and modify the file system with exists(), isRegularFileExists(), isDirectoryExists(), fileSize(), makeDir(), makeDirs() (creates missing parents), removeFile() and removeFileRecursive().

APath cache = APath::getDefaultPath(APath::HOME) / ".cache" / "myapp";
cache.makeDirs();

Use APath::copy(from, to) and APath::move(from, to) to copy and move files.

docs.title: Well-known locations
docs.text:
APath::getDefaultPath returns HOME, TEMP or APPDATA of the current user on every platform. To store your own application's settings or databases, prefer AApplication::dataDir().

For scratch files use APath::nextRandomTemporary(), which returns a non-existent path in the temp directory, and wrap it in an APathOwner to have the file removed automatically:

APathOwner scratch(APath::nextRandomTemporary());
AFileOutputStream(scratch.value()) << "temporary";
// the file is removed when `scratch` is destroyed

docs.title: Listing a folder
docs.text:
listDir() returns an ADeque<APath> with the children; each path includes the folder it was listed from. . and .. are skipped. Pass flags such as AFileListFlags::DIRS or AFileListFlags::REGULAR_FILES to choose what you get.

for (const APath& child : APath("/home/user/work").listDir()) {
    if (child.isRegularFileExists() && child.extension() == "txt") {
        ALogger::info("Demo") << child.filename() << ": " << child.fileSize() << " bytes";
    }
}

docs.title: Reading files
docs.text:
AFileInputStream opens a file for reading and throws an AIOException subclass (for example AFileNotFoundException) if it can't. The easiest way to get all data out of a stream is AByteBuffer::fromStream:

auto bytes = AByteBuffer::fromStream(AFileInputStream("config.txt"));
AString text = AString::fromUtf8(bytes);

For big files, read in chunks instead. read() returns how many bytes it has put in the buffer, and 0 means the end of the stream.

AFileInputStream file("big.bin");
char buffer[0x1000];
while (auto size = file.read(buffer, sizeof(buffer))) {
    process(buffer, size);
}

docs.title: Writing files
docs.text:
AFileOutputStream creates (or truncates) the file. Pass true as the second argument to append. operator<< accepts strings, AByteBuffers, and numbers (numbers are written as raw bytes in native byte order, not as text).

{
    AFileOutputStream out("log.txt", true /* append */);
    out << "line\n";
}

The file is closed when the stream is destroyed.

_new<AFileOutputStream>("test.txt")->write("test", 4);

APath::copy("test.txt", "test-copy.txt");

char buf[0x100];
auto s = _new<AFileInputStream>("test-copy.txt")->read(buf, sizeof(buf));
ASSERT_TRUE(s == 4);
ASSERT_TRUE(memcmp(buf, "test", 4) == 0);

docs.title: Streams
docs.text:
Files are just one kind of IInputStream and IOutputStream. Code that takes the interfaces works with files, network sockets, memory buffers and compressed data alike:

AString readAll(IInputStream& is) {
    return AString::fromUtf8(AByteBuffer::fromStream(is));
}

Besides files, aui::core provides AByteBufferInputStream (stream over a buffer), AConcatInputStream (several streams in a row), ALimitedInputStream (first N bytes of a stream) and APipe (an in-process pipe). IInputStream also has readExact(), which keeps reading until the requested number of bytes arrive and throws if the stream ends.

Note

Reading from a stream may block. Don't do it on the UI thread if the source can be slow; see Background tasks and timers.

To store and restore structures, JSON is the convenient choice: Writing JSON and Parsing JSON.

docs.title: Smart pointers
docs.text: AUI objects are normally owned by shared pointers. This page describes the pointer types and the shortcuts around them.

docs.title: AArc, AWeakArc and AUnique
docs.text:
Type Based on Notes aui::Arc, AArc<T> std::shared_ptr "atomic reference counter" aui::WeakArc, AWeakArc<T> std::weak_ptr lock() returns an AArc AUnique<T> std::unique_ptr

They inherit from the standard types, so they work with any API expecting std::shared_ptr and so on.

The _<T>, _weak<T> and _unique<T> aliases are older, shorter names of the same types. You'll see them all over the examples, but the header marks them as deprecated in favor of the A-prefixed spelling.

_<MyClass> a;     // same as AArc<MyClass>

docs.title: Creating objects
docs.text:
_new<T>(args...) is std::make_shared that returns an aui::Arc:

auto view = _new<AButton>("Click me");

An aui::Arc cannot be constructed from a raw pointer by accident: that constructor is deleted. Say how the memory is managed instead:

auto owned = aui::ptr::manage_shared(new Legacy());   // delete is called when the last reference dies
auto notOwned = aui::ptr::fake_shared(&someGlobal);   // destructor does nothing

Use fake_shared when an API demands a shared pointer but your object lives on the stack or in a static.

docs.title: Setting up an object in place
docs.text:
Creating an object and configuring it with a few setters usually takes a variable and several lines. Two helpers let you keep it in one expression. AUI_LET runs a block right after the expression, with the object named it:

auto builder = _new<SomeBuilderClass>() AUI_LET {
    it->setUsername("John");
    it->setAge(23);
};


ASSERT_EQ(builder->getUsername(), "John");
ASSERT_EQ(builder->getAge(), 23);

AUI_PERFORM_AS_MEMBER makes the block behave as a member function of the object, so there is no need to repeat its name:

auto builder = _new<SomeBuilderClass>();
AUI_PERFORM_AS_MEMBER(*builder, {
   setUsername("John");
   setAge(23);
});

ASSERT_EQ(builder->getUsername(), "John");
ASSERT_EQ(builder->getAge(), 23);

aui::Arc also has a connect builder, which makes it possible to wire up signals without leaving the expression:

auto receiver = _new<ReceiverObject>();

auto sender = _new<SendObject>()
        .connect(&SendObject::someSignal, receiver, &ReceiverObject::receiveSignal);


AUI_PERFORM_AS_MEMBER(*sender, {
    invokeSignal();
});

ASSERT_TRUE(receiver->mSignalInvoked);

See signal_slot for what signals and slots are.

docs.title: Weak references
docs.text:
weak() makes an aui::WeakArc; lock() gives back an aui::Arc, which is empty if the object is gone. Use it to avoid reference cycles and to keep an async callback from extending the lifetime of an object.

void MyWindow::watch(const _<MyView>& view) {
    mCallback = [weakView = view.weak()] {
        if (auto view = weakView.lock()) {
            view->setVisibility(Visibility::GONE);
        }
    };
}

docs.title: this as a shared pointer
docs.text:
AObject derives from std::enable_shared_from_this. Calling shared_from_this() on a derived class returns a pointer to the base, so AUI provides aui::ptr::shared_from_this(this) and aui::ptr::weak_from_this(this) that return a pointer of the right type:

auto self = aui::ptr::shared_from_this(this);   // AArc<MyView>
auto weakSelf = aui::ptr::weak_from_this(this); // AWeakArc<MyView>

docs.title: Pointer to a member of a shared object
docs.text:
AUI_PTR_ALIAS(owner, field) returns a shared pointer to owner->field that keeps the whole owner alive. It's useful to pass a part of a state object to some component without the component knowing about the entire state.

struct State {
    AProperty<bool> checked;
};

_<State> state = _new<State>();
_<AProperty<bool>> checked = AUI_PTR_ALIAS(state, checked);

docs.title: Casting
docs.text:
_cast<To>(ptr) is dynamic_pointer_cast for aui::Arc:

if (auto button = _cast<AButton>(view)) {
    // view is actually a button
}

docs.title: Working with text
docs.text:
This page covers everyday string tasks with AString, AStringView and AStringVector.

AString is a UTF-8 string derived from std::string, so it works wherever std::string does. Positions and sizes are measured in bytes, as in std::string, while text-aware operations (case conversion, trimming by a set of symbols, conversion to other encodings) understand Unicode. When you need to count in characters, use utf8().

docs.title: Creating strings
docs.text:
A string literal converts to AString implicitly. The _as suffix makes a literal an AString right away, which is handy for chaining calls:

AString hello = "Привет, мир";
auto length = "hello"_as.length();

If your data is in some other encoding, use AString::fromUtf8, fromUtf16, fromUtf32 or fromLatin1. To get the data back, use toUtf16(), toUtf32() or encode().

AString str("Привет, 🤡, Как твои дела?");
EXPECT_EQ(str.toUtf16(), u"Привет, 🤡, Как твои дела?");
EXPECT_EQ(str.toUtf32(), U"Привет, 🤡, Как твои дела?");

docs.title: Characters vs bytes
docs.text:
length(), substr(), erase() and the like operate on bytes, because that's what std::string does. A single character such as 嗨 takes three bytes in UTF-8. To work with characters, switch to the UTF-8 view with utf8(). It provides length(), substr(), iterators and other operations in terms of Unicode code points. See AUtf8View.

EXPECT_EQ("嗨"_as, "嗨");
EXPECT_EQ("嗨"_as.length(), 3);
EXPECT_EQ("嗨"_as.utf8().length(), 1);
EXPECT_EQ("嗨"_as.toStdString(), "嗨");

AString str("🤡, как твои дела?");
EXPECT_EQ(str.utf8().substr(0, 1), "🤡");
EXPECT_EQ(str.utf8().substr(1), ", как твои дела?");
EXPECT_EQ(str.utf8().substr(1, 3), ", к");

insert() and erase() on AString take byte positions, but insert() also accepts an AChar, which gets encoded properly. Mind that the position must not point into the middle of a multibyte character:

auto s = "AB"_as;
s.insert(1, U'🤡');
EXPECT_EQ(s, "A🤡B");
EXPECT_EQ(s.bytes().size(), 6);

docs.title: Converting to and from numbers
docs.text:
Parsing never throws. toInt(), toLong(), toUInt(), toFloat(), toDouble() and friends return an AOptional that is empty if the whole string is not a valid number or the value doesn't fit. Hexadecimal literals starting with 0x are understood too.

EXPECT_EQ("123"_as.toInt(), 123);
EXPECT_EQ("0"_as.toInt(), 0);
EXPECT_EQ("-251"_as.toInt(), -251);
EXPECT_EQ("123abs"_as.toInt(), std::nullopt);
EXPECT_EQ("1a23"_as.toInt(), std::nullopt);
EXPECT_EQ("a123"_as.toInt(), std::nullopt);
EXPECT_EQ("0x"_as.toInt(), 0);
EXPECT_EQ("0x123"_as.toInt(), 0x123);
EXPECT_EQ("0xabcdef"_as.toInt(), 0xabcdef);
EXPECT_EQ("0xabcdef123456"_as.toInt(), std::nullopt); // overflow
EXPECT_EQ("123456214214"_as.toInt(), std::nullopt); // overflow

If you prefer exceptions, use the ...OrException variants (toIntOrException(), ...). Use AString::number() to format a number as a string.

docs.title: Formatting
docs.text:
AString uses the fmt library. Call format() on a string or use the _format literal:

EXPECT_EQ("test {}"_format("azaza"), "test azaza");

Format specifiers work as in fmt:

EXPECT_EQ("test {:.2}"_format(1.2f), "test 1.2");

_format is declared in AUI/Traits/strings.h. Standard containers and AString itself can be passed as arguments.

docs.title: Searching, replacing and trimming
docs.text:
EXPECT_EQ("Ку🤡Ку"_as.utf8().startsWith(U'К'), true);
EXPECT_EQ("Ку🤡Ку"_as.startsWith("Ку"), true); // russian letters

EXPECT_EQ("Ку🤡Ку"_as.utf8().startsWith(U'K'), false);
EXPECT_EQ("Ку🤡Ку"_as.startsWith("Ky"), false); // english letters

replaceAll() and removeAll() modify the string in place, while replacedAll() and removedAll() return a modified copy.

EXPECT_EQ("abcdef"_as.replaceAll("ab", "12"), "12cdef");

uppercase() and lowercase() are Unicode-aware:

EXPECT_EQ("a"_as.uppercase(), "A"); // ascii
EXPECT_EQ("å"_au8.uppercase(), "Å"); // unicode

trim(), trimLeft() and trimRight() remove a single symbol (a space by default)...

EXPECT_EQ(AString("  a b  ").trim(), "a b");
EXPECT_EQ(AString("xxaxx").trim('x'), "a");
// only the given symbol is removed
EXPECT_EQ(AString("\t a \n").trim(), "\t a \n");

... or any symbol of a set:

EXPECT_EQ(AString("\t a b \r\n").trim(" \t\r\n"), "a b");
EXPECT_EQ(AString("xyhixyx").trim("xy"), "hi");

Note

Trimming returns an AStringView into the original string and doesn't allocate. Don't let the view outlive the string it was made from. Construct an AString from the view if you need a copy.

docs.title: Splitting and joining
docs.text:
split() returns an AStringVector; join() of AStringVector does the opposite.

EXPECT_EQ("1x2"_as.split('x'), AStringVector({"1", "2"}));

auto parts = "a, b, c"_as.split(", ");     // { "a", "b", "c" }
AString joined = parts.join('-');          // "a-b-c"

docs.title: Passing strings around
docs.text:
Take AStringView for read-only parameters. It converts from AString, std::string_view and string literals without copying. Return or store AString when you need ownership.

bool isGreeting(AStringView text) {
    return text.startsWith("Hello");
}

docs.title: Printing
docs.text:
AString can be streamed to std::ostream and to the logger, and is accepted by fmt as is.

ALogger::info("MyApp") << "Hello, " << name;

See also Binary data, compression and identifiers for raw bytes and Base64, and i18n for translating user-visible strings.

docs.title: aui::core
docs.text: Main central library.

docs.title: Detailed Description
docs.text:
aui::core is the main module of AUI. All other modules are built on top of aui::core. It implements several basic features:

  • strings and text processing
  • containers and optionals
  • smart pointers
  • signal-slot and properties
  • background tasks, futures and timers; interruptable threads
  • files, paths and streams
  • binary data, compression, UUIDs
  • i18n
  • logging
  • urls
  • reflection
  • data models
  • trait classes
