docs.title: Replacing AUI mobile project
docs.text:
Note

This page describes an advanced scenario of integrating AUI. For basic usage, see Crosscompiling (Android and iOS)

Some projects may require their custom mobile project (Android Studio or Xcode), for example to specific mobile features (such as Google Play Games integration, Face ID, etc). In this case, you would have to create your own project and link AUI as a library.

You will need a toolchain file which describes your target platform.

In Android, a Gradle-driven project provides the toolchain for you. You don't even need to specify CMAKE_TOOLCHAIN_FILE, Gradle does it for you.

In iOS, there's no "official" toolchain so there are community-provided toolchains (like the one used in AUI).

AUI.Boot forwards CMAKE_TOOLCHAIN_FILE across all the dependencies.

docs.title: Android
docs.text:
1. Create new Android Studio project with native C++ support.
  2. In your app/src/cpp/CMakeLists.txt, add_subdirectory your C++ application or directly auib_import the AUI framework (unrecommended because you will experience difficulties when compiling for other platforms).
  3. Copy & paste AUI's native Java code for Android to your project. You may also want to adjust your app.gradle and AndroidManifest.xml.
  4. To draw AUI, you should use GLSurfaceView and pass rendering routines to AUI. Also, take care of handling user input. Also, you can inflate AuiView to your own Android layout.

docs.title: iOS
docs.text:
1. Create new Xcode project.
  2. Since Xcode does not support CMake, you will have to compile AUI (and your C++ AUI application) by yourself (by creating Xcode rules or manually dropping compiled binaries to Xcode project).
  3. Take a look on how does AUI handles its routines on iOS and implement them by yourself in your project.

docs.title: Crosscompiling (Android and iOS)
docs.text:
AUI provides the unified way to cross-compile your application with AUI_BUILD_FOR CMake configure variable. When specified, CMake does the whole configure routine as if the project is compiled for the host system but it generates extra project directory for the target platform's development environment once the apps target is invoked.

To build target platform's final application package, run build the apps target.

docs.title: Workflow
docs.text:
Android: 

mkdir build # or whatever name
cd build
cmake -DAUI_BUILD_FOR=android ..
cmake --build . -t apps

iOS: 

mkdir build # or whatever name
cd build
cmake -DAUI_BUILD_FOR=ios ..
cmake --build . -t apps

These commands produce an Android Studio/Xcode project in build/app_project directory and build it. You can now open it in Android Studio/Xcode to upload the application to your device and debug. Both support C++, so you can continue development of your app there.

docs.title: Supported platforms
docs.text: AUI_BUILD_FOR value Host platform Target platform Project environment Project dir android Windows Linux macOS Android Gradle (can be opened with Android Studio) ${CMAKE_BINARY_DIR}/app_project ios macOS iOS Xcode ${CMAKE_BINARY_DIR}/app_project

docs.title: Limitations
docs.text:
1. Variables defined in the configure step (including the ones specified with command line by -DVAR=VALUE syntax) are not forwarded to the child CMake configure process. To bypass the limitation, use auib_mark_var_forwardable(VAR) function, where VAR is your variable name.
  2. As like CMake's generated projects, the projects generated by AUI are not portable too.

docs.title: Hashing and HMAC
docs.text:
AHash provides message digests and HMAC. All functions return the raw digest as an AByteBuffer; use toHexString() or toBase64String() to get text.

Function Digest size AHash::md5 16 bytes AHash::sha1 20 bytes AHash::sha256 32 bytes AHash::sha512 64 bytes AHash::sha256hmac 32 bytes

Warning

MD5 and SHA-1 are broken for security purposes. Use them only to interoperate with existing formats.

docs.title: Hashing a buffer
docs.text:
#include <AUI/Crypt/AHash.h>

AByteBuffer digest = AHash::sha256(AByteBuffer::fromString("hello"));
ALogger::info("Sample") << digest.toHexString();

docs.title: Hashing a file or other stream
docs.text:
Every digest has an overload accepting an input stream. The stream is read until its end, so there is no need to load the whole file in memory:

auto checksum = AHash::sha256(AFileInputStream("big.iso")).toHexString();

The overload takes aui::no_escape<IInputStream>, so it accepts a stream object (temporary or lvalue), a pointer or a shared pointer (for example _new<AByteBufferInputStream>(buffer)).

docs.title: Verifying a download
docs.text:
Compare the hex digest with the published one. Hex output is lowercase.

bool matches = AHash::sha256(AFileInputStream(path)).toHexString() == expectedSha256;

docs.title: HMAC
docs.text:
AHash::sha256hmac(in, key) computes HMAC-SHA256 of in with a secret key. It is used to authenticate a message with a shared secret (webhook signatures, signed cookies, etc...):

auto signature = AHash::sha256hmac(AByteBuffer::fromString(body), AByteBuffer::fromString(secret));
if (signature.toHexString() != receivedSignature) {
    throw AException("bad signature");
}

Note

The == comparison above is not constant-time. Whether that matters depends on your threat model.

docs.title: Passwords
docs.text:
A plain digest, even salted, is a poor way to store passwords: this module does not implement a password hashing function (bcrypt, scrypt, PBKDF2, argon2).

See also crypt for the module overview.

docs.title: Random bytes
docs.text:
ACrypto::safeRandom() (AUI/Crypt/Random.h) returns an _<AByteBuffer> of 4096 cryptographically secure random bytes. They are produced by a CTR_DRBG generator (mbedTLS) which is seeded from the system entropy source on every call, so it is suitable for key material, tokens and nonces.

#include <AUI/Crypt/Random.h>

_<AByteBuffer> bytes = ACrypto::safeRandom();

The function throws AException if the generator can't be seeded. Seeding makes each call relatively expensive; if you need a lot of random numbers, call it once and take what you need from the buffer.

For non-security randomness (shuffling, test data), use ARandom from aui::core.

Key generation in ARsa does not use this function; it seeds its own mbedTLS generator from the same entropy source.

See also crypt for the module overview.

docs.title: RSA keys and encryption
docs.text: ARsa holds an RSA key and encrypts or decrypts data with it. Instances are created through static factories and are returned as _<ARsa>.

docs.title: Generating a key pair
docs.text:
#include <AUI/Crypt/ARsa.h>

auto keys = ARsa::generate();      // 2048 bits
auto big = ARsa::generate(4096);

Generation of large keys takes noticeable time; do it off the UI thread.

docs.title: Exporting and importing keys
docs.text:
Keys are exchanged in PEM format. getPrivateKeyPEM() and getPublicKeyPEM() return the PEM text as a byte buffer, so it can be written to a file directly. The private key is written unencrypted.

AFileOutputStream("private.pem") << keys->getPrivateKeyPEM();
AFileOutputStream("public.pem") << keys->getPublicKeyPEM();

ARsa::fromPrivateKeyPEM and ARsa::fromPublicKeyPEM read them back. Both throw AException on malformed input.

auto both = ARsa::generate();
auto priv = ARsa::fromPrivateKeyPEM(both->getPrivateKeyPEM());

auto someData = ARandom().nextBytes(10000);
auto result = priv->decrypt(both->encrypt(someData));

docs.title: Sending data to someone who has only the public key
docs.text:
The holder of the public key encrypts, the holder of the private key decrypts:

auto both = ARsa::generate();
auto pub = ARsa::fromPublicKeyPEM(both->getPublicKeyPEM());

auto someData = ARandom().nextBytes(10000);
auto result = both->decrypt(pub->encrypt(someData));

(In this test the same instance is used for decryption; in a real application the private key stays on the other side.)

docs.title: Data size
docs.text:
encrypt accepts input of any length. It is split into chunks of getKeyLength() - 11 bytes (PKCS#1 v1.5 padding), and each chunk becomes a getKeyLength() byte block of the output. The output is therefore larger than the input, and decrypt expects exactly the concatenation of such blocks.

RSA is slow and the output grows, so for bulk data it is usually used to protect a small secret rather than the data itself. This module has no symmetric cipher; bring your own.

Warning

ARsa offers encryption only. It does not sign or authenticate data, and it uses PKCS#1 v1.5 padding. Review whether this fits your protocol before relying on it.

Errors in encryption or decryption (for example, decrypting corrupted or foreign data) throw AException.

docs.title: aui::crypt
docs.text: Cryptography: hashing, HMAC and RSA.

docs.title: Detailed Description
docs.text:
aui::crypt is a small module built on top of mbedTLS. It provides:

  • message digests (MD5, SHA-1, SHA-256, SHA-512) and HMAC-SHA256, see Hashing and HMAC;
  • RSA key generation, PEM import/export and encryption, see ARsa and RSA keys and encryption;
  • a weak helper for gathering random bytes, see Random bytes.

Results are returned as AByteBuffer, which can be converted to hex or base64 text with toHexString() and toBase64String().

To use the module, link it to your target:

auib_import(aui https://github.com/aui-framework/aui COMPONENTS core crypt VERSION ${AUI_VERSION})
aui_link(${PROJECT_NAME} PRIVATE aui::crypt)

Note

The module does not cover symmetric ciphers (AES etc...), signatures or TLS. HTTPS requests are handled by curl.

docs.title: Related Pages
docs.text:
• ARsa

    Stores public and/or private RSA key and encrypts/decrypts data with it.

docs.title: Async requests and downloads
docs.text: ACurl::Builder offers several ways of not blocking the caller. Everything described here keeps the UI responsive.

docs.title: runAsync
docs.text:
runAsync() schedules the request on the global ACurlMulti (a background thread serving all simultaneous requests) and returns AFuture<ACurl::Response>. Network errors are delivered as an exception of the future.

ACurl::Builder("https://example.com/api/items").runAsync().onSuccess([this](const ACurl::Response& r) {
    // not the UI thread; hop to it before touching views.
    AUI_UI_THREAD_X [this, text = AString::fromUtf8(r.body)] {
        mLabel->setText(text);
    };
});

Inside a pool/coroutine task, you may simply dereference the future (future->body), which suspends the task rather than the thread.

To use a dedicated multi instead of the global one, pass it: runAsync(curlMulti).

docs.title: Downloading to a file
docs.text:
Pick a destination instead of buffering the body in memory: withOutputStream takes any IOutputStream.

ACurl a(ACurl::Builder("https://github.com").withOutputStream(_new<AFileOutputStream>("temp.html")));
a.run();

For a large file, call run() on a worker thread (for example, with AThreadPool), or enqueue the ACurl into ACurlMulti. Progress is available through getNumberOfBytesDownloaded() and getContentLength().

Resuming or fetching a part: withRanges(begin, end).

docs.title: Reading a response as a stream
docs.text:
toInputStream() returns an IInputStream fed by a background request. Reads block until data arrives, so it suits parsers working with streams:

auto stream = ACurl::Builder("https://example.com/data.json").toInputStream();
auto json = AJson::fromStream(*stream);

docs.title: Cancelling
docs.text: ACurl::close() is thread-safe and non-blocking. After it is called, neither success nor fail is emitted.

docs.title: Signals
docs.text:
ACurl emits success and fail (carrying ErrorDescription). Use withOnSuccess and withErrorCallback on the builder, or connect to the signals if you construct ACurl yourself and add it with ACurlMulti::global() << curl.

Note

ACurlMulti processes additions on its own thread, so right after operator<< its curls() may still be empty.

docs.title: HTTP requests with aui::curl
docs.text: Requests are described with ACurl::Builder and executed either synchronously (this page) or asynchronously (see Async requests and downloads). Builder methods return Builder&, so calls are chained.

docs.title: Simple GET
docs.text:
runBlocking() performs the request on the calling thread and returns a Response with code, contentType and body.

AByteBuffer buffer = ACurl::Builder("https://github.com").runBlocking().body;

Warning

runBlocking() blocks the thread. Never call it from the UI thread; use runAsync() instead.

docs.title: Query parameters
docs.text:
For GET, withParams encodes key-value pairs and appends them to the url.

auto response = ACurl::Builder("https://example.com/search")
    .withParams({
        { "q", "hello world" },
        { "page", "2" },
    })
    .runBlocking();

docs.title: Headers
docs.text:
auto response = ACurl::Builder("https://example.com/api/me")
    .withHeaders({
        "Authorization: Bearer " + token,
        "Accept: application/json",
    })
    .runBlocking();

To read response headers, set withHeaderCallback; it is called for each received header line.

docs.title: POST, PUT, DELETE
docs.text:
withMethod accepts ACurl::Method::HTTP_GET (default), HTTP_POST, HTTP_PUT and HTTP_DELETE.

A form-encoded POST is made with withParams:

ACurl::Builder("https://example.com/login")
    .withMethod(ACurl::Method::HTTP_POST)
    .withParams({
        { "user", "alex" },
        { "password", "secret" },
    })
    .runBlocking();

For an arbitrary body (JSON, for instance) use withBody with a string, and set Content-Type yourself. The reply can be parsed with Parsing JSON:

auto reply = ACurl::Builder("https://example.com/api/items")
    .withMethod(ACurl::Method::HTTP_POST)
    .withHeaders({ "Content-Type: application/json; charset=utf-8" })
    .withBody(AJson::toString(AJson::Object { { "name", "box" } }).toStdString())
    .runBlocking();
auto json = AJson::fromBuffer(reply.body);

withBody also has overloads accepting a read callback, and withInputStream uploads from any IInputStream, such as a file.

docs.title: Uploading files
docs.text:
AFormMultipart builds a multipart/form-data body; pass it to withMultipart.

AFormMultipart form;
form["comment"] = { .value = AString("Nice") };
form["file"] = { .value = _new<AFileInputStream>("photo.png"), .filename = AString("photo.png") };
ACurl::Builder("https://example.com/upload")
    .withMethod(ACurl::Method::HTTP_POST)
    .withMultipart(form)
    .runBlocking();

docs.title: Error handling
docs.text:
There are two kinds of errors.

A protocol error, such as 404, is not a failure from curl's point of view. Check response.code:

if (response.code != ACurl::ResponseCode::HTTP_200_OK) {
    // handle
}

A network error (DNS failure, timeout, TLS problem) throws ACurl::Exception from runBlocking(); curlStatus() holds the libcurl code. When using ACurl directly (ACurl(builder).run()), exceptions are off by default; enable them with throwExceptionOnError(true), or use withErrorCallback (which also disables throwing).

ACurl a(ACurl::Builder("https://snonejklgnjkwernjkg3ernjknerjk.sfjgsjknsdgjknsdgjknjksdgnjkzdg")
            .withOutputStream(_new<AFileOutputStream>("temp.html"))
            .throwExceptionOnError(true));
EXPECT_THROW(a.run(), ACurl::Exception);

Note

withTimeout is the same as withLowSpeedTime: it sets how long the transfer speed may stay below the low speed limit (1 KiB/s by default, see withLowSpeedLimit) before the request is aborted. It is not a limit of the total request duration.

docs.title: Custom window titlebar blur
docs.text:
Example's page

This page describes an example listed in the ui category.

Window with extended decoration, whose titlebar blurs the contents scrolled under it.

This example demonstrates AWindow::Init::DecorationExtended with declarative::Titlebar overlaid on top of an AScrollArea using AStackedLayout.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
The window contents are a declarative::Stacked of two layers:

  1. Content layer: a declarative::Vertical with an ASpacerFixed on top and the AScrollArea below it. The spacer's height is bound to the titlebar's measured height (AUI_REACT(AMetric(titlebar->size()->y, AMetric::T_PX))), so the initial position of the contents is shifted from beneath the titlebar, while scrolled content can still go under it.
  2. Titlebar layer: a declarative::Vertical with declarative::Titlebar at the top and a SpacerExpanding below, so the titlebar does not capture the rest of the window. Its style sets a translucent background (BackgroundSolid with a half-transparent white) and ass::Backdrop with Backdrop::GaussianBlur, which blurs whatever is rendered underneath the titlebar.

By default, the scroll area clips its contents to the bounds of AScrollAreaViewport. Since the scroll area no longer extends under the titlebar, its viewport is switched to AOverflow::VISIBLE with an extra stylesheet (the view is marked with the .scrollarea-viewport-hack class and the rule targets t<AScrollAreaViewport>()). The content is then not clipped and can slide under the titlebar overlay; as a consequence, it ends up in the backdrop and gets blurred.

Without this, the titlebar would blur only the content that lies within the scroll area, and scrolled content would disappear at the edge of the viewport instead of being blurred.

docs.title: src/main.cpp
docs.text:
#include "AUI/Platform/AMessageBox.h"
#include "AUI/View/AButton.h"
#include "AUI/View/ASpacerFixed.h"

#include <AUI/Platform/Entry.h>
#include <AUI/Platform/AWindow.h>
#include <AUI/Util/UIBuildingHelpers.h>
#include <AUI/View/AScrollArea.h>
#include <AUI/View/ATitlebar.h>
#include <AUI/View/ADrawableView.h>

using namespace declarative;
using namespace ass;

static AArc<AView> actualContent() {
    auto scrollarea =
        AScrollArea::Builder()
            .withContents(Centered {
                Icon { ":logo.svg" } AUI_OVERRIDE_STYLE { FixedSize { 1024_dp } },
            })
            .withExpanding()
            .build();

    // important: for scrollarea, we hjacking its AScrollAreaViewport so it shows its overflow
    // TODO: declarative version of ScrollArea should provide viewport modifier so we don't need to mess up
    // with the stylesheets
    scrollarea << ".scrollarea-viewport-hack";
    scrollarea->setExtraStylesheet(AStylesheet {
        {
            c(".scrollarea-viewport-hack") >> t<AScrollAreaViewport>(),
            AOverflow::VISIBLE,
        },
    });
    return scrollarea;
}

AUI_ENTRY {
    auto window = _new<AWindow>(AWindow::Init {
        .title = "Custom window titlebar blur",
        .width = 600_dp,
        .height = 500_dp,
        .decoration = AWindow::Init::DecorationExtended {},
    });

    AArc<AView> titlebar =
        Titlebar {
            Horizontal {
                Centered {
                    Button {
                        .content = Label { "Before" },
                        .onClick = [w = window.get()] { AMessageBox::show(w, "Test", "Test"); },
                    },
                },
                // shows window->title() and is aligned the way the OS aligns titles.
                WindowTitle {},
                Centered {
                    Button {
                        .content = Label { "After" },
                        .onClick = [w = window.get()] { AMessageBox::show(w, "Test", "Test"); },
                    },
                },
            },
        } AUI_OVERRIDE_STYLE {
            Backdrop {
                Backdrop::GaussianBlur { 32_dp },
            },
            BackgroundSolid { AColor::WHITE.transparentize(0.5f) },
        };

    window->setContents(Stacked {
        Vertical::Expanding { // content layer
            // keep contents out of the system UI (titlebar controls strip)
            SpacerFixed { AUI_REACT(AMetric(window->safeAreaInsets->top, AMetric::T_PX)) },
            actualContent(),
        },
        Vertical::Expanding {  // titlebar layer
            titlebar,
            SpacerExpanding {},   // blank space
        },
    });

    window->show();
    return 0;
}

docs.title: aui::data
docs.text:
Outdated

aui::data is not maintained. It is excluded from the build (see the commented-out define_aui_component(data) in the root CMakeLists.txt) and its README states that it needs reworking. It depends on APIs that no longer exist in aui::core (Autumn, AVariant), so it does not compile against current AUI.

aui::data was meant to be a thin SQL access layer. The sources live in aui.data/src/AUI/Data and contain:

  • ASqlDatabase - connection object. ASqlDatabase::connect picks a driver by name ("sqlite", "mysql") and query/execute run SQL with positional ? parameters.
  • ASqlBuilder - a small query builder (insert, select, update, remove, where) plus experimental mapping of rows to model structs (AModelMeta, ASqlModel).
  • ASqlBlueprintTable - schema definition for tables.
  • AMigrationManager - runs registered migrations once, remembering progress in a key-value table (AMeta).
  • SQLException - error type.

None of these classes carries a documentation comment, so there are no generated reference pages for them, and this documentation intentionally gives no usage examples: they could not be verified against a working build.

If you need a database in an AUI application today, use a database library directly (for instance SQLite's C API imported with auib_import, see aui.boot) and run blocking calls off the UI thread.

See also aui::sqlite for the SQLite driver of this module.

docs.text:
View that displays a single color.

Header:#include <AUI/View/AColorPicker.h> CMake:aui_link(my_target PUBLIC aui::views)

docs.title: Detailed Description
docs.text:
The ColorView simply renders a solid rectangle matching the provided color contract. It is intended to be used as a visual preview of a color value.

#include <AUI/Platform/Entry.h>
#include <AUI/Platform/AWindow.h>
#include <AUI/View/AColorPicker.h>

using namespace ass;
using namespace declarative;


class MainWindow : public AWindow {
public:
    MainWindow() : AWindow("Color picker", 600_dp, 300_dp) {
        auto color = _new<AProperty<AColor>>(AColor::RED);
        setContents(Vertical {
          GroupBox {
            Label { "View" },
            color_picker::ColorView { AUI_REACT(**color) } AUI_OVERRIDE_STYLE {
                  FixedSize(40_dp, 20_dp),
                  Border { 1_px, AColor::BLACK },
                  Padding { 2_px },
                },
          },
          GroupBox {
            Label { "Sliders RGB" },
            color_picker::SlidersRGB {
              .color = AUI_REACT(**color),
              .onColorChanged = [color](AColor c) { *color = c; },
            },
          },
        });
    }

};

AUI_ENTRY {
    _new<MainWindow>()->show();
    return 0;
}

declarative::Slider
docs.text:
Slider control.

Header:#include <AUI/View/ASlider.h> CMake:aui_link(my_target PUBLIC aui::views)

docs.title: Detailed Description
docs.text:
The Slider represents a horizontal slider control that can be used in declarative UI definitions. It exposes a single value in the range [0, 1] and emits a signal whenever the value changes. The visual representation consists of a track and a handle view. By default the track and handle are created using the static helper functions defaultTrack() and defaultHandle(), but users may provide custom implementations by overriding the corresponding member variables.

The slider automatically handles mouse and keyboard input. When the user drags the handle, the onValueChanged slot is invoked.

docs.title: Examples
Public fields and Signals
docs.text:
_<AView> handle

View representing the slider handle.

The default implementation is provided by defaultHandle().

contract::Slot<aui::float_within_0_1> onValueChanged

Slot that is called whenever the slider value changes.

The slot receives the new value as a float_within_0_1. The implementation expects the consumer to update the value contract inside this slot.

_<AView> track

View representing the slider track.

By default this is created by defaultTrack(value) which creates a simple rectangular track. Users can replace this with a custom view to change the appearance.

contract::In<aui::float_within_0_1> value

Current slider value in the range [0, 1].

The value is a contract input, meaning it can be bound to other components or data models. Changing this value programmatically will update the handle position.

docs.title: Examples
Public Methods
docs.text:
static _<AView> Slider::defaultHandle()

Creates a default handle view.

Returns A view representing the handle.

The handle is a draggable element that the user can move along the track. It updates the value contract when dragged.

_<AView> Slider::defaultHandle() {
    return _new<AView>() AUI_OVERRIDE_STYLE {
        BackgroundSolid { AStylesheet::getOsThemeColor() },
        FixedSize { 8_dp },
        BorderRadius { 4_dp },
    };
}

static _<AView> Slider::defaultTrack(const contract::In<aui::float_within_0_1>& value)

Creates a default track view.

Arguments value The slider value contract. Returns A view representing the track.

The returned view is a simple rectangle that visually represents the slider's range. It listens to the value contract to update its visual state.

_<AView> Slider::defaultTrack(const contract::In<aui::float_within_0_1>& value) {
    return ProgressBar { .progress = value } AUI_OVERRIDE_STYLE {
        FixedSize { {}, 4_dp },
        MinSize { 150_dp, {} },
    };
}

docs.text:
Titlebar of the window which contents extend into the titlebar area (AWindow::Init::DecorationExtended).

Header:#include <AUI/View/ATitlebar.h> CMake:aui_link(my_target PUBLIC aui::views)

docs.title: Detailed Description
docs.text:
Titlebar is the AUI's equivalent of GtkWindowHandle + AdwHeaderBar. It lays out as Horizontal { window controls (start), contents (expanding), window controls (end) }. Its height is the maximum of the contents' height and the window controls' height, so making the titlebar higher is as simple as putting a taller view in it.

Titlebar is always a window drag handle: dragging any point under it, except buttons (AButton) and views with .override-title-dragging ASS class, moves the window; double click maximizes/restores it.

setContents(Stacked {
    content,
    Vertical {
        Titlebar { Horizontal { Label { "My app" } } },
        SpacerExpanding {},
    },
});

docs.title: declarative::WindowTitle
docs.text:
Displays the title of the window it is placed in, the way the OS displays it in its own titlebar.

Header:#include <AUI/View/ATitlebar.h> CMake:aui_link(my_target PUBLIC aui::views)

docs.title: Detailed Description
docs.text:
The text is bound to AWindow::title of the window WindowTitle is placed in, so AWindow::setTitle updates both the OS-visible title (taskbar, window switcher) and the title drawn inside the window. There is nothing to keep in sync.

Where the OS can draw the title of a DecorationExtended window itself (see AWindow::hasNativeWindowTitle), it does: WindowTitle placed into declarative::Titlebar is a blank space, and the native title is drawn over it with the system font, color and inactive window look. The native title is shown only while the window's titlebar contains a WindowTitle.

  • macOS: the title is drawn by AppKit, centered over the whole window horizontally (the horizontal position of WindowTitle doesn't matter) and centered vertically in declarative::Titlebar.
  • Linux GTK/adw: the title is a native header bar title. Like in a regular header bar, it is centered over the window while it fits into WindowTitle, and is shifted into WindowTitle otherwise.

Elsewhere (Windows, X11, Extended windows with AUI-drawn controls, Borderless windows) there is no native title to reuse, and WindowTitle is a label drawn by AUI: left-aligned on Windows, centered on Linux. Style it with t<AWindowTitle>() ASS selector. ASS text properties have no effect on the native title.

WindowTitle is expanding horizontally.

Titlebar {} without contents contains WindowTitle. Put WindowTitle explicitly to combine it with other views:

Titlebar {
  Horizontal {
    Icon { ":img/logo.svg" },
    WindowTitle {},
    Button { Label { "Settings" } },
  },
}

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: This document lists a collection of code samples and tutorials designed to help both newcomers and experienced developers with AUI Framework app development. These projects cover diversity of topics, from fundamental views usage through to complete application assembly.

docs.title: Building the Examples
docs.text:
To build these examples, simply clone AUI repository and configure CMake with -DAUI_BUILD_EXAMPLES=TRUE.

CLion VS Code Terminal
  1. Open Settings: Ctrl+Alt+S.
  2. Go to Build, Execution, Deployment > CMake.
  3. Add -DAUI_BUILD_EXAMPLES=TRUE to CMake options.

  1. Open Settings: Ctrl+,.
  2. Search for CMake Configure Args.
  3. Press button Add item
  4. Enter -DAUI_BUILD_EXAMPLES=TRUE.

git clone https://github.com/aui-framework/aui
cd aui
mkdir build
cd build
cmake .. -DAUI_BUILD_EXAMPLES=TRUE -GNinja
cmake --build . --parallel
cd bin

# launch any program
./aui.example.views

Some of these examples are located outside AUI's build tree; such examples should be compiled as regular CMake projects.

docs.title: App
docs.text:
These examples typically go beyond single-file projects and delve into more substantial applications that showcase how multiple techniques can be integrated to create nearly production-ready applications. Each example not only demonstrates specific features of the AUI Framework but also covers practical aspects such as dependency management, data binding and user interface customization.

Name Description Minesweeper Game Minesweeper game implementation driven by ass. App Template ⚡ GitHub-hosted app project with CI/CD building, testing, releasing, auto updating, code quality checking and more. AUI Telegram Client (AUIgram) Using AUI Framework from perspective of a Telegram client. This project shows how to solve typical problems of a UI application (i.e., dependency management, data binding, styling, asynchronous data loading, packaging, deploying). Fractal Example Fractal viewer application demonstrating usage of custom shaders. Game of Life Game of Life implementation that uses advanced large dynamic data rendering techniques such as ITexture, AImage to be GPU friendly. The computation is performed in AThreadPool. docs.text:
When choosing a font rendering mode, consider:

docs.title: Forking AUI
docs.text:
It's a common scenario when you want to fork AUI's repository. Reasons might include:

  1. Zero trust policy. Of course, we value our reputation, but it's completely okay you might want to mitigate security risks by obtaining full control of the code that appears in your project.
  2. AUI development. You want to improve AUI or make your own version of AUI in your project.

This page describes how to do so.

You can fork AUI to whatever source hosting provider you want, but in general, it's recommended to fork AUI on GitHub:

  1. AUI's original infrastructure setup is on GitHub already. You'll benefit from complete build, docs gen and testing pipelines without asking your devops to support them on your behalf.

Additionally, you won't lose Prebuilt packages "AUI.Boot's precompiled binaries" feature by publishing your fork on GitHub and enabling GitHub Actions (AUI's license does not obligate you to publish byproducts, e.g., compiled binaries or documentation). 2. As soon as you publish your project with modified version of AUI, you'll need to publish changes to AUI anyway (a requirement of MPL2).

docs.title: Steps
docs.text:
1. Mirror/clone/fork AUI's repo from https://github.com/aui-framework/aui.
  2. If you follow zero trust policy, you will need to fork all AUI's dependencies to your controlled zone as well. You can search them by auib_import keyword. Once discovered, fork the dependencies and update URLs in your AUI repo accordingly.
  3. (Optionally) update URLs in .github directory in your AUI repo or make adjustments that suit your particular project needs.
  4. Don't forget to update URL to AUI.Boot and auib_import boilerplate in your project.

Once done, you don't depend on 3rd parties anymore. It is now up to you when and how change AUI's code.

//

//

#include "FractalView.h"
#include "AUI/Render/IRenderer.h"
#include <glm/gtc/matrix_transform.hpp>

static gl::Program::Uniform UNIFORM_TR("tr");
static gl::Program::Uniform UNIFORM_SQ("sq");
static gl::Program::Uniform UNIFORM_RATIO("ratio");
static gl::Program::Uniform UNIFORM_ITERATIONS("iterations");

FractalView::FractalView() : mTransform(1.f) {
    setExpanding();
    mShader.load(R"(
#version 330 core

in vec4 pos;
in vec2 uv;
out vec2 pass_uv;
uniform float ratio;
uniform mat4 SL_uniform_transform;

void main() {
    gl_Position = SL_uniform_transform * pos;
    pass_uv = (uv - 0.5) * 2.0;
    pass_uv.x *= ratio;
}
)",
    R"(
#version 330 core

in vec2 pass_uv;

#define product(a, b) vec2(a.x*b.x-a.y*b.y, a.x*b.y+a.y*b.x)
#define conjugate(a) vec2(a.x,-a.y)
#define divide(a, b) vec2(((a.x*b.x+a.y*b.y)/(b.x*b.x+b.y*b.y)),((a.y*b.x-a.x*b.y)/(b.x*b.x+b.y*b.y)))

uniform float c;
uniform int iterations;
uniform mat4 tr;
uniform sampler2D tex;

out vec4 color;

void main() {
    vec2 tmp_pass_uv = (tr * vec4(pass_uv, 0.0, 1.0)).xy;
    vec2 v = vec2(0, 0);
    int i = 0;
    for (; i < iterations; ++i) {
        v = product(v, v) + tmp_pass_uv;
        vec2 tmp = v * v;
        if ((v.x + v.y) > 4) {
            break;
        }
    }
    if (i == iterations) {
        color = vec4(0, 0, 0, 1);
    } else {
        float theta = float(i) / float(iterations);
        color = texture(tex, vec2(theta, 0));
    }
}
)", { "pos", "uv" }, gl::GLSLOptions { .custom = true });
    mShader.compile();
    mShader.use();
    mShader.set(UNIFORM_TR, mTransform);
    mShader.set(UNIFORM_SQ, 1.f);

    mTexture = _new<gl::Texture2D>();
    mTexture->tex2D(*AImage::fromUrl(":img/color_scheme_wikipedia.png"));
}

void FractalView::render(ARenderContext context) {
    AView::render(context);

    mShader.use();
    mTexture->bind();
    context.render.rectangle(ACustomShaderBrush {}, { 0, 0 }, getSize());
}

void FractalView::onLayout(glm::ivec2 size) {
    AView::onLayout(size);
    mShader.use();
    mShader.set(UNIFORM_RATIO, mAspectRatio = float(size.x) / float(size.y));
}

void FractalView::setIterations(unsigned it) {
    mShader.use();
    mShader.set(UNIFORM_ITERATIONS, int(it));
}

void FractalView::onScroll(const AScrollEvent& event) {
    AView::onScroll(event);
    auto projectedPos = (glm::dvec2(event.origin) / glm::dvec2(getSize()) - glm::dvec2(0.5)) * 2.0;
    projectedPos.x *= mAspectRatio;
    mTransform = glm::translate(mTransform, glm::vec3 { projectedPos, 0.0 });
    mTransform = glm::scale(mTransform, glm::vec3(1.0 - event.delta.y / 1000.0));
    mTransform = glm::translate(mTransform, -glm::vec3 { projectedPos, 0.0 });

    handleMatrixUpdated();

    redraw();
}

void FractalView::reset() {
    mTransform = glm::dmat4(1.0);
    handleMatrixUpdated();
    redraw();
}

void FractalView::handleMatrixUpdated() {
    mShader.use();
    mShader.set(UNIFORM_TR, mTransform);
    emit centerPosChanged(getPlotPosition(), getPlotScale());
}

/// [key_handling]
void FractalView::onKeyDown(AInput::Key key) {
    AView::onKeyDown(key);
    onKeyRepeat(key);
}

void FractalView::onKeyRepeat(AInput::Key key) {
    AView::onKeyRepeat(key);
    constexpr float SPEED = 0.2f;
    switch (key) {
        case AInput::UP:
            mTransform = glm::translate(mTransform, { 0, -SPEED, 0 });
            break;
        case AInput::DOWN:
            mTransform = glm::translate(mTransform, { 0, SPEED, 0 });
            break;
        case AInput::LEFT:
            mTransform = glm::translate(mTransform, { -SPEED, 0, 0 });
            break;
        case AInput::RIGHT:
            mTransform = glm::translate(mTransform, { SPEED, 0, 0 });
            break;
        case AInput::PAGEDOWN:
            mTransform = glm::scale(mTransform, glm::vec3 { 0.99 });
            break;
        case AInput::PAGEUP:
            mTransform = glm::scale(mTransform, glm::vec3 { 1.01 });
            break;

        default:
            return;
    }
    handleMatrixUpdated();
}
/// [key_handling]

glm::dvec2 FractalView::getPlotPosition() const { return glm::dvec2(mTransform[3]); }

double FractalView::getPlotScale() const { return mTransform[0][0]; }

void FractalView::setPlotPositionAndScale(glm::dvec2 position, double scale) {
    mTransform = glm::dmat4(scale);
    mTransform[3] = glm::dvec4 { position, 0, 1 };
    handleMatrixUpdated();
}

docs.title: Game of Life
docs.text:
Example's page

This page describes an example listed in the app category.

Game of Life implementation that uses advanced large dynamic data rendering techniques such as ITexture, AImage to be GPU friendly. The computation is performed in AThreadPool.

Conway's Game of Life, a cellular automaton devised by the mathematician John Conway. The game consists of a grid where each cell can be either alive or dead, and its state evolves over time according to simple rules based on the states of adjacent cells.

Every cell interacts with its eight neighbours, which are the cells that are horizontally, vertically, or diagonally adjacent. At each step in time, the following transitions occur:

  • Any live cell with fewer than two live neighbours dies, as if by underpopulation.
  • Any live cell with two or three live neighbours lives on to the next generation.
  • Any live cell with more than three live neighbours dies, as if by overpopulation.
  • Any dead cell with exactly three live neighbours becomes a live cell, as if by reproduction.

Wikipedia

Represents the grid of cells with their states (CellState::ALIVE or CellState::DEAD). It has methods for initialization and randomization, as well as accessors to get the size and state of individual cells.

Computations are handled asynchronously by an AThreadPool, improving performance during state transitions or rule computations in large grids.

#include <range/v3/all.hpp>

#include <AUI/Platform/AWindow.h>
#include <AUI/Platform/Entry.h>
#include <AUI/Util/UIBuildingHelpers.h>
#include <AUI/View/AButton.h>
#include <AUI/View/AScrollArea.h>
#include <AUI/View/ATextArea.h>

using namespace declarative;
using namespace ass;
using namespace std::chrono_literals;

enum class CellState : std::uint8_t {
    DEAD,
    ALIVE,
};

constexpr CellState operator!(CellState s) {
    return s == CellState::ALIVE ? CellState::DEAD : CellState::ALIVE;
}

using CellsImage = AFormattedImage<APixelFormat::RGBA_BYTE>;

class Cells : public AObject {
public:
    Cells(glm::ivec2 size) {
        mSize = size;
        for (auto s : { &mStorage, &mNextPopulation }) {
            s->resize(size.x * size.y);
        }

        connect(mTimer->fired, me::frame);
        connect(isRunning.changed, AUI_SLOT(mTimer)::setRunning);
    }

    void frame() {
        mFrame = AThreadPool::global() * [&] {
            for (int y = 0; y < mSize.y; ++y) {
                for (int x = 0; x < mSize.x; ++x) {
                    glm::ivec2 i { x, y };
                    get(mNextPopulation, i) = [&] {
                        auto around = cellsAround(i);
                        switch (around) {
                            default:
                                return CellState::DEAD;
                            case 2:
                                return get(mStorage, i);
                            case 3:
                                return CellState::ALIVE;
                        }
                    }();
                }
            }
            std::swap(mStorage, mNextPopulation);

            emit frameComplete;
        };
    }

    [[nodiscard]] glm::ivec2 size() const noexcept { return mSize; }

    [[nodiscard]] const AVector<CellState>& storage() const noexcept { return mStorage; }

    [[nodiscard]] CellState& operator[](glm::ivec2 position) { return get(mStorage, position); }

    void randomize() {
        ranges::generate(mStorage, [&] {
            static std::default_random_engine re;
            static std::uniform_int_distribution d(0, 10);
            return d(re) > 7 ? CellState::ALIVE : CellState::DEAD;
        });
        emit frameComplete;
    }

    AProperty<bool> isRunning = false;
    emits<> frameComplete;

private:
    _<ATimer> mTimer = _new<ATimer>(100ms);
    AFuture<> mFrame;
    glm::ivec2 mSize {};
    AVector<CellState> mStorage;
    AVector<CellState> mNextPopulation;

    CellState& get(AVector<CellState>& storage, glm::ivec2 position) {
        position %= mSize;
        if (position.x < 0) {
            position.x = mSize.x + position.x;
        }
        if (position.y < 0) {
            position.y = mSize.y + position.y;
        }
        return storage[position.y * mSize.x + position.x];
    }

    unsigned cellsAround(glm::ivec2 position) {
        unsigned accumulator = 0;
        for (int y = -1; y <= 1; ++y) {
            for (int x = -1; x <= 1; ++x) {
                if (x == 0 && y == 0) {
                    continue;
                }
                accumulator += get(mStorage, position + glm::ivec2 { x, y }) == CellState::ALIVE ? 1 : 0;
            }
        }
        return accumulator;
    }
}; /// end

class CellsView : public AView {
public:
    static constexpr auto SCALE = 8_dp;

    CellsView(_<Cells> cells) : mCells(std::move(cells)) { connect(mCells->frameComplete, me::updateTexture); }

    void render(ARenderContext ctx) override {
        AView::render(ctx);
        if (mTexture) {
            ctx.render.rectangle(ATexturedBrush { mTexture }, { 0, 0 }, float(SCALE) * glm::vec2(mCells->size()));
        }
        auto drawGrid = [&] {
            ASmallVector<std::pair<glm::vec2, glm::vec2>, 128 * 2> points;
            for (int i = 1; i < mCells->size().x; ++i) {
                points << std::make_pair(glm::vec2(i * SCALE, 0.f), glm::vec2(i * SCALE, getSize().y));
            }
            for (int i = 1; i < mCells->size().y; ++i) {
                points << std::make_pair(glm::vec2(0.f, i * SCALE), glm::vec2(getSize().x, i * SCALE));
            }
            ctx.render.lines(ASolidBrush { AColor::GRAY }, points);
        };
        drawGrid();
    }

    void onPointerPressed(const APointerPressedEvent& event) override {
        AView::onPointerPressed(event);
        glm::ivec2 position = glm::ivec2(event.position / float(SCALE));
        (*mCells)[position] = !(*mCells)[position];
        updateTexture();
    }

    glm::ivec2 onIntrinsicMeasure(AConstraints constraints) override {
      return mCells->size() * int(SCALE);
    }

private:
    _<Cells> mCells;
    _<ITexture> mTexture;

    void updateTexture() {
        if (!mTexture) {
            mTexture = ASurface::current()->getRenderingContext()->renderer().getNewTexture();
        }

        CellsImage image(mCells->size());
        for (unsigned y = 0; y < image.height(); ++y) {
            for (unsigned x = 0; x < image.width(); ++x) {
                image.set(
                    { x, y },
                    AFormattedColorConverter(
                        (*mCells)[glm::ivec2(x, y)] == CellState::ALIVE
                            ? AColor::WHITE
                            : AColor::TRANSPARENT_BLACK));
            }
        }
        mTexture->setImage(image);
        redraw();
    }
}; /// end

class GameOfLifeWindow : public AWindow {
public:
    GameOfLifeWindow() : AWindow("Game of Life") {
        setContents(Vertical {
          Centered {
            Horizontal {
              _new<AButton>("Randomize") AUI_LET {
                      connect(it->clicked, AUI_SLOT(mCells)::randomize);
                  },
              _new<AButton>() AUI_LET {
                      it & mCells.isRunning > [](AButton& b, bool isRunning) {
                          b.setText(isRunning ? "Pause" : "Run");
                      };
                      connect(it->clicked, [&] { mCells.isRunning = !mCells.isRunning; });
                  },
            } AUI_OVERRIDE_STYLE { LayoutSpacing { 4_dp } },
          },
          Centered {
            _new<CellsView>(aui::ptr::fake_shared(&mCells)) AUI_OVERRIDE_STYLE {
                  Expanding(),
                  BackgroundSolid(AColor::BLACK),
                },
          },
        } AUI_OVERRIDE_STYLE { LayoutSpacing { 4_dp } });
    }

private:
    Cells mCells { { 64, 64 } };
}; /// end

AUI_ENTRY {
    auto w = _new<GameOfLifeWindow>();
    w->pack();
    w->show();
    return 0;
}

Windows macOS Ubuntu Fedora

Install Windows updates

You may want to ignore this, but in case of errors, please ensure you have installed Windows updates.

Install MSVC compiler

CLion comes with MinGW by default. It works okayish, but we recommend using de-facto standard compiler for Windows instead.

VS Code does not come with any compiler by default.

You are not forced to use Visual Studio IDE, you can use whatever IDE you want. We just want the compiler part.

Visual Studio Community edition is sufficient.

Install msvc or clang, if you haven't already, and reboot.

Press Win, type Visual Studio Installer and launch.

Choose Individual components tab.

Search and select the following components:

  1. Windows Universal C Runtime
  2. MSVC v142 or newer
  3. Windows 10 SDK or newer
  4. Windows Universal CRT SDK

Click Install.

Don't forget to reboot!

Configure CLion to use MSVC compiler instead of MinGW

While you can use MinGW for your AUI project, it is recommended to use commonly accepted compiler for Windows.

If you use VS Code, it will pick up the correct compiler automatically.

If you use CLion:

  1. Ctrl+Alt+S, navigate to "Build, Execution, Deployment" > "Toolchains".
  2. Press +.
  3. Choose Visual Studio. CLion should pick up it automatically.

  1. Select Visual Studio.
  2. Press "arrow up" button to raise priority. Visual Studio compiler should be by default!
  3. Press OK.

Install Xcode.

sudo apt update
sudo apt install pkg-config libglew-dev zlib1g-dev libssl-dev libcurl4-openssl-dev libgtk-3-dev libdbus-1-dev libfontconfig-dev ninja-build libpulse-dev git cmake g++

docs.text:
AUI does not provide "traditional" installation methods that involve manual downloading and deploying; instead, package managers are used to ensure easily reproducible builds. They compile and link all required dependencies automatically to free you from dependency management and focus you right to development of your application.

AUI App TemplateManual Setup CMakeXMake

You can use our App Template ⚡ to set up a new project quickly with AUI's .clang-format, Github Actions and other features out-of-the-box. The template is based on CMake and aui.boot.

Clone https://github.com/aui-framework/example_app with your IDE or via terminal:

git clone https://github.com/aui-framework/example_app

and open that directory in your IDE.

Recommended: Create a new repo

From App Template ⚡ repository, you can generate a completely separate repo with clean git history:

  1. Open http://github.com/aui-framework/example_app
  2. Click Create a new repository.

  1. Clone your own repo into IDE.

A full-fledged XMake-based app template is available at github.com/aui-framework/xmake_example_app. It comes pre-configured with GitHub Actions CI/CD, .clang-format, .clang-tidy, Valgrind suppression, auto-updating (Windows), and a ready-to-run AUI window — everything you need to start shipping an app.

AUI version support

The XMake app template currently targets AUI v7.1.2. Newer versions of AUI (v8.x and above) are not yet supported. Track progress in the xmake_example_app repository.

Recommended: Create a new repo from the template
  1. Open https://github.com/aui-framework/xmake_example_app

  2. Click Use this template → Create a new repository.

  3. Clone your new repo and open it in your IDE.

The template includes the following GitHub Actions workflows:

  • Build — triggered on push and pull_request. Builds for all supported platforms, runs tests, generates installable packages, and prepares a GitHub Release draft.
  • Code Quality — triggered on pull_request. Runs clang-tidy static analysis and valgrind dynamic analysis on tests.

To create a release, bump the version in CMakeLists.txt and push — the pipeline creates a GitHub Release draft for you automatically.

AUI provides support to several package managers, to choose at your own.

AUI BootCPMXMake

aui.boot is *official* way of using AUI. It is a CMake-based package manager that requires nothing but CMake.

Download AUI.Boot (one-time):

curl https://raw.githubusercontent.com/aui-framework/aui/refs/heads/master/aui.boot.cmake -o aui.boot.cmake

Create CMakeLists.txt:

CMakeLists.txt
# Standard routine
cmake_minimum_required(VERSION 3.16)
project(project_template)

# Use AUI.Boot
include(aui.boot.cmake)

# import AUI
auib_import(
    aui https://github.com/aui-framework/aui 
    COMPONENTS core views
    VERSION v8.0.0-rc.8
    )


# Create the executable. This function automatically links all sources from the src/ folder, creates CMake target and
# places the resulting executable to bin/ folder.
aui_executable(project_template)

# Link required libs
aui_link(project_template PRIVATE aui::core aui::views)

CMake's missing package manager is a small CMake script for setup-free, cross-platform, reproducible dependency management.

Download CPM to your project directory:

mkdir -p cmake
wget -O cmake/CPM.cmake https://github.com/cpm-cmake/CPM.cmake/releases/latest/download/get_cpm.cmake

Then, create a CMakeLists.txt:

CMakeLists.txt
# Standard routine
cmake_minimum_required(VERSION 3.16)
project(project_template)

# import AUI
include(cmake/CPM.cmake)
CPMAddPackage("gh:aui-framework/aui#v7.1.2")

# Create the executable. This function automatically links all sources from the src/ folder, creates CMake target and
# places the resulting executable to bin/ folder.
aui_executable(project_template)

# Link required libs
aui_link(project_template PRIVATE aui::core aui::views)

XMake is a lightweight, cross-platform build utility with built-in package management. It requires no external package manager — AUI is fetched and compiled automatically from xmake-repo.

AUI version support

XMake package support currently targets AUI v7.1.2. Newer versions (v8.x and above) are not yet available in xmake-repo. If you need the latest AUI, use AUI Boot or CPM instead.

Install XMake

Windows macOS Ubuntu / Debian Fedora / RHEL

Install via winget (recommended):

winget install xmake

Or download the installer from xmake.io and run it.

Note

After installation, reopen your terminal so that xmake is available on the PATH.

Install via Homebrew:

brew install xmake

curl -fsSL https://xmake.io/shget.text | bash

Or install via apt (may be an older version):

sudo add-apt-repository ppa:xmake-io/xmake
sudo apt update
sudo apt install xmake

curl -fsSL https://xmake.io/shget.text | bash

Verify the installation:

xmake --version

Create xmake.lua

Create the following xmake.lua in your project root:

xmake.lua
-- Specify available build configurations
add_rules("mode.release", "mode.debug")

-- Output compile_commands.json for clangd / VS Code IntelliSense
add_rules("plugin.compile_commands.autoupdate", {outputdir = ".vscode", lsp = "clangd"})

-- AUI requires C++20
set_languages("c++20")

-- Fetch AUI v7.1.2 from xmake-repo (latest version supported via XMake)
add_requires("aui v7.1.2")

-- Define the executable target
target("project_template")
    -- Collect all .cpp files from the src/ directory
    add_files("src/*.cpp")
    add_includedirs("src")
    -- Link AUI with only the components you need
    add_packages("aui", {components = {"core", "image", "views", "xml"}})
    -- Group AUI components into link groups to resolve circular dependencies
    add_linkgroups("aui.views", "aui.xml", "aui.image", "aui.core", {whole = true})

Create src/ directory and entry point

XMake picks up all .cpp files from src/ automatically. Create at minimum:

src/main.cpp
#include <AUI/Platform/Entry.h>
#include <AUI/Platform/AWindow.h>

AUI_ENTRY {
    _new<AWindow>("Hello AUI", 300_dp, 200_dp)->show();
    return 0;
}

Build and run

xmake          # configure dependencies and build
xmake run      # run the resulting executable

On the first run, XMake will download and compile AUI and all its dependencies. This may take a few minutes. Subsequent builds are incremental and fast.

Switching between Debug and Release 
xmake f -m debug    # switch to debug configuration
xmake               # rebuild
xmake f -m release  # switch back to release
xmake
VS Code integration

The plugin.compile_commands.autoupdate rule in xmake.lua automatically generates .vscode/compile_commands.json on every build. This enables full IntelliSense and code navigation in VS Code via the vscode-clangd extension — no additional configuration needed.

See Minimal UI Template XMake for a full ready-to-use example with MainWindow.

aui_executable hooks all CPP files from src/ directory. You need to create src/ directory and a CPP file in it.

src/main.cpp
/*
 * AUI Framework - Declarative UI toolkit for modern C++20
 * Copyright (C) 2020-2025 Alex2772 and Contributors
 *
 * SPDX-License-Identifier: MPL-2.0
 *
 * This Source Code Form is subject to the terms of the Mozilla Public
 * License, v. 2.0. If a copy of the MPL was not distributed with this
 * file, You can obtain one at http://mozilla.org/MPL/2.0/.
 */

/// [AButton_example]
#include <AUI/Platform/Entry.h>
#include <AUI/Platform/AWindow.h>
#include <AUI/Util/UIBuildingHelpers.h>
#include <AUI/View/AButton.h>

using namespace ass;
using namespace declarative;

AUI_ENTRY {
    auto window = _new<AWindow>("Button", 600_dp, 300_dp);
    window->setContents(Centered {
      Button {
        .content = Label { "Click me" },
        .onClick = [] { ALogger::info("Test") << "Hello world!"; },
      },
    });
    window->show();
    return 0;
}
/// [AButton_example]

Why CMake or IDE doesn't recognize a new CPP file?

This indicates that the IDE's build system needs to be initialized or refreshed.

Reload CMake project to hook up a newly added CPP file:

CLion VS Code Terminal

File > Reload CMake Project or right-click on CMakeLists.txt > Load/Reload CMake project.

  1. Please make sure you have followed setup procedure listed in the beginning on this page.
  2. F1 >CMake: Configure. If it asks for a toolchain, choose Unspecified.
cmake -S . -B build

  3. Right click on project's target > Set Build target and Set Launch/Debug target.
  4. F1 >CMake: Debug.

gl::Texture2DArray
docs.text:
Represents a 2D texture array.

Header:#include <AUI/GL/Texture2DArray.h> CMake:aui_link(my_target PUBLIC aui::views)

docs.title: Detailed Description
docs.text:
A 2D texture array is a texture that contains multiple 2D textures, each accessible by its index. It's useful for storing and accessing multiple textures with the same dimensions.

After creating a 2D texture array, you can use update to update a single texture in the array. You cannot update dimensions of the texture array, so you should create a new one if you want to change the size of the texture array.

docs.title: Public Methods
docs.text:
Texture2DArray::Texture2DArray(glm::uvec2 textureSize, unsigned textureCount)

Initializes the 2D texture array with empty data.

Arguments textureSize The size of the 2D texture (width and height). textureCount The number of layers in the texture array.

This function allocates storage for a 2D texture array with the specified size and texture count. It binds the texture and uses glTexStorage3D to allocate the storage.

void Texture2DArray::update(unsigned texture, AImageView image)

Updates a single texture of the 2D texture array.

Arguments texture The index of the texture to be updated. image The image to be used as the new texture.

This function binds the texture and uploads the provided image as a texture in the 2D texture array. It uses glTexSubImage3D to update the texture.

This function expects the image to have the same size as the texture size initialized earlier, otherwise, an assertion error is thrown.

docs.title: IAudioPlayer
docs.text:
Interface for audio playback.

Header:#include <AUI/Audio/IAudioPlayer.h> CMake:aui_link(my_target PUBLIC aui::audio)

docs.title: Detailed Description
docs.text:
Experimental Feature

This API is experimental. Experimental APIs are likely to contain bugs, might be changed or removed in the future.

One IAudioPlayer plays one sound. Create it with IAudioPlayer::fromUrl or IAudioPlayer::fromStream; the returned object is backed by the native audio API of the current platform.

auto player = IAudioPlayer::fromUrl(":sound/click.ogg");
player->setVolume(128);
player->play();

Playback state is changed with play, pause and stop. Use setLoop to repeat the sound and setVolume to change the volume (0 to 256, 256 is the original volume). The finished signal is emitted when the sound ends.

Several players can play simultaneously; their output is mixed by AAudioMixer.

See Playing sounds and Custom sound sources for more.

Warning

A player created from a stream can't be restarted after it has ended or has been stopped, and can't loop: restarting requires reopening the source, which is only possible when the player knows the url. Create a new player instead, or use fromUrl.

docs.title: IInspectable
docs.text:
Interface for objects that can expose debug inspector information.

Header:#include <AUI/Util/IInspectable.h> CMake:aui_link(my_target PUBLIC aui::views)

docs.title: Detailed Description
docs.text:
Analogue to Jetpack Compose's debugInspectorInfo. Objects implementing this interface expose a set of named properties describing their state to debugging/inspection tooling (e.g. devtools, ViewPropertiesView).

Properties are stored as an ordered sequence of name-value pairs, preserving insertion order (as Compose's properties does). Each property value is an AInspectable, which carries the original typed value and knows how to render itself both as a plain string (CLI / agentic AI profiler) and as a rich view (GUI devtools).

To add inspector support for a custom type, either ensure fmt::formatter<T> is available (the default AInspectableValue<T> will use it automatically), or specialise AInspectableValue<T> to override renderAsView() / renderAsString().

docs.title: Adding a custom image format
docs.text: AUI decodes images through IImageLoaders kept in the AImageLoaderRegistry. To support a format that is not built in, implement the interface and register it once at startup.

docs.title: Raster formats
docs.text:
A raster loader implements two methods: matches, which looks at the first bytes of the file, and getRasterImage, which decodes it.

class QoiImageLoader : public IImageLoader {
public:
    bool matches(AByteBufferView buffer) override {
        return buffer.size() >= 4 && std::memcmp(buffer.data(), "qoif", 4) == 0;
    }

    _<AImage> getRasterImage(AByteBufferView buffer) override {
        glm::uvec2 size = readQoiSize(buffer);
        auto image = _new<AImage>(size, APixelFormat::RGBA_BYTE);
        decodeQoi(buffer, image->modifiableBuffer());
        return image;
    }
};

(readQoiSize and decodeQoi stand for your decoder.) modifiableBuffer() gives direct access to the pixel storage of the freshly created AImage.

Register the loader before the first image is loaded, e.g., at the start of AUI_ENTRY:

AImageLoaderRegistry::inst().registerRasterLoader(_new<QoiImageLoader>(), "qoi");

The name is used by supportedFormats() only. After that, AImage::fromUrl and IDrawable::fromUrl handle .qoi files like any other.

docs.title: Vector and animated formats
docs.text:
Formats that are rasterized on demand (svg) or change over time (gif) return an IImageFactory from getImageFactory and are registered with registerVectorLoader or registerAnimatedLoader. The factory's provideImage(size) renders the image at the requested size. Animated factories derive from IAnimatedImageFactory and also report hasAnimationFinished(); isNewImageAvailable() tells the drawable whether the next frame is ready.

Note

AImage::fromUrl uses raster loaders only. Vector and animated loaders serve drawables.

docs.title: Order matters
docs.text:
The registry asks the loaders in registration order and takes the first one whose matches returns true, so make matches strict enough not to steal other formats' files.

Exceptions thrown from a loader are swallowed by the registry, and the next loader is tried; a loader returning nullptr is skipped the same way.

docs.title: Loading images
docs.text: This page describes how to decode image files into AImage. To work with the pixels afterwards, see Processing images. To display an image in a view, use drawables (IDrawable::fromUrl) rather than AImage; both share the same loaders.

docs.title: From a url, file or buffer
docs.text:
AImage::fromUrl accepts any AUrl, including file:// urls and builtin assets (:img/icon.png, see AUI Assets).

auto image = AImage::fromUrl(":target.bmp");

ASSERT_TRUE(image != nullptr);
ASSERT_EQ(image->width(), 16);
ASSERT_EQ(image->height(), 16);

AImage::fromFile takes an APath, and AImage::fromBuffer decodes a file that is already in memory (for example, downloaded by curl or received from a socket).

auto fromDisk = AImage::fromFile("photo.jpg");
auto fromMemory = AImage::fromBuffer(downloadedBytes);

The format is detected by the file contents, not by the extension.

docs.title: Handling errors
docs.text:
All three return _<AImage>. On failure (file not found, unknown or corrupted format) they log the reason with ALogger and return nullptr instead of throwing. Always check the result:

if (auto image = AImage::fromFile(path)) {
    ALogger::info("Image") << "Loaded " << image->width() << "x" << image->height();
} else {
    // show an error to the user
}

Note

fromUrl reads the whole stream into memory, up to 256 MiB.

docs.title: Supported formats
docs.text:
Out of the box: bmp, png, jpg and webp. AImage only decodes raster formats. Vector (svg) and animated (gif, animated webp) files are intended for drawables, which rasterize them at the size required.

The list of registered formats is available at runtime:

for (const auto& format : AImageLoaderRegistry::inst().supportedFormats()) {
    ALogger::info("Image") << format;
}

Support for another format can be added with a custom loader, see Adding a custom image format.

docs.title: Processing images
docs.text: This page covers reading and modifying pixels with AImage and AImageView. For getting an image from a file, see Loading images.

docs.title: Creating an image
docs.text:
An image is a size, a pixel format (APixelFormat) and a buffer. The simplest way to make one is to specify the size and format; the pixels are allocated by AImage.

AImage canvas({256, 256}, APixelFormat::RGBA_BYTE);
canvas.fill(0x202020_rgb);
canvas.set({10, 20}, 0xff0000_rgb);

fill and set accept a universal AColor, which is converted to the image's format automatically. You can also construct an image from an existing AByteBuffer of pixels: AImage(buffer, size, format).

docs.title: Reading pixels
docs.text:
get returns an AColor regardless of the actual format:

AColor color = canvas.get({10, 20});
AColor average = canvas.averageColor();

Positions outside of the image are an assertion failure in debug builds and undefined behaviour in release.

docs.title: Fast per-pixel access
docs.text:
get/set have to dispatch on the format at each call. In hot loops use visit: it resolves the format once and calls your lambda with a statically typed image whose Color is a concrete struct (r, g, b, a members) and which can be iterated with begin()/end().

canvas.visit([](auto& image) {
    for (auto& pixel : image) {
        pixel.r /= 2; // halve the red component
    }
});

The lambda is instantiated for every supported layout (R, RG, RGB, RGBA, ARGB, BGRA, each as bytes or floats), so it must compile for all of them: r always exists, but g, b and a do not. Use if constexpr or restrict the format with convert (below).

docs.title: Converting the pixel format
docs.text:
If your code works with one format only, ask for it. convert<format> passes the image to the callback as is when it already has this format, and converts a temporary copy otherwise:

image->convert<APixelFormat::RGBA_BYTE>([](const AFormattedImageView<APixelFormat::RGBA_BYTE>& rgba) {
    for (const auto& pixel : rgba) {
        // pixel.r, pixel.g, pixel.b and pixel.a are bytes
    }
});

When the format is known only at runtime, image->convert(APixelFormat::RGB_BYTE) returns a new AImage.

Conversion to a format without an alpha channel drops it; conversion in the other direction sets alpha to fully opaque.

docs.title: Cropping, resizing, mirroring
docs.text:
These return a new image and leave the original intact:

AImage part = image->cropped({16, 16}, {32, 32});    // position, size
AImage small = image->resizedLinearDownscale({64, 64});
AImage flipped = image->mirroredVertically();

mirrorVertically() flips an AImage in place. resizedLinearDownscale is meant for shrinking: it uses bilinear sampling without prefiltering, so large reductions can look aliased.

docs.title: Composing images
docs.text:
insert copies another image (converting the format if necessary) into this one at the given position. Parts that do not fit are clipped.

AImage atlas({512, 512}, APixelFormat::RGBA_BYTE);
atlas.fill(0x00000000_argb);
atlas.insert({0, 0}, *icon1);
atlas.insert({64, 0}, *icon2);

insert overwrites pixels, it does not blend alpha.

docs.title: Views over foreign memory
docs.text:
AImageView looks at pixels owned by someone else, without copying. It optionally takes a stride (bytes per row), which makes it possible to view a part of a larger buffer.

APixelFormat pf = APixelFormat::RGBA_BYTE;
std::vector<uint8_t> some_bytes(100 * 100 * pf.bytesPerPixel());
AByteBufferView data(reinterpret_cast<const char*>(some_bytes.data()), some_bytes.size());

AImageView view_big(data, 100 * pf.bytesPerPixel(), {100, 100}, pf);
AImageView view_small(data, 100 * pf.bytesPerPixel(), {50, 50}, pf);

ASSERT_EQ(view_big.get({40, 40}), view_small.get({40, 40}));

Here view_small reads a 50x50 region of the same 100x100 buffer. An AImage converts to an AImageView implicitly.

docs.title: Infinite Lazy List
docs.text:
Example's page

This page describes an example listed in the ui category.

Usage of AUI_DECLARATIVE_FOR to make an infinite lazy list.

This example demonstrates making an optimal infinite list. That is, when you infinitely scroll down to load new items, the older items are unloaded from memory.

The "loading" action is performed on a worker thread and a delay is simulated by AThread::sleep.

As a bonus, we've added a spinner to indicate that loading is in progress.

In this example, we've used functional style and decomposition technique instead of making custom view classes. The idea is hide the implementation specifics of myLazyList that makes a basic AView in return. The overall state of produced lazy list object is controlled by list model.

myLazyList is limited to specific type of model by intention. AUI does not provide some kind of generalization on its own. In fact, we're demonstrating the whole concept in less than 100 lines of code. You certainly can make a generalization that suits your project's needs.

docs.text:
#include <range/v3/all.hpp>

#include <AUI/Platform/Entry.h>
#include "AUI/Platform/AWindow.h"
#include "AUI/Util/UIBuildingHelpers.h"
#include "AUI/View/AScrollArea.h"
#include "AUI/View/ASpinnerV2.h"
#include "AUI/View/AForEachUI.h"
#include "AUI/Model/AListModel.h"
#include "AUI/Thread/AAsyncHolder.h"

using namespace declarative;
using namespace ass;
using namespace std::chrono_literals;

struct Item {
    AProperty<AString> value;
};

struct State {
    AProperty<AVector<_<Item>>> items;
    AProperty<bool> needMore = false;
    AAsyncHolder asyncTasks;
};

_<AView> myLazyList(_<State> state) {
    // note that we observe for transition to true here, not the current state of property
    // see PropertyTest_Observing_changes for more info
    AObject::connect(state->needMore.changed, AObject::GENERIC_OBSERVER, [state](bool newState){
        if (!newState) { // we're interested in transitions to true state only.
            return;
        }
        auto loadFrom = state->items->size(); // base index to load from.
        state->asyncTasks << AUI_THREADPOOL {
            // perform "loading" task on a worker thread.

            AThread::sleep(500ms); // imitate hard work here

            // aka "loaded" from backend storage of some kind
            auto loadedItems = AVector<_<Item>>::generate(20, [&](size_t i) {
                return aui::ptr::manage_shared(new Item { .value = "Item {}"_format(loadFrom + i) });
            });

            AUI_UI_THREAD { // back to main thread.
                state->items.writeScope()->insertAll(loadedItems);
                state->needMore = false;
            };
        };
    });

    return Vertical {
        AUI_DECLARATIVE_FOR(i, *state->items, AVerticalLayout) { return Label{} & i->value; },
        Centered {
          _new<ASpinnerV2>() AUI_LET {
                  AObject::connect(it->redrawn, AObject::GENERIC_OBSERVER, [state] {
                      // when a spinner appears, we indicate that we need more items.
                      state->needMore = true;
                  });
              },
        },
    };
}

AUI_ENTRY {
    auto window = _new<AWindow>("Infinite Lazy List", 200_dp, 300_dp);
    window->setContents(Stacked { AScrollArea::Builder().withContents(myLazyList(_new<State>())) });
    window->show();

    return 0;
}

docs.title: iOS (operating system)
docs.text:
iOS is an operating system developed by Apple, designed for their mobile devices such as iPhone, iPad, and iPod touch. It provides a secure, user-friendly interface to manage apps, files, music, photos, and other content.

Early Access Feature

At the moment, support of iOS in AUI Framework is in early stage and lacks a lot of features.

iOS shares its XNU kernel and codebase with macOS (operating system).

docs.title: Key considerations
docs.text:
• iOS is easier to support than Android (operating system) due to limited number of devices and OS versions
  • You'd need a macOS (operating system) machine to build and run an iOS app
  • smartphones come with high density displays, so you need to use density-independent dimension units such as _dp
  • AApplication::activated (Application lifetime & instancing) is not wired to openURL yet, so it is never emitted on iOS. AApplication::requestSingleInstanceLock always succeeds.

docs.title: Detailed Description
docs.text:
The rendering engine provides graphics rendering capabilities for the AUI Framework's user interface system. It offers both hardware-accelerated (OpenGL) and software-based rendering backends. The engine handles drawing primitives, text rendering, visual effects, and maintains consistent rendering behavior across different platforms and hardware capabilities.

The renderer is shared across windows and manages its own resources such as textures, but each window has its own rendering context.

docs.title: Core Renderer Interface
docs.text:
Category Key Methods Purpose Shape Drawing rectangle(), roundedRectangle(), rectangleBorder() Basic geometric shapes Line Drawing line(), lines(), points() Vector graphics primitives Text Rendering string(), prerenderString(), newMultiStringCanvas() Text output and caching Visual Effects boxShadow(), boxShadowInner(), squareSector() Advanced visual effects State Management setColor(), setTransform(), setBlending() Rendering context control Masking pushMaskBefore(), pushMaskAfter(), popMaskBefore(), popMaskAfter() Stencil-based clipping

The renderer maintains internal state including:

  • Current color multiplier (mColor)
  • Transformation matrix (mTransform)
  • Target window (mWindow)
  • Stencil depth for masking (mStencilDepth)
  • Texture pool for resource management (mTexturePool)

docs.title: HiDPI (High‑DPI) support
docs.text:
The framework uses logical units dp for layout and drawing. All logical values are multiplied by the window pixel ratio before they reach the renderer. The renderer works with physical pixels only (px).

This ensures that the UI appears consistent across displays with varying pixel densities.

virtual void IRenderer::setBlending(Blending blending)

Sets blending mode.

Arguments blending new blending mode

Blending Modes and Effects

The rendering engine supports multiple blending modes for advanced visual effects:

enum class Blending Blending mode.

Terminology used in this documentation:

Source color (S) Source color is a color of the brush (i.e. texture color matching current position) multiplied by the current renderer color, i.e. when drawing a black rectangle onto the white canvas the source color is black. Destination color (D) Destination color is a color of the framebuffer you're drawing to, i.e. when drawing a black rectangle onto the white canvas the destination color is white. S.rgb Source color without the alpha component. S.a Source's alpha component without the color itself. D.rgb Destination color without the alpha component. D.a Destination's alpha component without the color itself. Alpha-based Alpha-based blending mode is a blending mode that uses the alpha component in it's formula. Color-based Color-based blending mode is a blending mode that does not use the alpha component in it's formula. Constant Description Blending::NORMAL Normal blending. Formula S.rgb * S.a + D.rgb * (1 - S.a) Type Alpha-based Behaviour

When S.a is 0, NORMAL does not drawElements anything.

When S.a is 1, NORMAL ignores D. Blending::ADDITIVE Simply sums S and D colors. Formula S.rgb + D.rgb Type Color-based Behaviour

When S is black, ADDITIVE does not drawElements anything.

When S is white, ADDITIVE draws white.

Blending::INVERSE_DST Inverses destination color and multiplies it with the source color. Formula S.rgb * (1 - D.rgb) Type Color-based Behaviour

When S is black, INVERSE_DST does not drawElements anything.

When S is white, INVERSE_DST does full inverse.

Blending::INVERSE_SRC Inverses source color and multiplies it with the destination color. Formula (1 - S.rgb) * D.rgb Type Color-based Behaviour

When S is black, INVERSE_SRC does not drawElements anything.

When S is white, INVERSE_SRC draws black.

docs.title: IXmlEntityVisitor
docs.text:
Visits an xml entity (element).

Header:#include <AUI/Xml/IXmlEntityVisitor.h> CMake:aui_link(my_target PUBLIC aui::xml)

docs.title: Detailed Description
docs.text:
One instance corresponds to one element. The parser calls its methods in document order:

  • visitAttribute for each attribute in the opening tag. An attribute without a value gets an empty string.
  • visitTextEntity for text between tags.
  • visitEntity for each nested element. Return a visitor which will receive the nested element, or nullptr to skip the element along with its contents.

All methods have empty default implementations, so override only what you need.

struct Point: IXmlEntityVisitor {
    int x = 0, y = 0;
    void visitAttribute(const AString& name, AString value) override {
        if (name == "x") x = value.toInt().valueOr(0);
        if (name == "y") y = value.toInt().valueOr(0);
    }
};

See Parsing XML.
