docs.title: Signal-slot
docs.text: Signal-slots is an object messaging mechanism that creates seamless relations between objects.

docs.title: Detailed Description
docs.text:
Signal-slots were originally implemented in Qt and it has proven themselves as an object messaging mechanism making it easy to implement the observer pattern without boilerplate code. Signal-slot tracks object existence on the both ends so destruction of either sender or receiver object breaks the link between them. When the sender or receiver object is destroyed slot execution is never possible even in a multithreaded environment. Almost any signal can be connected to almost any slot (even lambda) by any code.

All classes that inherit from AObject or one of its subclasses (e.g., AView) can contain signals and slots. Signals are emitted by objects when they change their state in a way that may be interesting to other objects. This is all the object does to communicate. It does not know or care whether anything is receiving the signals it emits. This is true information encapsulation, and ensures that the object can be used as a software component.

Signal declarations (emits) are special public fields of any class that inherit from AObject. 

class Counter: public AObject {
public:
  Counter() = default;

  void setValue(int value) {
    mValue = value;
    emit valueChanged;
  }

signals:
  emits<> valueChanged;

private:
  int mValue = 0;
};

They can specify arguments: 

emits<int> valueChanged;
...
emit valueChanged(mValue);

Any member function of a class can be used as a slot.

You can connect as many signals as you want to a single slot, and a signal can be connected to as many slots as you need.

docs.title: Signals
docs.text:
Signals are publicly accessible fields that notify an object's client when its internal state has changed in some way that might be interesting or significant. These signals can be emitted from various locations, but it is generally recommended to only emit them from within the class that defines the signal and its subclasses.

The slots connected to a signal are generaly executed immediately when the signal is emitted like a regular function call. \c emit returns control after all slots are called. If receiver has AObject::setSlotsCallsOnlyOnMyThread set to true and \c emit was called on a different thread, \c emit queues slot execution to the AEventLoop associated with receiver's thread. All AView have this behaviour enabled by default.

docs.title: Slots
docs.text:
A slot is triggered by the emission of a related signal. Slot is no more than a regular class method with a signal connected to it.

When called directly, slots follow standard C++ rules and syntax. However, through a signal-slot connection, any component can invoke a slot regardless of its accessibility level. Visibility scope matters only when creating connection (AObject::connect). This means a signal from one class can call a private slot in another unrelated class if connection is created within class itself (with access to its private/protected methods).

Furthermore, slots can be defined as virtual functions, which have been found to be beneficial in practical application development.

Compared to callbacks, the signals and slots system has some performance overhead due to its increased flexibility. The difference is typically insignificant for real-world applications. In general, emitting a signal connected to various slots can result in an execution time roughly ten times slower than direct function calls. This delay comes from locating the connection object and safely iterating over connections.

The trade-off between the signals and slots mechanism's simplicity and flexibility compared to pure function calls or callbacks is well-justified for most applications, given its minimal performance cost that users won't perceive.

docs.title: Basic example
docs.text:
Let's use \c Counter from our previous example: 

class Counter: public AObject {
public:
  Counter() = default;

  void setValue(int value) {
    mValue = value;
    emit valueChanged(value);
  }

signals:
  emits<int> valueChanged;

private:
  int mValue = 0;
};

class MyApp: public AObject {
public:
  MyApp() {}

  void run() {
    connect(mCounter->valueChanged, this, &MyApp::printCounter);
    mCounter->setValue(123); // prints "New value: 123"
  }

private:
  _<Counter> mCounter = _new<Counter>();

  void printCounter(int value) {
    ALogger::info("MyApp") << value;
  }
};

AUI_ENTRY {
  auto app = _new<MyApp>();
  app->run();
  return 0;
}

If connect(mCounter->valueChanged, this, &MyApp::printCounter); looks too long for you, you can use AUI_SLOT macro: 

connect(mCounter->valueChanged, AUI_SLOT(this)::printCounter);

Furthermore, when connecting to this, AUI_SLOT(this) can be replaced with me: 

connect(mCounter->valueChanged, me::printCounter);

Lambda can be used as a slot either: 

connect(mCounter->valueChanged, this, [](int value) {
  ALogger::info("MyApp") << value;
});

As with methods, this can be omitted: 

connect(mCounter->valueChanged, [](int value) {
  ALogger::info("MyApp") << value;
});

docs.title: UI example
docs.text:
Knowing basics of signal slots, you can now utilize UI signals: 

mOkButton = _new<AButton>("OK");
...
connect(mOkButton->clicked, [] { // the signal is connected to "this" object
    ALogger::info("Example") << "The button was clicked";
});

Pitfall

In lambda, do not capture shared pointer (AUI's _) of signal emitter or receiver object by value. This would cause a memory leak: 

mOkButton = _new<AButton>("OK");
...
connect(mOkButton->clicked, [view] { // WRONG!!!
    view->setText("clicked");
});
Do this way: 
mOkButton = _new<AButton>("OK");
...
connect(mOkButton->clicked, [view = view.get()] { // ok
    view->setText("clicked");
});

docs.title: Going further
docs.text:
Let's take our previous example with Counter and make an UI app. Signal slot reveals it's power when your objects have small handy functions, so lets add increase method to our counter:

class Counter: public AObject {
public:
  Counter() = default;

  void setValue(int value) {
    mValue = value;
    emit valueChanged(value);
  }

  void increase() {
    setValue(mCounter + 1);
  }

signals:
  emits<int> valueChanged;

private:
  int mValue = 0;
};

class MyApp: public AWindow {
public:
  MyApp() {
    auto label = _new<ALabel>("-");
    auto button = _new<AButton>("Increase");

    using namespace declarative;
    setContents(Vertical {
      label,
      button,
    });

    connect(button->clicked, AUI_SLOT(mCounter)::increase); // beauty, huh?
    connect(mCounter->valueChanged, label, [label = label.get()](int value) {
      label->setText("{}"_format(value));
    });
  }

private:
  _<Counter> mCounter = _new<Counter>();
};

AUI_ENTRY {
  auto app = _new<MyApp>();
  app->show();
  return 0;
}

This way, by clicking on "Increase", it would increase the counter and immediately display value via label.

Let's make things more declarative and use AUI_LET syntax to set up connections: 

MyApp() {
  using namespace declarative;
  setContents(Vertical {
    _new<ALabel>("-") AUI_LET {
      connect(counter->valueChanged, label, [label = it.get()](int value) {
        label->setText("{}"_format(value));
      });
    },
    _new<AButton>("Increase") AUI_LET {
      connect(it->clicked, AUI_SLOT(mCounter)::increase);
    },
  });
}

See also property-system for making reactive UI's on trivial data.

docs.title: Arguments
docs.text:
If signal declares arguments (i.e, like AView::keyPressed), you can accept them: 

view = _new<ATextField>();
...
connect(view->keyPressed, [](AInput::Key k) { // the signal is connected to "this" object
    ALogger::info("Example") << "Key was pressed: " << k;
});

The signals and slots mechanism is type safe: The signature of a signal must match the signature of the receiving slot. Also, a slot may have a shorter signature than the signal it receives because it can ignore extra arguments: 

view = _new<ATextField>();
...
connect(view->keyPressed, [] { // the signal is connected to "this" object
    ALogger::info("Example") << "Key was pressed";
});

docs.title: Differences between Qt and AUI implementation
docs.text:
Suppose we want to emit statusChanged signal with a string argument and connect it with showMessage slot:

Qt AUI Signal declaration 
signals:
  void statusChanged(QString str);

signals:
  emits<AString> statusChanged;
Slot declaration 
slots:
  void showMessage(QString str);

  void showMessage(AString str);
Connect from this to this 
connect(this, SIGNAL(statusChanged(QString), this, SLOT(showMessage(QString)));

  connect(statusChanged, me::showMessage);
Connect from the emitter object to the sender object 
 QObject::connect(emitter, SIGNAL(statusChanged(QString), receiver, SLOT(showMessage(QString)));

  AObject::connect(emitter->statusChanged, AUI_SLOT(receiver)::showMessage);

docs.title: aui::sqlite
docs.text:
Outdated

aui::sqlite is not maintained and is not part of the current build. It is a plugin for aui::data, which itself does not compile against current AUI.

aui::sqlite consists of the ASqlite driver class (aui.sqlite/src/AUI/ASqlite.h) and a vendored copy of SQLite 3 in 3rdparty. Loaded as a plugin, it registers itself with ASqlDatabase::registerDriver so that connecting with the driver name "sqlite" works; the database name is a file path or :memory:.

The module's tests (aui.sqlite/tests) cover the query builder, the migration manager and the key-value metadata table, but they are not built either, and the ORM test is commented out. ASqlite has no documentation comment, so no reference page is generated.

For SQLite in an application, import the official library with auib_import (see aui.boot) and keep database calls off the UI thread.

docs.title: Detailed Description
docs.text:
Derive your suite from UITest and use TEST_F. Before each test, UITest replaces the window manager with a stub one (windows are not shown on the screen, rendering goes to a software renderer). After each test, it closes all windows and destroys the window manager.

class UIMyWindow : public testing::UITest {
protected:
    void SetUp() override {
        UITest::SetUp();   // do not forget to call the base
        _new<MyWindow>()->show();
    }
};

TEST_F(UIMyWindow, Hello) {
    By::text("Say hello").perform(click());
}

Warning

If you override SetUp or TearDown, call UITest::SetUp() first and UITest::TearDown() last. Release every window and view you own before calling UITest::TearDown().

Every failed assertion made via UIMatcher saves a screenshot to reports/<suite>/fail-<test>.png with the matched views outlined in red; a screenshot of the final state of every test is saved as reports/<suite>/finish-<test>.png.

For views to update (layout, styles, pending messages), the UI must be processed; actions and checks of UIMatcher do that for you. In other cases, call uitest::frame().

docs.title: Troubleshoot list
docs.text: If neither of these suggestions helped and you think you encountered an AUI's issue, consider reporting it on GitHub.

docs.title: Linking problems
docs.text:
1. Make sure you are using aui_link instead of target_link_libraries at least for AUI's components.

  2. Try using static build instead of shared libraries.

    cd build
cmake .. -DBUILD_SHARED_LIBS=OFF

docs.title: Assets
docs.text:
See also: AUI Assets

  1. Ensure you have called aui_compile_assets() in your CMakeLists.txt.
  2. Make sure you are using aui_link instead of target_link_libraries at least for AUI's components.
  3. If you are aui_link'ing asset-containing modules (i.e. aui::views) against static library, consider link them also with the final executable (PUBLIC linking does not solve this issue on Linux).
  4. Try using WHOLEARCHIVE flag.

docs.title: Build cache invalidation
docs.text:
Symptoms:

  1. Linking problems
  2. Newly added/removed files not being recognized by the build system
  3. Changes in CMake scripts are not "visible" in IDE
  4. Other weird issues

Cache invalidation is one of the software engineering problems (along with naming). There's cheatsheet on how to invalidate caches:

  1. Reload CMake cache
  2. In CLion: File > Reload CMake Project
  3. In Visual Studio Code: F1 > CMake: Configure
  4. In CLI: 
    cd <YOUR_BUILD_DIR>
cmake ..
    or 
    cmake --build <YOUR_BUILD_DIR>
  5. Delete CMakeCache.txt from your CMake binary dir (cmake-build-debug or cmake-build-release in CLion).
  6. Delete your CMake binary dir.
  7. Change AUI version (also may need CMakeCache.txt to be deleted)
  8. Delete aui.boot cache dir (~/.aui (AUI.Boot Cache Dir) unless otherwise specified)

docs.title: Animating views
docs.text: AUI has two ways to make things move: animators attached to a view, and animating a property yourself.

docs.title: Animators
docs.text:
An animator (AAnimator) transforms how a view is painted over a period of time. Create one, set the duration in seconds and assign it to the view. The view is repainted continuously until the animation finishes.

auto animator = _new<ATranslationAnimator>(glm::vec2 { -100, 0 });   // slide in from the left
animator->setDuration(0.3f);
view->setAnimator(animator);

The other stock animators are ARotationAnimator (between two AAngleRadians, i.e., 0_deg and 90_deg) and ASizeAnimator. AAnimator::combine({ a, b }) runs several at once; setRepeating(true) makes the animation loop (useful for a busy indicator like ASpinner); setCurve replaces the easing. Ready-made curves live in aui::animation_curves (Linear, CubicBezier, Standard).

Animators change only the painting: the layout and hit testing of the view are not affected, except for ASizeAnimator, which really changes the size.

A custom animator is a class overriding doAnimation(view, theta, renderer) where theta goes from 0 to 1.

docs.title: Animating a property
docs.text:
Anything that is a function of a property can be animated by changing that property over time. Drive it with an ATimer, and let reactive expressions or signals do the rest. The timer example (7GUIs) updates the current time ten times a second, and a progress bar follows:

class TimerWindow : public AWindow {
public:
    TimerWindow() : AWindow("AUI - 7GUIs - Timer", 300_dp, 50_dp) {
        setContents(Centered {
          Vertical::Expanding {
            Horizontal {
              Label { "Elapsed Time:" },
              Centered::Expanding {
                _new<AProgressBar>() AUI_LET {
                        it & mElapsedTimeRatio;
                        it->setCustomStyle({ Expanding { 1, 0 } });
                    },
              },
            } AUI_OVERRIDE_STYLE { LayoutSpacing { 4_dp } },
            Label { AUI_REACT("{:.1f}s"_format(duration_cast<milliseconds>(*mElapsedTime).count() / 1000.f)) },
            Horizontal {
              Label { "Duration:" },
              /// [timer_slider]
              Slider {
                .value = AUI_REACT(float(mDuration->count()) / float(MAX_DURATION.count())),
                .onValueChanged =
                    [this](aui::float_within_0_1 newValue) {
                        mDuration =
                            high_resolution_clock::duration(long(float(MAX_DURATION.count()) * float(newValue)));
                    },
              } AUI_OVERRIDE_STYLE { Expanding { 1, 0 } },
              /// [timer_slider]
            } AUI_OVERRIDE_STYLE { LayoutSpacing { 4_dp } },
            _new<AButton>("Reset Timer") AUI_OVERRIDE_STYLE {
                  Expanding { 1, 0 },
                } AUI_LET { connect(it->clicked, me::reset); },
          } AUI_OVERRIDE_STYLE { LayoutSpacing { 4_dp } },
        });

        connect(mTimer->fired, me::update);
        mTimer->start();
    }

private:
    _<ATimer> mTimer = _new<ATimer>(100ms);
    high_resolution_clock::time_point mStartTime = high_resolution_clock::now();
    AProperty<high_resolution_clock::time_point> mCurrentTime;
    AProperty<high_resolution_clock::duration> mDuration = 30s;

    APropertyPrecomputed<high_resolution_clock::duration> mElapsedTime = [&] {
        return std::min(mCurrentTime - mStartTime, *mDuration);
    };

    APropertyPrecomputed<aui::float_within_0_1> mElapsedTimeRatio = [&] {
        return float(mElapsedTime->count()) / float(mDuration->count());
    };

    void update() { mCurrentTime = high_resolution_clock::now(); }

    void reset() { mStartTime = high_resolution_clock::now(); }
};

For indeterminate waiting, ASpinner and ASpinnerV2 rotate by themselves; use AProgressBar when you know the progress.

docs.title: Performance
docs.text: Every frame of an animation is a repaint. Keep animated areas small and do not animate in a view that is expensive to paint; consider Render to texture to cache a complex subtree.

docs.title: UI Building Overview
docs.text: AUI Framework provides a comprehensive set of tools and libraries for building robust, scalable, and maintainable user interfaces. With its modular architecture and extensive feature set, developers can create complex UI components with ease. See Getting started with AUI for quick start.

docs.title: Views
docs.text: Views are basic units to build UIs with AUI. There is a wide range of pre-built views for common UI elements, such as buttons, labels, and text inputs.

docs.title: Layout
docs.text: Layout is flexible and customizable way of managing your views in a logical and visually appealing manner. From simple linear layouts to complex grid-based adaptive arrangements.

docs.title: Styles
docs.text: ASS supports for custom themes and styling using CSS-like syntax. Customize the look and feel of your UI using robust styling and theming capabilities.

docs.title: Event handling with signal-slot
docs.text:
signal_slot can be used to handle UI events and respond to them accordingly.

mOkButton = _new<AButton>("OK");
connect(mOkButton->clicked, [] { 
    ALogger::info("Example") << "The button was clicked";
});

docs.title: Data Binding
docs.text: Data binding, based on signal_slot "signal-slot", allows to establish a connection between UI and application data objects.

docs.title: Devtools
docs.text: AUI Devtools provide a set of features that makes it easier to design, test, and debug your UI components. With visual debugging tools, and more, you can streamline your development workflow and focus on building amazing user experiences.

docs.title: API Reference
docs.text:
• All Views
  • ASS
    • Selectors
    • Properties

docs.title: Creating a custom view and custom painting
docs.text: When no standard view does what you need, derive from AView. A custom view is responsible for three things: telling its size, painting itself and reacting to input. Everything else (styling, focus, hover, data binding) it inherits.

docs.title: Painting
docs.text:
Override render(ARenderContext). Call the base implementation first so the view's background and border from the stylesheet are painted below your content, then draw with ctx.render, which is an IRenderer. Coordinates are in pixels relative to the top left corner of the view.

void render(ARenderContext ctx) override {
    AView::render(ctx);

    for (const auto& circle : *mState->circles) {
        if (&circle == mHoveredCircle) {
            ctx.render.roundedRectangle(
                ASolidBrush { AColor::GRAY }, circle.position - *circle.radius, glm::vec2(circle.radius * 2.f),
                circle.radius);
        }
        ctx.render.roundedRectangleBorder(
            ASolidBrush { AColor::BLACK }, circle.position - *circle.radius, glm::vec2(circle.radius * 2.f),
            circle.radius, 1);
    }
}

The view above (from the 7GUIs Circle Drawer) also sets its look up in the constructor with setCustomStyle, so it needs no stylesheet. Whatever IRenderer has to offer can be used: rectangles, rounded rectangles, borders, lines, strings, drawables. Brushes (ASolidBrush, gradients...) define how the shape is filled.

When data your view displays changes, call redraw(). The example does this by connecting signals of its state:

connect(mState->circles.changed, me::redraw);
connect(mHoveredCircle.changed, me::redraw);

Warning

render may be called many times per second or, on the contrary, be skipped when nothing changes; moreover AUI may cache the view's picture (see Render to texture). Do not mutate application state in render; only paint.

docs.title: Sizing
docs.text:
By default, a custom view has a minimal size which can be changed from the stylesheet (MinSize, FixedSize, Expanding, MaxSize; see ass_properties). Setting Expanding() makes the view fill the available space, which is what the circle drawer does.

If the preferred size depends on the contents, override onIntrinsicMeasure. It receives constraints and returns the size of the content area in pixels. Measurement must not change the layout; if something that affects the size has changed, call requestLayout() and the view will be measured again.

glm::ivec2 onIntrinsicMeasure(AConstraints constraints) override {
    return { 100, int(mValues.size()) * 20 };
}

The layout system is described in layout-managers. If the view contains child views, derive from AViewContainerBase and set a layout instead.

docs.title: Reacting to input
docs.text:
Override the pointer and keyboard functions; see Handling input events for the full list. The circle drawer finds the circle under the pointer in onPointerMove and adds a new one in onPointerReleased. Always call the base implementation, otherwise clicked and hover state stop working.

Set the cursor with setCursor(ACursor::POINTER), and offer a right click menu by overriding composeContextMenu(), see Dialogs, menus and popups.

docs.title: Exposing state
docs.text:
Views in AUI are expected to cooperate with the property system and be usable from the declarative DSL, like Label { AUI_REACT(...) } or Slider { .value = ..., .onValueChanged = ... }. The idiomatic way to achieve this is to put the view behind a struct in namespace declarative: its fields are the inputs (contract::In for values flowing in, a callback or contract::Slot for events flowing out), and operator() builds the view out of existing ones.

namespace declarative {
struct Chip {
    contract::In<AString> text;
    contract::Slot<> onClick;

    _<AView> operator()() {
        return Button {
            .content = Label { .text = std::move(text) },
            .onClick = std::move(onClick),
        }();
    }
};
}   // namespace declarative

Usage is the same as with the built-in views:

Chip {
    .text = AUI_REACT("Clicked {} times"_format(state->count)),
    .onClick = [=] { ++state->count; },
}

The struct does not own any state; it displays what it is given and reports what the user did.

See declarative::Slider (ASlider.h) for a complete reference implementation, and property-system for details on reactive expressions.

docs.title: Drawing with OpenGL
docs.text: A view can draw with raw OpenGL, too. In render, restore the GL state AUI relies on after your calls. The examples/ui/opengl_simple example draws a triangle this way, and examples/app/fractal renders a fractal with a shader in a custom view.

docs.title: Images
docs.text: To show a picture, you don't need a custom view: Icon { ":img/logo.svg" } (backed by ADrawableView) shows an SVG or raster image from the assets (see AUI Assets), and ass has BackgroundImage.

docs.title: Dialogs, menus and popups
docs.text:
AUI offers several ways to ask the user something, from OS-native modal boxes to windows and menus made of regular views.

Need Use tell something or ask yes/no, urgently AMessageBox choose a file or a folder ADesktop::browseForFile / browseForDir custom dialog with arbitrary contents a child AWindow with WindowStyle::MODAL right click menu AView::composeContextMenu, see AMenu list of options attached to a button ADropdownList

docs.title: Message box
docs.text:
AMessageBox shows a native dialog. The call blocks until the user dismisses it and returns which button was pressed.

auto response = AMessageBox::show(this,
                  "Title",
                  "Message",
                  AMessageBox::Icon::NONE,
                  AMessageBox::Button::OK);
ALogger::info("Example") << "Response: " << int(response);

Because of the blocking, it's better saved for things the application can't continue without. For anything else, show the information inline.

AMessageBox::show can be used with a nullptr parent if there's no window around.

docs.title: File and folder choosers
docs.text:
ADesktop::browseForFile and ADesktop::browseForDir open the native dialog and return an AFuture<APath>. Do not call a blocking getter on the future from the UI thread; subscribe with onSuccess. An empty path means the user cancelled.

mAsync << ADesktop::browseForFile(this).onSuccess([&](const APath& f) {
    if (f.empty()) {
        AMessageBox::show(this, "Result", "Cancelled");
    } else {
        AMessageBox::show(this, "Result", "File: {}"_format(f));
    }
});

The example keeps the future in an async holder (mAsync) owned by the window. The file dialog accepts a list of ADesktop::FileExtension ({ "Images", "png" }) as a filter.

docs.title: Custom dialog window
docs.text:
A dialog is just another AWindow. Pass the parent and WindowStyle::MODAL (no resizing, no minimize/maximize buttons), fill it with views, and show() it. The circle drawer example opens such a window to adjust the radius of a circle:

auto popup = _new<AWindow>("Radius", 200_dp, 50_dp, dynamic_cast<AWindow*>(ASurface::current()), WindowStyle::MODAL);
popup->setContents(Vertical {
    Label { "Adjust radius." },
    Slider {
        .value = AUI_REACT(circle->radius / MAX_RADIUS),
        .onValueChanged = [circle](aui::float_within_0_1 s) { circle->radius = s * MAX_RADIUS; },
    },
});
connect(popup->closed, [] { /* commit the changes */ });
popup->show();

closed is emitted when the window is closed; close it from code with close(). Note that MODAL only affects the look of the window. If the user should not interact with the parent meanwhile, call blockUserInput() on the parent and blockUserInput(false) before the dialog is destroyed (see ASurface).

docs.title: Context menus
docs.text:
Override composeContextMenu() in a view. It returns an AMenuModel, which is a vector of AMenuItems. It's called every time the user right clicks (or long presses) the view, so the content can depend on the current state. Returning an empty vector shows no menu.

AMenuModel composeContextMenu() override {
    auto circle = *mHoveredCircle;
    if (circle == nullptr) {
        return {};
    }
    return {
        {
            .name = "Adjust radius...",
            .onAction = [this, circle] { showRadiusDialog(circle); },
        },
        { .type = AMenu::SEPARATOR },
        {
            .name = "Delete",
            .shortcut = AInput::DEL,
            .onAction = [this, circle] { remove(circle); },
            .enabled = canDelete(),
        },
    };
}

Items can be nested with .type = AMenu::SUBLIST and .subItems. Text views such as ATextField already provide cut/copy/paste/select all this way.

To open a menu without a right click, call AMenu::show(model).

docs.title: Popups attached to a view
docs.text: Dropdown lists and menus use overlapping surfaces: lightweight windows drawn above the window contents. ASurface::createOverlappingSurface(position, size) creates one; fill it with views and call pack(). view->getPositionInWindow() helps to place it below a view. See the doc comment of createOverlappingSurface in ASurface for an example.

docs.title: Building a form
docs.text: A form is a bunch of input views whose values are kept in your data. This page goes through the input views and ways to connect them to your state. For the layout side, see layout-managers.

docs.title: Input views at a glance
docs.text: Need View one line of text ATextField multiple lines of text ATextArea integer in a range ANumberPicker flag ACheckBox one of a few options ARadioButton, ADropdownList value between 0 and 1 declarative::Slider action AButton

docs.title: State and layout first
docs.text:
Keep the values of a form in a state object made of properties, and describe the form with Vertical / Horizontal containers. Anything that depends on the state is written as AUI_REACT(...): AUI tracks the properties read inside the expression and updates the view when they change. No manual refresh code is needed.

struct Booking {
    AProperty<AString> name;
    AProperty<int> passengers = 1;
    AProperty<bool> isReturnFlight = false;

    bool isValid() const { return !name->empty() && *passengers > 0; }
};

...
setContents(Vertical {
    Horizontal {
        Label { "Name:" },
        _new<ATextField>() && state->name,
    },
    Label { AUI_REACT("Hello, {}!"_format(state->name)) },
    Label { AUI_REACT("Passengers: {}"_format(state->passengers)) },
    Button {
        .content = Label { AUI_REACT(state->isValid() ? "Book" : "Fill in the form") },
        .onClick = [=] { book(*state); },
    } AUI_LET { AObject::connect(AUI_REACT(state->isValid()), AUI_SLOT(it)::setEnabled); },
} AUI_OVERRIDE_STYLE { LayoutSpacing { 4_dp } });

Label { AUI_REACT(...) } and Button { .content = Label { AUI_REACT(...) } } are the main tools: the form reads as a description of what is shown for the given state, and handlers (.onClick) only change the state.

docs.title: Text input and two-way binding
docs.text:
The text() property of ATextField and ATextArea can be bound to an AProperty<AString> of your state with &&. Typing updates the property; assigning the property updates the field.

_form({
  { "Name:", _new<ATextField>() && mEditedUser.name },
  { "Surname:", _new<ATextField>() && mEditedUser.surname },
}) AUI_OVERRIDE_STYLE { LayoutSpacing { 4_dp } },

_form lays out { label, view } pairs in two columns. The same state can feed several views, because properties notify all of their observers. Here, mEditedUser.name is bound to the text field; when the user presses "Create", the code simply reads (and resets) it, and the text field goes empty by itself.

docs.title: Enabling a button when the form is valid
docs.text:
Express validity as a reactive expression over the state and connect it to setEnabled of the button:

Button {
    .content = Label { "Book" },
    .onClick = [=] { /* ... */ },
} AUI_LET { AObject::connect(AUI_REACT(state->isValid()), AUI_SLOT(it)::setEnabled); },

This is how the 7GUIs "Flight Booker" does it. If the validity is used in several places, give it a name with APropertyPrecomputed, which recomputes whenever a property it read has changed, as the 7GUIs "CRUD" (examples/7guis/crud) does:

APropertyPrecomputed<bool> mCreateEnabled = [this] { return !(mEditedUser.surname->empty() || mEditedUser.name->empty()); };
...
Button { Label { "Create" }, { me::createClicked } } & mCreateEnabled > &AView::setEnabled,

For details on properties and reactive expressions, see property-system.

docs.title: Validating text
docs.text:
The field accepts whatever is typed. To validate, observe the text, parse it, and change the style of the field to signal an error. The example parses the text of a field as a date and makes the background red if it is not one.

auto dateTextField(_<DateTextFieldState> state) {
    return _new<ATextField>() AUI_LET {
        AObject::connect(
            state->parsed, it, [&it = *it, &state = *state](const AOptional<system_clock::time_point>& value) {
                if (!value) {
                    return;
                }
                if (state.userChangesText.is_locked()) {
                    return;
                }

                it.text() = formatDate(*value);
            });
        AObject::connect(it->text().changed, state->parsed, [&it = *it, &state = *state](const AString& s) {
            std::unique_lock lock(state.userChangesText);
            state.parsed = parseDate(s);
        });
        AObject::connect(
            AUI_REACT(ass::PropertyList { BackgroundSolid(!state->parsed->hasValue() ? AColor::RED : AColor::WHITE) }),
            AUI_SLOT(it)::setCustomStyle);
    };
}

If you want to forbid some characters altogether, subclass ATextField and override isValidText (see ANumberPicker's inner field for an example).

docs.title: Passwords, read-only fields, limits
docs.text:
auto password = _new<ATextField>();
password->setPasswordMode(true);          // hides symbols, disables copy
password->setMaxTextLength(64);

auto readOnly = _new<ATextField>();
readOnly->setEditable(false);

docs.title: Choosing from a list
docs.text:
ADropdownList takes a list model. Its selectionId() is a property, so it binds like anything else:

_new<ADropdownList>(AListModel<AString>::make({
  "Dropdown list 1",
  "Dropdown list 2",
  "Dropdown list 3",
  "Dropdown list 4",
  "Dropdown list 5",
  "Dropdown list 6",
})),

The flight booker connects it to a boolean this way:

AObject::connect(AUI_REACT(state->isReturnFlight ? 1 : 0), it->selectionId());
AObject::connect(it->selectionId().changed, AObject::GENERIC_OBSERVER, [=](int newSelection) {
    state->isReturnFlight = newSelection == 1;
});

docs.title: Numbers
docs.text:
ANumberPicker is an integer text field with plus/minus buttons. Set the range with setMin / setMax, read the value with getValue() or observe valueChanged (final) and valueChanging (on every keystroke):

auto picker = _new<ANumberPicker>();
picker->setMin(1);
picker->setMax(12);
picker->setValue(4);
AObject::connect(picker->valueChanged, AObject::GENERIC_OBSERVER, [](int64_t x) { /* ... */ });

ADoubleNumberPicker is the same for floating point numbers.

docs.title: Slider and progress
docs.text:
declarative::Slider works with a value from 0 to 1. It does not keep its own state: it displays .value and notifies you via .onValueChanged; you update the state, and the value flows back.

Slider {
  .value = AUI_REACT(float(mDuration->count()) / float(MAX_DURATION.count())),
  .onValueChanged =
      [this](aui::float_within_0_1 newValue) {
          mDuration =
              high_resolution_clock::duration(long(float(MAX_DURATION.count()) * float(newValue)));
      },
} AUI_OVERRIDE_STYLE { Expanding { 1, 0 } },

Multiply by your range to get a real value, as the timer does with its duration. A AProgressBar or CircleProgressBar showing the same property displays progress; see its page for styling.

docs.title: Grouping
docs.text: Wrap related inputs with AGroupBox (a frame with a title) and arrange them with Vertical, Horizontal or _form.

docs.title: Handling input events
docs.text: Views report what the user does through signals and virtual functions. For ordinary reactions, connect to a signal; for custom views, override the function.

docs.title: Reacting to a click
docs.text:
AView has the clicked signal, which every view emits when the user presses and releases the left mouse button (or taps) inside of it. A AButton is not special in this regard: a label or any other view can be clicked as well.

_new<ALabel>("Open website") AUI_LET {
    AObject::connect(it->clicked, AObject::GENERIC_OBSERVER, [] {
        APlatform::openUrl(AUrl("https://github.com/aui-framework/aui"));
    });
}

Related signals of AView:

Signal Emitted when clicked left button (or tap) released over the view clickedButton any button released over the view; carries APointerIndex clickedRight right button released over the view clickedRightOrLongPressed right click, or long press on touchscreens doubleClicked double click pressed / released pointer pressed / released mouseEnter / mouseLeave pointer enters / leaves the view scrolled mouse wheel or touch scrolling keyPressed / keyReleased keyboard key pressed / released while the view is focused focusAcquired / focusLost focus changes

To click a view from code (i.e., a hotkey that does the same as a button), call AView::click(); it emits clicked.

For buttons specifically, see the examples on the AButton page.

docs.title: Pointer events in a custom view
docs.text:
AView offers onPointerPressed, onPointerReleased, onPointerMove, onPointerDoubleClicked and onScroll. A view that is pressed continues to receive move and release events even if the pointer leaves it, so dragging works out of the box. Use AView::isMouseHover() to check whether the pointer is actually over the view.

Coordinates in the events are relative to the view's top left corner, in pixels.

void onPointerReleased(const APointerReleasedEvent& event) override {
    AView::onPointerReleased(event);   // always call the base implementation to keep `clicked` working
    if (event.asButton != AInput::LBUTTON) {
        return;
    }
    addPoint(event.position);
}

Note

Pointer events are unified for mouse and touchscreen. A finger touch is reported as a left button press; event.pointerIndex tells which finger or which mouse button caused the event.

A scroll event carries event.origin (where the pointer is) and event.delta (how much was scrolled). The fractal example uses them to zoom around the pointer.

docs.title: Keyboard
docs.text:
Keyboard events go to the focused view and then bubble up through its parents. A view overrides:

  • onKeyDown(AInput::Key) - a key was pressed (not a character: arrows, function keys, etc);
  • onKeyRepeat(AInput::Key) - the key is held and the OS autorepeat fires;
  • onKeyUp(AInput::Key);
  • onCharEntered(AChar) - a character was typed, with layout, shift and input methods already applied. Use this for text.
void FractalView::onKeyDown(AInput::Key key) {
    AView::onKeyDown(key);
    onKeyRepeat(key);
}

void FractalView::onKeyRepeat(AInput::Key key) {
    AView::onKeyRepeat(key);
    constexpr float SPEED = 0.2f;
    switch (key) {
        case AInput::UP:
            mTransform = glm::translate(mTransform, { 0, -SPEED, 0 });
            break;
        case AInput::DOWN:
            mTransform = glm::translate(mTransform, { 0, SPEED, 0 });
            break;
        case AInput::LEFT:
            mTransform = glm::translate(mTransform, { -SPEED, 0, 0 });
            break;
        case AInput::RIGHT:
            mTransform = glm::translate(mTransform, { SPEED, 0, 0 });
            break;
        case AInput::PAGEDOWN:
            mTransform = glm::scale(mTransform, glm::vec3 { 0.99 });
            break;
        case AInput::PAGEUP:
            mTransform = glm::scale(mTransform, glm::vec3 { 1.01 });
            break;

        default:
            return;
    }
    handleMatrixUpdated();
}

Keys are values of the AInput::Key enum. AInput::isKeyDown(key) polls the current state of a key anywhere in the code, which is handy for modifiers:

if (AInput::isKeyDown(AInput::LSHIFT)) {
    // ...
}

AInput::CMD_CTRL maps to Cmd on Apple platforms and to Ctrl elsewhere, which is what you want for hotkeys like copy or save.

docs.title: Keyboard shortcuts
docs.text:
AUI does not have a global hotkey registry; a shortcut is a key press handled by a view. A window is a view container as well, so the simplest place for application-wide shortcuts is the window itself:

class MainWindow : public AWindow {
public:
    void onKeyDown(AInput::Key key) override {
        AWindow::onKeyDown(key);
        if (AInput::isKeyDown(AInput::CMD_CTRL) && key == AInput::S) {
            save();
        }
    }
};

AShortcut (built with AInput::CMD_CTRL + AInput::S) is only a description which converts to a readable string like Ctrl+S; it is used for menu items, see AMenu.

docs.title: Intercepting a key before the text field
docs.text:
A key that is not consumed by the focused view bubbles up: for instance, Enter typed in an ATextField reaches the onKeyDown of its parents. Overriding onCharEntered is the way to change what a text view does with typed characters. The notes example turns Enter in the title into "go to the next field":

class TitleTextArea : public ATextArea {
public:
    using ATextArea::ATextArea;
    void onCharEntered(AChar c) override {
        if (c == '\r') {
            ASurface::current()->focusNextView();
            return;
        }
        ATextArea::onCharEntered(c);
    }
};

docs.title: Focus
docs.text:
Only one view of a window has focus. Views that handle keyboard input take it when clicked or when the user tabs to them. In code:

  • view->focus() gives the view focus (a freshly shown text field typically wants this);
  • view->isFocused() / view->hasFocus() query the state, focusAcquired / focusLost / focusState signals report changes;
  • ASurface::focusNextView() moves focus like Tab does.

The focused state can be used in ass selectors to highlight the view.

docs.title: Mouse cursor
docs.text:
The shape of the pointer over a view is set with AView::setCursor or the cursor ASS property, which takes ACursor:

Label { "link" } AUI_OVERRIDE_STYLE { ACursor::POINTER }

Besides the system cursors (ACursor::POINTER, TEXT, MOVE, EW_RESIZE, NS_RESIZE), a cursor can be built from an image or a drawable.

docs.title: Context menu
docs.text: Override AView::composeContextMenu() to return a menu model that is shown on right click or long press. See Dialogs, menus and popups.

docs.title: Testing input
docs.text: UI tests simulate clicks, key presses and typing against a real window; see Writing tests and the aui.uitests module (By::type<ATextField>().perform(click()), keyDownAndUp(AInput::RETURN), type("text")).

docs.title: Lists, scrolling and tabs
docs.text: This page is about views that hold and organize other content. To create views from a collection of your data (the usual, reactive way), see AForEachUI; the classic model-based views are described below.

docs.title: Scrolling
docs.text:
Wrap contents with AScrollArea to make them scrollable. The area expands by default, so give it room in the parent layout (or limit it with MaxSize / FixedSize).

AScrollArea::Builder().withContents(
    Vertical {
        Label { "Lots of..." },
        Label { "...content" },
    }
).build()
  • setStickToEnd(true) keeps the area scrolled to the end as the content grows, which fits chats and logs;
  • scrollTo(view) scrolls so that the given view is visible;

ATextArea does not scroll by itself, to avoid nested scrolling: put it into a scroll area, as the notes example does.

docs.title: List of views from data
docs.text: AForEachUI and the AUI_DECLARATIVE_FOR macro create one view per item of an AProperty<AVector<...>> and keep them in sync with it.. See AForEachUI.

docs.title: Model-based list
docs.text:
AListView displays a model of strings. A model is a class implementing IListModel<AString>, which only needs to tell the number of items and to return an item by its index. When the data changes, the model emits dataInserted, dataRemoved or dataChanged so the view updates.

size_t DemoListModel::listSize() {
    return mListSize;
}

AString DemoListModel::listItemAt(const AListModelIndex& index) {
    return "List item #{}"_format(index.getRow() + 1);
}

void DemoListModel::addItem() {
    mListSize += 1;
    emit dataInserted(range({mListSize - 1}));
}

void DemoListModel::removeItem() {
    if (mListSize > 0) {
        mListSize -= 1;
        emit dataRemoved(range({mListSize}));
    }
}

[] {   // lambda style inlining
    auto model = _new<DemoListModel>();

    return Vertical {
        Horizontal {
          _new<AButton>("Add").connect(&AButton::clicked, AUI_SLOT(model)::addItem),
          _new<AButton>("Remove").connect(&AButton::clicked, AUI_SLOT(model)::removeItem),
        } AUI_OVERRIDE_STYLE { LayoutSpacing { 4_dp } },
        _new<AListView>(model) AUI_OVERRIDE_STYLE {
          MinSize { 60_dp, 60_dp },
        }
    } AUI_OVERRIDE_STYLE { LayoutSpacing { 4_dp } };
}(),

AListModel<T> is a ready-to-use model backed by a vector, and the one that ADropdownList takes: AListModel<AString>::make({ "one", "two" }).

The selection is available as getSelectionModel() and the selectionChanged signal. setAllowMultipleSelection(true) enables multiple selection; itemDoubleClicked tells when an item was double clicked.

Prefer AForEachUI when items need more than a string. AListView suits simple lists, especially with an existing model.

docs.title: Trees
docs.text:
ATreeView shows an ATreeModel<AString>: an item has a name and optional children. Selection and hovering are reported with itemSelected, itemMouseClicked, itemMouseDoubleClicked and itemMouseHover.

_new<ATreeView>(_new<ATreeModel<AString>>(AVector<ATreeModel<AString>::Item>{
    { "dir1", { { "file1" }, { "file2" } } },
    { "dir2", { { "file3" } } },
}))

docs.title: Tabs
docs.text:
ATabView has a row of tab buttons and switches between added views:

auto tabs = _new<ATabView>();
tabs->addTab(Centered { Label { "General settings" } }, "General");
tabs->addTab(Centered { Label { "About the app" } }, "About");

If tabs should be switched by something else (a sidebar, a wizard's "Next" button), use APageView and its APageSwitch.

docs.title: Splitters
docs.text:
ASplitter lets the user redistribute space between views by dragging the border:

ASplitter::Horizontal().withItems({ listView, details }).build()

Mark one of the items Expanding, so there is a view to take the free space. See the notes example, which has a list of notes and an editor in a splitter.

docs.title: Group boxes and dragging
docs.text: AGroupBox draws a titled frame around related controls. ADragArea lets the user drag views around inside it: ADragArea::convertToDraggable(view, false) makes a view draggable.

docs.title: UIMatcher
docs.text:
A lazy selector of views in all opened windows, with actions and checks to run on them.

Header:#include <AUI/Test/UI/UIMatcher.h> CMake:aui_link(my_target PUBLIC aui::uitests)

docs.title: Detailed Description
docs.text:
Obtain UIMatcher from the By functions (By::text, By::name, By::type, By::exactType, By::value). The matcher does not remember views: every perform, check, one, toSet and toVector call walks all windows of the window manager and finds the views that match at that moment. Therefore, the same matcher can be reused after UI has changed.

Only views with Visibility::VISIBLE are matched (and views inside invisible containers are not reachable), unless includeInvisibleViews() is called or an assertion that ignores visibility is used (visible(), notVisible(), gone(), isParentOf).

By::text("Say hello").perform(click());
By::name("#hello").check(visible()).check(text("Hello!"));

Matchers are combined with operator| (either) and operator& (both):

(By::text("OK") | By::text("Cancel")).check(sameWidth());

perform and check return the matcher itself, so they can be chained.

Note

check fails the test when nothing is matched, and perform on an empty selection does nothing, only prints a message. Do not assume that a perform found its target.

See Finding views, Simulating user input and Checking views.

docs.title: Public Methods
docs.text:
UIMatcher UIMatcher::allChildren()

Matches the views whose parent is matched by this matcher.

Combined with parent(), selects siblings: By::name("a").parent().allChildren().

Examples:

examples/ui/views/tests/LayoutManagerTest.cpp

Views Example — All-in-one views building example.

TEST_F(UILayoutManager, ButtonsAlignment) {
    // buttons column should be perfectly aligned
    By::name("Common button")
        .parent()
        .allChildren()
        .check(leftRightAligned(), "elements should be perfectly aligned");
}

template<class Assertion >
UIMatcher& UIMatcher::check(Assertion&& assertion, const char* msg = "no msg")

Checks that every matched view satisfies the assertion.

Arguments assertion `visible()`, `text("...")`, `width(...)` etc... or any callable `bool(const _&)`. msg message to print when the check fails. Returns this matcher, to chain further calls.

Failing is non-fatal (EXPECT_* semantics): the test continues. An empty selection fails the check.

Examples:

UIMatcher UIMatcher::findNearestTo(UIMatcher matcher)

Finds the nearest view to the specified one.

Arguments matcher UIMatcher of a view to find the nearest to. The UIMatcher is expected to match only one view. Returns the nearest view

Finds the nearest view to the bottom right corner of the specified view. The bottom right corner is chosen in order to simulate human eye scanning (which is from top-left to bottom-right).

Useful when finding fields by their labels: 

_new<ALabel>("Login"),
_new<ATextField>(),
_new<ALabel>("Password"),
_new<ATextField>(),
...
By::type<ATextField>().findNearestTo(By::text("Login")) // <- matches the first ATextField
By::type<ATextField>().findNearestTo(By::text("Password")) // <- matches the second ATextField


UIMatcher& UIMatcher::includeInvisibleViews()

Makes this matcher consider views that are not Visibility::VISIBLE as well.

_<AView> UIMatcher::one()

Returns the first matched view, or nullptr if nothing is matched.

Use it to get the actual view for direct inspection:

auto field = _cast<ATextField>(By::name("#username").one());

The order of views is unspecified; when several views match, make the selector more precise.

UIMatcher UIMatcher::parent()

Matches containers that have a direct child matched by this matcher.

Examples:

template<class Action >
UIMatcher& UIMatcher::perform(Action&& action)

Runs an action (click(), type("..."), scroll(...) etc...) on every matched view.

Returns this matcher, to chain further calls.

The UI is processed (uitest::frame()) before the first and after every action.

docs.title: uitest_util::InkGaps
docs.text:
Empty pixel rows above and below the dark text of a view on a white background.

Header:#include <aui.uitests/tests/InkGaps.h> CMake:aui_link(my_target PUBLIC )

docs.title: Simulating user input
docs.text:
Actions are objects that are passed to UIMatcher::perform. Each action is applied to every matched view, and the UI is processed (uitest::frame()) after each step, so a handler's reaction is visible immediately. Input goes through the same window entry points the platform uses (onPointerPressed, onCharEntered, onKeyDown and so on), so the views see what they would see from a real user.

By::text("Say hello").perform(click());

docs.title: Clicks
docs.text:
click() presses and releases the left button at the center of the view. clickRight() does the same with the right button.

TEST_F(UIClick, RightClick) {
    // check clicked right or long pressed signal emitted
    EXPECT_CALL(*mTestWindow, onButtonClickedRightOrLongPressed).Times(1);

    // press the button
    By::text("Say hello").perform(clickRight());
}

Pass a position relative to the view's top-left corner to click somewhere else. This is how the text field tests place a cursor:

TEST_F(UITextField, CursorAppearsAtTheEnd) {
    By::type<ATextField>().perform(click({299_dp, 0_dp})) // click at the right border
                          .check(selectionMatches(12));
}

doubleClick() takes an optional position, too:

TEST_F(UITextField, DoubleClickWordSelection1) {
    By::type<ATextField>().perform(doubleClick({20_dp, 0_dp})) // click at the first word
                          .check(selectionMatches(0, 5));
}

gestureLongPress() emits a long press gesture, the touch counterpart of the right click:

TEST_F(UIClick, LongPress) {
    // check clicked right or long pressed signal is emitted
    EXPECT_CALL(*mTestWindow, onButtonClickedRightOrLongPressed).Times(1);

    // press the button
    By::text("Say hello").perform(gestureLongPress());
}

For pointer sequences, use the separate steps: mousePress(), mouseRelease() and mouseMove() (and mousePressRight(), mouseReleaseRight()). pointerPress, pointerRelease and pointerMove are there for the cases when a pointer index has to be specified.

If you need a pointer event that the actions do not cover, call the window directly, as UIClickTest does:

mTestWindow->onPointerPressed({ .position = view->getCenterPointInWindow(), .asButton = AInput::LBUTTON });

docs.title: Typing
docs.text:
type("text") focuses the view and enters the string character by character, as if typed on the keyboard. It does not clear the field; select all first if you want to replace the contents.

TEST_F(UIType, HelloAppearsAfterClick) {
    // type "Steve" to the text field
    By::name("#username").perform(type("Steve"));

    // press the button
    By::text("Say hello").perform(click());

    // check label is appeared and contains text "Hello, Steve!"
    By::name("#hello").check(visible(), "label is not appeared")
                      .check(text("Hello, Steve!"), "invalid text");
}

docs.title: Key presses
docs.text:
keyDownAndUp(key) focuses the view and presses and releases a key. The argument is an AShortcut, so combinations are formed with +:

TEST_F(UITextField, CtrlA) {
    By::type<ATextField>()
            .perform(keyDownAndUp(AInput::LCONTROL + AInput::A))
            .perform(type("replace"))
            .check(text("replace"));
}

Actions can be chained on the same matcher, interleaved with checks. The following test moves the cursor with the keyboard and checks its position after each step (selectionMatches is a custom assertion, see Checking views):

TEST_F(UITextField, HomeEnd) {
    By::type<ATextField>()
            .perform(click({0, 0}))
            .check(selectionMatches(0))
            .perform(keyDownAndUp(AInput::END))
            .check(selectionMatches("hello world!"sv.length()))
            .perform(keyDownAndUp(AInput::HOME))
            .check(selectionMatches(0))
            ;
}

docs.title: Scrolling and hovering
docs.text:
scroll({ dx, dy }) delivers a scroll event to the view. mouseMove() moves the pointer to the view (with an optional offset), which updates hover state.

TEST_F(UIScrollTest, ContainedViewExpanded) {
    By::type<AScrollArea>().perform(scroll({0, 500}));
    (By::name(".container") | By::type<AScrollArea>()).check(areBottomAligned());
}

To scroll a particular child into view, call AScrollArea::scrollTo(view) directly; actions are only needed when the scroll itself is what you test.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
Action What it does click(), clickRight() Press and release the left or right button doubleClick() Two clicks and a double click event gestureLongPress() Long press gesture mousePress(), mouseRelease() Press or release the left button mouseMove() Move the pointer type("...") Enter characters into the focused view keyDownAndUp(key) Press and release a key or a shortcut scroll({ dx, dy }) Mouse wheel

Position arguments are relative to the view's top-left corner and accept _dp literals, as in click({ 23_dp, 0_dp }).

docs.title: Checking views
docs.text:
UIMatcher::check applies an assertion to every matched view. The assertion is a function object that takes a view and returns bool; the second argument of check is the message shown when it fails.

By::name("#hello").check(visible(), "label is not appeared")
                  .check(text("Hello, Steve!"), "invalid text");

Failures are non-fatal (EXPECT_*): the test goes on and reports every problem. Empty selection fails the check, so a typo in a selector does not make the test pass silently. check returns the matcher, so checks and actions can be chained.

docs.title: Visibility and text
Sizes
docs.text:
width(metric) and height(metric) compare with an exact size. widthIsMinimal() and heightIsMinimal() check that the view is not larger than its minimum size. sameWidth() and sameHeight() check that all matched views have equal sizes, whatever it is.

TEST_F(UILayoutTest, ExpandingWithMinSize1) {
    inflate(Horizontal::Expanding {
      _new<AView>() << ".expanding_minsize" AUI_OVERRIDE_STYLE { Expanding {}, MinSize { 200_dp, {} } },
      _new<AView>() << ".expanding" AUI_OVERRIDE_STYLE { Expanding {} },
    } AUI_OVERRIDE_STYLE { FixedSize(300_dp, {}) });

    By::name(".expanding_minsize").check(width(200_dp), "width of .expanding_minsize is invalid");
    By::name(".expanding").check(width(100_dp), "width of .expanding is invalid");
}

TEST_F(UILayoutTest, LayoutSpacing2) {
    inflate(Horizontal::Expanding {
      Button { Label { "1" } } AUI_OVERRIDE_STYLE { Expanding {} },
      Button { Label { "2" } } AUI_OVERRIDE_STYLE { Expanding {} },
    } AUI_OVERRIDE_STYLE { LayoutSpacing { 8_dp }, FixedSize(200_dp, {}) });

    By::type<AButton>().check(sameWidth(), "widths of the buttons are not equal");
}

Sizes in width(...) and height(...) accept _dp, so tests do not depend on the screen density.

docs.title: Alignment and order
docs.text:
areLeftAligned(), areRightAligned(), areTopAligned(), areBottomAligned(), areLeftRightAligned() and areTopBottomAligned() check that all matched views share the edge (or both edges). The assertion remembers the first view's edge, so the check is relative: the views are aligned to each other.

isTopAboveTopOf(matcher), isTopBelowTopOf(matcher), isBottomAboveBottomOf(matcher) and isBottomBelowBottomOf(matcher) compare an edge with the same edge of all views matched by another matcher. That is the way to check if something is scrolled out of an area:

TEST_F(UIScrollTest, ContainedViewExpanded) {
    By::type<AScrollArea>().perform(scroll({0, 500}));
    (By::name(".container") | By::type<AScrollArea>()).check(areBottomAligned());
}

isParentOf(view) passes for the matched views that contain view somewhere inside.

By::type<AScrollArea>().check(isParentOf(label));

docs.title: Negation
docs.text:
uitest::impl::not$(assertion) inverts an assertion. It lives in the impl namespace, but it is the way to say "not":

By::text("Content").check(uitest::impl::not$(isTopAboveTopOf(By::type<AScrollArea>())));

docs.title: Colors
docs.text: averageColor(color, inaccuracy) and pixelColorAt({ x, y }, color, inaccuracy) look at the rendered pixels. See Screenshots and pixels.

docs.title: Custom assertions
docs.text:
Any callable bool(const _<AView>&) is an assertion. It may use GTest macros inside, which gives much better messages than a bare false:

namespace {
    struct SelectionMatchesAssert {
        ACursorSelectable::Selection selection;

        SelectionMatchesAssert(unsigned begin, unsigned end) : selection{begin, end} {}

        SelectionMatchesAssert(unsigned s) : selection{s, s} {}

        bool operator()(const _<AView>& view) const {
            if (auto t = _cast<ACursorSelectable>(view)) {
                EXPECT_EQ(t->selection(), selection);
            }
            return true;
        }
    };

    using selectionMatches = SelectionMatchesAssert;
}

Use it as By::type<ATextField>().check(selectionMatches(0, 5)).

By default, an assertion is evaluated on visible views only. If it should see invisible ones (like notVisible() does), add using IGNORE_VISIBILITY = std::true_type; to the assertion type.

Matchers can be extended in the same way: derive from IMatcher, implement matches(const _<AView>&) and wrap it in UIMatcher:

class HasTooltip : public IMatcher {
public:
    bool matches(const _<AView>& view) override {
        return view->getAssNames().contains(".has-tooltip");
    }
};
auto matcher = UIMatcher(_new<HasTooltip>());

docs.title: Your first UI test
docs.text: This page shows how to set up a UI test suite and run a complete scenario. For the general test setup (aui_enable_tests, running Tests), see Writing tests. An overview of the module is at uitests.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
A UI test creates real windows and views, but no native window is opened. testing::UITest switches to AStubWindowManager and a software renderer, so the test runs on a machine without a display. The views are laid out, styled and rendered as usual, the screenshot of any moment is available, and input is delivered to the window the same way the platform would do it.

Include <AUI/UITest.h>; it brings By, all actions, all assertions and GTest.

docs.title: Fixture
docs.text:
Derive your suite from testing::UITest. Create and show the window in SetUp, and call the base class methods.

class UIClick : public testing::UITest {
public:

protected:
    class TestWindow : public AWindow {
    private:
        _<ALabel> mHelloLabel;

    public:
        TestWindow() {
            setContents(Centered {
              Vertical {
                _new<AButton>("Say hello")
                        .connect(&AView::clicked, this,
                                 [&] {
                                     mHelloLabel->setVisibility(Visibility::VISIBLE);
                                     onButtonClicked();
                                 })
                        .connect(&AView::clickedRightOrLongPressed, this, [&] { onButtonClickedRightOrLongPressed(); })
                        .connect(&AView::doubleClicked, this, [&] { onButtonDoubleClicked(); }) AUI_LET { it->setDefault(); },
                mHelloLabel = _new<ALabel>("Hello!") AUI_LET { it->setVisibility(Visibility::INVISIBLE); },
              },
            });

            pack();
        }

        MOCK_METHOD(void, onButtonClicked, (), ());
        MOCK_METHOD(void, onButtonDoubleClicked, (), ());
        MOCK_METHOD(void, onButtonClickedRightOrLongPressed, (), ());
    };

    void SetUp() override {
        UITest::SetUp();

        mTestWindow = _new<TestWindow>();
        mTestWindow->show();
    }

    void TearDown() override {
        mTestWindow = nullptr;
        UITest::TearDown();
    }

    _<TestWindow> mTestWindow;
};

The application under test here is a button "Say hello" that reveals a "Hello!" label. Note GMock: the window exposes MOCK_METHODs that the signal handlers call, so the test can tell whether the click was delivered.

Tip

Place the window in the fixture class as a nested class, as above, when it is only needed for tests. To test a window of your application, include its header and _new<MyWindow>()->show() it.

docs.title: Test body
docs.text:
Find a view, perform an action, check the outcome:

TEST_F(UIClick, HelloAppearsAfterClick) {
    EXPECT_CALL(*mTestWindow, onButtonClicked).Times(1);
    // press the button
    By::text("Say hello").perform(click());

    // check label is appeared
    By::text("Hello!").check(visible(), "label is not appeared");
}

By::text("Say hello") finds the button, click() clicks the center of it, and By::text("Hello!") finds the label and visible() checks that it is shown. See Finding views, Simulating user input and Checking views.

docs.title: Typing and reading values
docs.text:
Views can be found by their ASS name (<< "#username" in the view tree). The following window has a text field and a button; the test types a name, presses the button and checks the label.

class UIType: public testing::UITest {
public:
protected:
    void SetUp() override {
        UITest::SetUp();

        class TestWindow: public AWindow {
        private:
            _<ATextField> mTextField;
            _<ALabel> mHelloLabel;

        public:
            TestWindow() {
                setContents(Centered {
                        Vertical {
                                Horizontal {
                                        mTextField = _new<ATextField>() << "#username",
                                        _new<AButton>("Say hello").connect(&AView::clicked, this, [&] {
                                            if (mTextField->getText().empty()) {
                                                mHelloLabel->setVisibility(Visibility::INVISIBLE);
                                                return;
                                            }
                                            mHelloLabel->text() = "Hello, {}!"_format(mTextField->getText());
                                            mHelloLabel->setVisibility(Visibility::VISIBLE);
                                        }) AUI_LET { it->setDefault(); },
                                },
                                mHelloLabel = _new<ALabel>() AUI_LET {
                                    it->setVisibility(Visibility::INVISIBLE);
                                    it << "#hello";
                                }
                        }
                });

                pack();
            }
        };

        // prepare the window
        _new<TestWindow>()->show();
    }

    void TearDown() override {
        UITest::TearDown();
    }
};

TEST_F(UIType, HelloAppearsAfterClick) {
    // type "Steve" to the text field
    By::name("#username").perform(type("Steve"));

    // press the button
    By::text("Say hello").perform(click());

    // check label is appeared and contains text "Hello, Steve!"
    By::name("#hello").check(visible(), "label is not appeared")
                      .check(text("Hello, Steve!"), "invalid text");
}

docs.title: Processing the UI
docs.text:
A UI is not updated by itself in a test; nothing runs an event loop for you. Layout, style changes and queued messages (for example, lambdas posted with AUI_UI_THREAD) are processed when you call uitest::frame(). Every perform and check of UIMatcher calls it before and after the action, so most tests never need it. Call it explicitly when you changed something directly and want to look at the result:

label->setVisibility(Visibility::GONE);
uitest::frame();
EXPECT_EQ(otherView->getPosition().x, 0);

uitest::frame() also repacks every window (see AStubWindowManager::drawFrame), so a window is shrunk to the size of its contents unless the contents are expanding. Use AUI_REPEAT(10) { uitest::frame(); } to let a layout settle if it needs several passes.

Note

Timers and other asynchronous work do not advance on their own either. If your code waits for an AThread::sleep or a background task, call AThread::processMessages() after waiting, and prefer to make the code under test injectable (for instance, pass the delay as a parameter) so the test does not have to sleep.

docs.title: Testing data binding
docs.text:
Reactive UI is checked the same way: change the state and look at the views.

TEST_F(UIReactiveTest, Label) {
    // Test that a reactive label updates its text when the bound property changes.
    // The test creates a simple state object with a reactive string property
    // and binds it to a label using the AUI_REACT macro. It then verifies
    // the initial rendered text and the updated text after changing the
    // property.
    using namespace ass;

    struct State {
        AProperty<AString> name;
    };
    auto state = _new<State>();

    mWindow->setContents(Vertical {
        Label { AUI_REACT("{}!"_format(state->name)) }
    });

    // Initially, the property is empty, so the label should display "!".
    EXPECT_EQ(*_cast<ALabel>(By::type<ALabel>().one())->text(), "!");
    // Update the property; the label should automatically reflect the new value.
    state->name = "Hello";
    EXPECT_EQ(*_cast<ALabel>(By::type<ALabel>().one())->text(), "Hello!");
}

docs.title: Cleaning up
docs.text: Release the windows and views you hold before calling UITest::TearDown(), as the fixtures above do (mTestWindow = nullptr;). UITest::TearDown() closes all windows and destroys the window manager.

docs.title: Screenshots and pixels
docs.text: The software renderer used by UI tests is deterministic, so what is drawn can be verified in a test. It is the last resort for custom drawing and styles; for layout and state, prefer Checking views.

docs.title: Colors of a view
docs.text:
averageColor(color, inaccuracy) takes a screenshot, clips it to the view and compares the average color. inaccuracy is in [0;1), where 0 demands the same color and 1 matches anything; the default is 0.1.

TEST_F(UIScreenAnalyzer, AverageColor) {
    // check the button is red
    By::text("Say hello").check(averageColor(0xff0000_rgb), "the button is not red");
    By::text("A basic button").check(uitest::impl::not$(averageColor(0xff0000_rgb)), "the button is red");
}

pixelColorAt({ x, y }, color, inaccuracy) checks one pixel. The position is relative to the view and within [0;1]: { 0, 0 } is the top-left corner, { 1, 1 } is the bottom-right, { 0.5f, 0.5f } is the center.

TEST_F(UIStyleTest, Merge) {
    testing::InSequence s;
    using namespace ass;

    mWindow->setExtraStylesheet(AStylesheet {
      {
        t<ASurface>(),
        BackgroundSolid { AColor::BLACK },
      },
      {
        ass::c("test1"),
        BackgroundImage { ":uni/caption/close.svg", {}, {}, Sizing::COVER }, // white cross
        FixedSize(32_px),
      },
      {
        ass::c("test2"),
        BackgroundImage { {}, AColor::RED },
      },
    });
    By::type<View>().check(pixelColorAt({0.5f, 0.5f}, AColor::BLACK)); // no white cross
    mView->addAssName("test1");
    By::type<View>().check(pixelColorAt({0.f, 0.5f}, AColor::BLACK)); // outside of cross
    By::type<View>().check(pixelColorAt({0.5f, 0.5f}, AColor::WHITE)); // within cross
    mView->addAssName("test2");
    By::type<View>().check(pixelColorAt({0.f, 0.5f}, AColor::BLACK)); // outside of cross
    By::type<View>().check(pixelColorAt({0.5f, 0.5f}, AColor::RED)); // within cross, overlayed by red
}

Pixel checks are the way to test ass rules: set an extra stylesheet, check the color.

docs.title: Custom analysis
docs.text:
ScreenshotAnalyzer gives access to the image. makeScreenshot() captures the window, clip(view) or clip(position, size) crops it, averageColor() and image() return the results.

auto shot = ScreenshotAnalyzer::makeScreenshot().clip(By::name("#preview").one());
EXPECT_EQ(shot.image().size(), glm::uvec2(64, 64));

docs.title: Seeing what the test sees
docs.text:
When a test fails, testing::UITest writes screenshots to the reports/ directory (relative to the working directory of the test run):

  • reports/<suite>/fail-<test>.png for every failed assertion, with the matched views outlined in red;
  • reports/<suite>/finish-<test>.png for the final state of every test.

To look at an intermediate state, call saveScreenshot("name") from the test body. The file is placed in reports/ and named <suite>.<test>_<name>.png.

TEST_F(UIDataBinding, Dropdown) {
    saveScreenshot("initial");
    By::type<ADropdownList>().perform(click());
    saveScreenshot("opened");
}

Tip

Upload reports/ as an artifact in your CI, so a red build comes with the pictures.

docs.title: Finding views
docs.text: Every UI test starts with finding the views to work with. By is a set of functions that return a UIMatcher; the matcher is then used to perform actions and check assertions. Matching is lazy: the view tree is searched on every call, so a matcher stays valid after the UI has changed.

docs.title: By text, name and type
docs.text:
By::text matches views whose text equals the string: labels, buttons, text fields, anything that converts to a string via IStringable (so AButton is matched by its caption).

By::text("Say hello").perform(click());

By::name matches by ASS name, which is assigned with << in the view tree ("#username", ".container") or with addAssName. A name is the most robust selector: it does not depend on a text that may be translated or changed.

mTextField = _new<ATextField>() << "#username",
...
By::name("#username").perform(type("Steve"));

By::type<T>() matches views of type T or derived from it, and By::exactType<T>() only of exactly T.

By::type<AButton>().check(sameWidth(), "widths of the buttons are not equal");

By::value(view) matches a particular view object, which is handy for combining it with other matchers.

Note

Only visible views are matched by default. A view with Visibility::INVISIBLE or Visibility::GONE, and everything inside it, is skipped. Assertions visible(), notVisible() and gone() are exceptions; they look at invisible views, too. Call includeInvisibleViews() to find invisible views with toSet(), one(), perform or check.

docs.title: Combining matchers
docs.text:
| selects views matched by any of the operands, & by both:

(By::text("Common button") | By::text("Show all views...")).check(sameHeight());
(By::type<AButton>() & By::name(".primary")).perform(click());

Mind that perform is applied to every matched view, in unspecified order. When you need exactly one view, make the selector precise enough, or use one().

docs.title: Getting the view itself
docs.text:
one() returns the first matched view as _<AView>, or nullptr if there is none. toSet() and toVector() return all of them. Cast to the concrete type to inspect it:

auto label = _cast<ALabel>(By::name("#hello").one());
ASSERT_TRUE(label);
EXPECT_EQ(*label->text(), "Hello, Steve!");

Position and size are in getPositionInWindow(), getSize() and getCenterPointInWindow(); these are what the click action uses to aim.

docs.title: Relatives
docs.text:
parent() selects containers that have a direct child matched by this matcher, allChildren() selects views whose parent is matched. Together they select siblings:

// every element in the same container as the "Common button"
By::name("Common button").parent().allChildren().check(areLeftAligned());

docs.title: Finding the nearest view
docs.text:
Forms usually pair a label with a field. findNearestTo picks, among the matched views, the one closest to another view, measured from its bottom-right corner (the way a person scans a form). The argument must match exactly one view.

// layout: Label "Login", ATextField, Label "Password", ATextField
By::type<ATextField>().findNearestTo(By::text("Login")).perform(type("alice"));
By::type<ATextField>().findNearestTo(By::text("Password")).perform(type("secret"));

docs.title: Many windows
docs.text: A matcher looks into all windows opened by the window manager, so dialogs and popups are found without extra effort. Make the selector narrow enough if the same text appears in several windows.

docs.title: aui::uitests
docs.text: UI testing: find views, simulate user input and check what is on the screen.

docs.title: Detailed Description
docs.text:
aui::uitests runs your real windows and views inside a GTest test, without a native window: a stub window manager and a software renderer are used, so tests are fast and work on a headless CI. A test finds views with By, acts on them as a user would (click, type, scroll) and checks the result.

#include <AUI/UITest.h>

class UIGreeting : public testing::UITest {};

TEST_F(UIGreeting, Click) {
    _new<MyWindow>()->show();
    By::text("Say hello").perform(click());
    By::name("#hello").check(visible()).check(text("Hello!"));
}

Include <AUI/UITest.h> to get everything. If your project uses aui_enable_tests and AUI was imported with the uitests component (auib_import(aui ... COMPONENTS core views uitests)), aui::uitests is linked to the Tests target automatically; see Writing tests for the general test setup.

Pages of this module:

  • Your first UI test - fixture, window, a complete test;
  • Finding views - finding views with By and combining matchers;
  • Simulating user input - clicks, typing, key presses, scrolling;
  • Checking views - built-in checks, layout checks and custom assertions;
  • Screenshots and pixels - pixel checks and failure reports.

testing::UITest is the base class of UI test suites, UIMatcher is the object returned by By.

docs.title: Related Pages
docs.text:
• UIMatcher

    A lazy selector of views in all opened windows, with actions and checks to run on them.

  • testing::UITest

    Base class of UI test suites.

  • ScreenshotAnalyzer

    A screenshot of the current window contents which can be analyzed in tests.

docs.title: UnixEventFd
docs.text:
File-descriptor object to trigger select/poll/epoll/kqueue

Header:#include <AUI/Platform/unix/UnixEventFd.h> CMake:aui_link(my_target PUBLIC aui::core)

docs.title: Detailed Description
docs.text: On Linux implemented with eventfd. On FreeBSD/Apple implemented with pipes.

docs.title: UnixIoThread
docs.text:
Poll-based event loop to handle events of file descriptors.

Header:#include <AUI/Platform/unix/UnixIoThread.h> CMake:aui_link(my_target PUBLIC aui::core)

docs.title: Public Methods
docs.text:
AFuture<ABitField<UnixPollEvent>> UnixIoThread::waitForEvent(int fd, ABitField<UnixPollEvent> flags)

A simplified version of registerCallback/unregisterCallback for waiting events on file descriptor.

Arguments fd file descriptor to watch on. flags which events to listen Returns AFuture with bitfield on which events was triggerred 
AAsyncHolder async;
async << []() -> AFuture<> {
   int signalFd = signalfd(-1, &procMask, SFD_CLOEXEC);
   for (;;) {
       co_await UnixIoThread::inst().waitForEvent(signalFd, UnixPollEvent::IN);
       read(signalFd, ...);
   }
   close(signalFd);
};

docs.title: Publishing releases for AUpdater
docs.text: AUpdater does not impose where the update comes from. What it needs is a ZIP archive with a complete copy of your application, found by checkForUpdatesImpl and downloaded by downloadUpdateImpl. This page shows the setup that App Template ⚡ uses: GitHub releases.

docs.title: Produce the archive
docs.text:
The update is always a ZIP portable. Build it with AUI_PORTABLE_ZIP packaging, see App Packaging:

cmake .. -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release -DAUI_APP_PACKAGING=AUI_PORTABLE_ZIP
cmake --build . --config Release
cpack . -c Release -B artifacts
gh release upload ${{ github.ref }} artifacts/*.*

The archive name contains the platform and the architecture, followed by -portable, i.e. myapp-1.2.3-linux-x86_64-portable.zip. Upload the archive for every platform and architecture you support to the same release. tar.gz archives are not supported by the updater.

If you distribute a Windows installer as well, it has to install into the user's directory so the updater can replace files without elevation; see Inno Setup.

docs.title: Pick the right asset
docs.text:
aui::updater::AppropriatePortablePackagePredicate tells whether a file name is a portable for the current platform and architecture. It is meant to be used with ranges::find_if. If you name archives differently, pass your own qualifier:

aui::updater::AppropriatePortablePackagePredicate p { .qualifier = "windows-x86_64" };
EXPECT_TRUE(p("app-windows-x86_64.zip"));
EXPECT_FALSE(p("app-windows-x86.zip"));

docs.title: Check GitHub and download
docs.text:
aui::updater::github::latestRelease (see aui::updater::github::LatestReleaseResponse) returns the latest non-draft, non-prerelease release of a repository together with its assets. The example below compares the tag with the current version, finds the matching asset, asks the user and starts the download.

static constexpr auto LOG_TAG = "MyUpdater";
class MyUpdater: public AUpdater {
public:
    ~MyUpdater() override = default;

protected:
    AFuture<void> checkForUpdatesImpl() override {
        return AUI_THREADPOOL {
            try {
                auto githubLatestRelease = aui::updater::github::latestRelease("aui-framework", "example_app");
                ALogger::info(LOG_TAG) << "Found latest release: " << githubLatestRelease.tag_name;
                auto ourVersion = aui::updater::Semver::fromString(AUI_PP_STRINGIZE(AUI_CMAKE_PROJECT_VERSION));
                auto theirVersion = aui::updater::Semver::fromString(githubLatestRelease.tag_name);

                if (theirVersion <= ourVersion) {
                    getThread()->enqueue([] {
                      AMessageBox::show(
                          nullptr, "No updates found", "You are running the latest version.", AMessageBox::Icon::INFO);
                    });
                    return;
                }
                aui::updater::AppropriatePortablePackagePredicate predicate {};
                auto it = ranges::find_if(
                    githubLatestRelease.assets, predicate, &aui::updater::github::LatestReleaseResponse::Asset::name);
                if (it == ranges::end(githubLatestRelease.assets)) {
                    ALogger::warn(LOG_TAG)
                        << "Newer version was found but a package appropriate for your platform is not available. "
                           "Expected: "
